title: CCNA 200-301
description: Cisco Certified Network Associate - routing, switching, security, automation.
long_description: The CCNA (Cisco Certified Network Associate) is THE gateway to networking careers. The 200-301 exam covers the fundamentals: routing (static, OSPF), switching (VLAN, STP, EtherChannel), IPv4/IPv6, security (ACL, port-security, basic VPN), wireless infrastructure, IP services (NAT, DHCP, QoS), and automation (Python, REST, JSON, Ansible). It's the most recognised Cisco certification in the world and the prerequisite to CCNP and then CCIE.
importance: The CCNA is explicitly required in most 'Network Engineer', 'NOC Analyst', or 'Systems and Networks Engineer' job postings, both in the US and internationally. It validates a technical foundation recruiters take seriously and unlocks the junior-to-mid salary brackets.
validity_note: Valid for 3 years. The official exam uses a scaled score of about 825/1000 (≈ 82.5%) - Cisco keeps the exact threshold confidential. Renewal: retake the exam, pass a higher-level Cisco exam (CCNP, CCIE), or accumulate 30 CE credits. No grace period.

course_blocks.text: Introduction

The **CCNA** (Cisco Certified Network Associate) is Cisco's associate-level certification for people who build, run and troubleshoot small to medium networks. It is earned by passing a single exam, **200-301 CCNA**. It validates that you understand how networks work (addressing, switching, routing, services, security, automation) and that you can configure and verify Cisco IOS devices from the command line.

It is aimed at junior network and system administrators, help desk and support technicians who want to move into networking, students, and developers or cloud engineers who need solid network foundations. There is no formal prerequisite, but Cisco suggests some hands-on experience with networks. If you have never configured a switch, plan more lab time.
The exam at a glance

rows.label: Number of questions
values: Not published by Cisco, and it can vary between candidates. Candidates commonly report roughly 100 to 120 items, but this is **not official**.

rows.label: Passing score
values: Not published by Cisco. Widely reported to be around 825 on a 300 to 1000 scale, but this is **not official** and may change.

rows.label: Language and delivery
values: Delivered by Pearson VUE, in a test center or online with a remote proctor. Check the languages offered when you book.

rows.label: Price
values: Around 300 USD plus local taxes. Check Cisco's exam page for the current price in your country.

rows.label: Validity
values: 3 years, renewed by retaking an exam or by earning continuing education credits.

course_blocks.text: Question types

items.definition: One correct option among several. The most common format.
The question states how many answers to pick (“Choose two”). Cisco does not say whether partial credit is given, so treat the question as all or nothing: one wrong pick may lose it.
Match items to categories or put steps in order, for example syslog levels to their names or DORA messages in sequence.
A simulated topology with a working CLI. You configure devices to meet stated requirements, and the result is graded on the final configuration and behavior.
A scenario (diagram or text) followed by several multiple choice questions about it.
A simulated network where you can run `show` commands (but usually not change the configuration) to answer several questions.

course_blocks.title: No going back (commonly reported)
course_blocks.body: Candidates commonly report that, once you validate an answer, you **cannot return** to a previous question, and that there is no review screen to flag questions for later. This is not an official Cisco guarantee and the rules shown at the start of your exam are what counts. Plan as if each answer is final.

course_blocks.text: The result is a **scaled score**, not a percentage of correct answers. Questions do not all carry the same weight and Cisco does not disclose how each item is scored, so do not try to compute your result during the exam. Aim for clear mastery of every domain rather than a target number.

course_blocks.title: Which version will you take?
course_blocks.body: This course follows the current **v1.1** blueprint. Cisco published a **v2.0** blueprint in May 2026, and third-party sources state it replaces v1.1 on 3 February 2027. If your exam date is close to that switch, read Part 7 and check the exact date on Cisco's site before booking.

course_blocks.text: The six domains of the v1.1 blueprint

Cisco publishes the exam topics as six weighted domains. The weight is the approximate share of the exam for that domain. This course follows the same structure: one part per domain, in the official order, with one section per objective.

rows.label: 4.0 IP Services

course_blocks.text: How to study with CertifLoop

items.title: Read one domain
items.body: Work through one part of this course, objective by objective. Type every configuration you see into a lab instead of only reading it.

items.title: Practice that domain
items.body: Take a mock exam, then on the exam results page use **Réviser** (Review) on the domain you just studied to get practice questions focused on it.

items.title: Drill subnetting every day
items.body: Use the unlimited subnetting drill on the CCNA page for 10 to 15 minutes a day until you find the network, broadcast, host range and mask of any address in well under a minute.

items.title: Take full mock exams
items.body: Once several domains are covered, take full timed mock exams in one sitting to build pace and stamina.

items.title: Review every mistake
items.body: For each wrong answer, find the reason (concept gap, misread question, default value forgotten), reread the matching section, and redo a focused review on that domain.

course_blocks.title: Time management rule of thumb
course_blocks.body: Count on roughly **1 minute per question**. Labs and simlets take longer (several minutes each), so keep a margin by answering simple questions quickly. If a question blocks you, eliminate what you can, choose the best remaining answer and move on: one hard question is not worth three easy ones left unanswered at the end.

course_blocks.title: Checking your pace
course_blocks.body: Suppose your exam has 110 items including 3 labs. If you budget 8 minutes per lab (24 minutes), about 96 minutes remain for 107 questions, a little under 1 minute each. At the 60-minute mark you should be past question 50 or so. If you are well behind, speed up on the recall questions.

course_blocks.text: 1.0 Network Fundamentals (20%)

This domain builds the foundation for everything else on the CCNA: what each network device does, how networks are laid out, which cables and interfaces connect them, how TCP and UDP carry data, how IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are structured, how wireless and virtualization fit in, and how a switch forwards frames. Questions mix theory (pick the right definition or default value) with hands-on tasks: calculating a subnet under time pressure, reading `show interfaces` counters, recognising an IPv6 address type or completing an interface configuration. Subnetting (1.6) and IPv6 (1.8, 1.9) deserve the most practice, because they come back in routing, ACL and NAT questions in the other domains.
1.1 Explain the role and function of network components

A network is a set of devices that each do one job well. To answer component questions, ask yourself at which OSI layer the device makes its decision and what it uses to decide: a MAC address (Layer 2), an IP address (Layer 3), or the content of the session and application (Layers 4 to 7).

items.definition: Layer 3 device that forwards packets between different IP networks using its routing table. Each interface is a separate broadcast domain. Routers connect LANs to the WAN and the internet and often run NAT, DHCP and ACLs.

Forwards Ethernet frames based on the destination MAC address, using a MAC address table it learns by itself. Each port is its own collision domain; all ports in the same VLAN form one broadcast domain.
A switch that can also route between VLANs in hardware, using SVIs (`interface vlan 10`) or routed ports (`no switchport`). Common in the distribution and core layers of a campus.

A stateful firewall that also inspects traffic up to the application layer: application visibility and control, URL filtering, user identity, malware protection and an integrated IPS. Cisco Secure Firewall (formerly Firepower) is an example.

Intrusion Prevention System placed inline: it compares traffic with attack signatures and behaviours and drops malicious packets in real time. An IDS only receives a copy of the traffic and alerts, it cannot block by itself. A next-generation IPS adds context (hosts, applications, reputation).
Connects wireless clients to the wired network by bridging 802.11 frames to Ethernet. An autonomous AP is configured individually; a lightweight AP is managed by a controller through a CAPWAP tunnel.

Centralises management and policy. A Wireless LAN Controller (WLC) manages many lightweight APs (configuration, RF, roaming, security). An SDN controller such as Cisco Catalyst Center (formerly DNA Center) manages switches and routers through APIs.
Any device at the edge that sends or receives user traffic: PCs, laptops, phones, IP phones, printers, cameras, IoT sensors.
A host that provides a service to clients: web, email, file, DNS, DHCP, database, authentication. Today it is often a virtual machine or a container rather than a dedicated physical box.

course_blocks.text: Power over Ethernet (PoE)

PoE lets a switch send electrical power over the same twisted-pair cable that carries data, so IP phones, APs and cameras need no local power outlet. The switch is the PSE (Power Sourcing Equipment) and the powered device is the PD. Before powering a port, the PSE detects a valid PD signature and can negotiate the power class (also through CDP or LLDP), so a normal PC plugged into a PoE port is not damaged.

columns: Max power per port at the PSE

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: An IDS works on a copy of the traffic (SPAN port or tap) and can only alert; an IPS sits inline and can drop packets. Also remember that a Layer 2 switch does not separate broadcast domains: only routers, Layer 3 interfaces and VLANs do.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Routers forward between IP networks and separate broadcast domains; L2 switches forward on MAC addresses.
A Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs with SVIs or routed ports.
NGFW = stateful firewall + application awareness + IPS; an IPS is inline, an IDS is not.
Lightweight APs are managed by a WLC through CAPWAP; autonomous APs stand alone.
PoE 15.4 W, PoE+ 30 W, 802.3bt up to 90 W; the switch is the PSE, the phone or AP is the PD.

course_blocks.text: 1.2 Describe characteristics of network topology architectures

A topology architecture is a repeatable design pattern. The goal is always the same: give users enough bandwidth, remove single points of failure and keep the network easy to grow. The exam expects you to recognise each pattern from a description or a diagram and to know which layer does what.
Campus designs: two-tier and three-tier

rows.label: Access
values: Many ports, PoE, VLAN assignment, port security, DHCP snooping, PortFast.

rows.label: Distribution
values: Aggregates access switches and connects them to the core.
Inter-VLAN routing, FHRP gateways, policy (ACL, QoS), boundary between L2 and L3.

rows.label: Core
values: High-speed backbone between distribution blocks, data center and WAN edge.
Fast, redundant Layer 3 links; avoid CPU-heavy features that slow forwarding.

course_blocks.text: A **two-tier** design (also called *collapsed core*) merges the distribution and core layers into one pair of switches. It suits a single building or a small campus because it costs less. A **three-tier** design adds a dedicated core when there are several buildings or distribution blocks: without a core, every distribution pair would need links to every other pair, which does not scale.
Spine-leaf (data center)

Modern data centers carry mostly **east-west** traffic (server to server) rather than north-south (client to server). In a spine-leaf fabric every leaf switch connects to every spine switch, leaves never connect to each other and spines never connect to each other. Servers, storage, firewalls and routers attach only to leaves. Any server reaches any other server in the same number of hops (leaf, spine, leaf), so latency is predictable, and you add capacity by adding a spine or ports by adding a leaf. Cisco ACI uses this design.

graph TD
  S1[Spine 1] --- L1[Leaf 1]
  S1 --- L2[Leaf 2]
  S1 --- L3[Leaf 3]
  S2[Spine 2] --- L1
  S2 --- L2
  S2 --- L3
  L1 --- SRV1[Servers]

course_blocks.caption: Spine-leaf: every leaf links to every spine, no leaf-to-leaf or spine-to-spine links.

course_blocks.text: WAN, SOHO, on-premises and cloud

items.definition: Connects sites over long distances through a provider or the internet: leased lines (point-to-point), MPLS VPN, Metro Ethernet, internet VPN (IPsec, DMVPN) and SD-WAN. Common topologies are point-to-point, hub-and-spoke, full mesh and partial mesh. A site with one link is single-homed; with two links to the same provider, dual-homed; with links to two providers, multihomed.
Small office/home office: one all-in-one device usually acts as router, switch, wireless AP, firewall, NAT and DHCP server, with an internet connection (DSL, cable, fiber or 4G/5G).
The organisation owns and runs the servers and network in its own building or data center: full control, but it pays upfront (CapEx) and handles power, cooling and upgrades.

Resources rented on demand from a provider and paid by use (OpEx). Service models: IaaS (you manage OS and apps), PaaS (you manage apps), SaaS (you just use the application). Deployment models: public, private, hybrid, community. Key traits: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: In spine-leaf, endpoints never connect to a spine, and two leaves are never cabled together. In a collapsed core (two-tier), the core is not missing: it is merged with the distribution layer.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Three-tier = access, distribution, core; two-tier collapses distribution and core.
Spine-leaf: each leaf connects to every spine, equal hop count, built for east-west traffic.
WAN options include leased lines, MPLS, Metro Ethernet, internet VPN and SD-WAN.
SOHO uses one all-in-one router for routing, switching, Wi-Fi, NAT and DHCP.
Cloud: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS; public, private, hybrid, community; pay per use.

course_blocks.text: 1.3 Compare physical interface and cabling types

Choosing a cable is a trade-off between distance, speed, cost and immunity to interference. Copper is cheap and easy to terminate but limited to 100 m and sensitive to electromagnetic interference (EMI). Fiber carries light, so it ignores EMI, goes much further and is the norm between buildings and for uplinks.
Single-mode fiber, multimode fiber and copper

rows.label: Light / signal source
values: LED or VCSEL, many paths of light

rows.label: Typical distance
values: Several km to tens of km
Up to a few hundred metres

course_blocks.text: On switches, fiber usually plugs into a transceiver module (SFP for 1 Gbps, SFP+ for 10 Gbps, QSFP for 40/100 Gbps) with LC connectors, while copper uses RJ-45. Multimode exhibits *modal dispersion*: the different light paths arrive at slightly different times, which is why it cannot go as far as single-mode.
Straight-through, crossover and Auto-MDIX

With 10BASE-T and 100BASE-TX, only two pairs are used: pins 1 and 2, and pins 3 and 6. PCs, routers, firewalls and APs transmit on pins 1-2 (MDI); switches and hubs transmit on pins 3-6 (MDI-X). When the two ends transmit on different pins, a **straight-through** cable works; when they transmit on the same pins, you need a **crossover** cable that swaps 1-2 with 3-6. Gigabit Ethernet (1000BASE-T) uses all four pairs in both directions.

rows.label: PC to switch, router to switch
Switch to switch, hub to switch
PC to PC, router to router, PC to router

course_blocks.text: **Auto-MDIX** detects the wrong cable type and swaps the transmit and receive pairs electronically, so either cable works. It is enabled by default on most modern Cisco switch ports and relies on speed and duplex autonegotiation (`mdix auto` interface command). The exam still expects you to know which cable the rule calls for.
Shared media versus point-to-point Ethernet

In the original **shared media** Ethernet (coaxial bus, then hubs), all devices share one collision domain, work in half duplex and use CSMA/CD: listen before sending, detect collisions, back off a random time and retry. A hub simply repeats bits out every port. In modern **point-to-point** Ethernet, each cable connects exactly two devices (for example a PC and a switch port), the link runs in full duplex, and collisions cannot happen, so CSMA/CD is not used. A serial WAN link or a leased line is also point-to-point.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Two switches need a crossover cable by the rule (both transmit on 3-6), even if Auto-MDIX makes a straight-through cable work. And a router connected to a PC is like-to-like (both MDI): crossover, not straight-through.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: SMF: thin core, laser, long distances; MMF: wider core, cheaper optics, shorter distances.
Copper UTP is limited to 100 m and is sensitive to EMI; fiber is immune.
Unlike devices: straight-through; like devices: crossover; Auto-MDIX fixes the mistake automatically.
Shared media = half duplex + CSMA/CD; point-to-point switched links = full duplex, no collisions.

course_blocks.text: 1.4 Identify interface and cable issues (collisions, errors, mismatch duplex, and/or speed)

Most Layer 1 problems show up in two places: the interface status line and the error counters of `show interfaces`. The status tells you whether the link is up at all; the counters tell you whether the frames that do cross the link arrive damaged.

rows.label: administratively down / down
values: The interface was shut down with `shutdown`; use `no shutdown`.

rows.label: down / down
values: Layer 1 problem: no cable, broken cable, far end off, speed mismatch. On a switch this shows as `notconnect`.

rows.label: up / down
values: Layer 1 is fine but Layer 2 fails, for example an encapsulation mismatch or keepalive problem on a serial link.

rows.label: down / down (err-disabled)
values: A protection feature (port security, BPDU guard...) disabled the port.

course_blocks.text: Here the port runs at **Half-duplex, 100Mb/s** and counts many **collisions** and **late collisions**. On a point-to-point switched link that is abnormal: it is the half-duplex side of a duplex mismatch. On the neighbour, which runs full duplex, you would typically see input errors, CRC errors and runts instead.

items.definition: Frames smaller than the 64-byte Ethernet minimum. Often fragments left by collisions or a faulty NIC.
Frames larger than the maximum allowed size (1518 bytes for a standard untagged Ethernet frame). Often an MTU mismatch or a faulty NIC.
Total of received errors, including runts, giants, CRC, frame, overrun and ignored.
The frame check sequence (FCS) computed on receipt does not match the one in the frame: bits were corrupted in transit. Typical causes: bad or too long cable, EMI, duplex mismatch.
Number of times the interface had to retransmit because of a collision. Normal only on half-duplex shared media; should be 0 on a full-duplex link.
Collisions detected after the first 64 bytes (512 bit times) of the frame were sent. Classic signs: duplex mismatch or a cable longer than the standard allows.

course_blocks.text: Duplex and speed mismatch

By default both ends autonegotiate speed and duplex. If you hard-code one side (for example `speed 100` and `duplex full`) and leave the other on auto, the auto side receives no negotiation messages. It can still sense the speed from the electrical signal, but it must assume the duplex: **half duplex at 10 or 100 Mbps**, full duplex at 1000 Mbps. The result is a duplex mismatch: the link is up, pings mostly work, but performance is poor and the counters climb. A **speed mismatch** is different: the link simply stays down.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# speed auto
SW1(config-if)# duplex auto
SW1(config-if)# end
SW1# show interfaces status
Port      Name               Status       Vlan       Duplex  Speed Type
Gi0/5     PC-ACCOUNTING      connected    10         a-full a-100 10/100/1000BaseTX
Gi0/6                        notconnect   10           auto   auto 10/100/1000BaseTX

course_blocks.text: In `show interfaces status`, the `a-` prefix means the value was autonegotiated (`a-full`, `a-100`); a value without the prefix was configured manually. The fix for a mismatch is to configure both ends the same way, ideally auto on both sides.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Late collisions on the half-duplex side and CRC/runts on the full-duplex side point to a duplex mismatch, not a bad cable. Also remember: when autonegotiation fails at 10/100 Mbps, IEEE defaults the duplex to half, not full.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: down/down = Layer 1; up/down = Layer 2; administratively down = `shutdown`.
Runts < 64 bytes, giants > 1518 bytes, CRC = corrupted frame (cable, EMI, duplex).
Collisions on a full-duplex link are abnormal; late collisions signal a duplex mismatch or an over-length cable.
Hard-coding one side and leaving the other on auto causes a duplex mismatch at 10/100 Mbps.
A speed mismatch keeps the link down; a duplex mismatch keeps it up but slow.

course_blocks.text: 1.5 Compare TCP to UDP

TCP and UDP are the two main Layer 4 (transport) protocols. Both use port numbers to deliver data to the right application, but they make opposite trade-offs. TCP adds reliability: it sets up a connection, numbers every byte, acknowledges what it receives and retransmits what is lost. UDP adds almost nothing on top of IP: it sends datagrams and forgets them, which keeps delay and overhead low.

rows.label: Ordering
values: Sequence numbers, data reassembled in order

rows.label: Typical uses
values: Voice and video (RTP), DNS queries, DHCP, TFTP, SNMP, syslog, NTP

course_blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server
  C->>S: SYN (seq=x)
  S->>C: SYN, ACK (seq=y, ack=x+1)
  C->>S: ACK (ack=y+1)
  Note over C,S: Connection established, data can flow
  C->>S: FIN
  S->>C: ACK
  S->>C: FIN
  C->>S: ACK
course_blocks.caption: TCP three-way handshake to open the connection and four-way exchange to close it.

course_blocks.text: **Windowing**: the receiver advertises a window size, the amount of data the sender may transmit before waiting for an acknowledgment. If all goes well the window grows so more data is in flight; if segments are lost or the receiver is busy, the window shrinks. This *sliding window* is TCP's flow control. Acknowledgments are cumulative: ACK 4001 means all bytes up to 4000 arrived and byte 4001 is expected next.

**Port numbers** identify the application: well-known ports are 0 to 1023, registered ports 1024 to 49151, and dynamic (ephemeral) ports 49152 to 65535, which clients pick as their source port. A socket is the combination of IP address, protocol and port; a TCP session is identified by both sockets.

course_blocks.title: Why does voice use UDP?
course_blocks.body: In a VoIP call, a packet that arrives 300 ms late is useless: the conversation has already moved on. Retransmitting it, as TCP would, only adds delay and jitter. UDP (with RTP on top) sends each voice sample once; a lost packet causes a tiny glitch, which is better than a growing delay. A file download is the opposite case: every byte must arrive intact, so it uses TCP.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: TFTP uses UDP 69 while FTP uses TCP 20/21; SNMP, syslog, NTP and DHCP are UDP. DNS uses both: UDP 53 for normal queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers. UDP has no handshake and no acknowledgments, so it cannot detect loss by itself.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered, flow control; UDP: connectionless, best effort, low overhead.
Three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK; closing uses FIN and ACK in both directions.
Windowing lets the receiver control how much data is sent before an acknowledgment.
Headers: TCP 20 bytes minimum, UDP 8 bytes.
Well-known 0-1023, registered 1024-49151, ephemeral 49152-65535; learn the common port numbers.

course_blocks.text: 1.6 Configure and verify IPv4 addressing and subnetting

An IPv4 address is 32 bits long, written as four decimal octets (dotted decimal). The subnet mask says which bits identify the network (mask bits set to 1) and which identify the host (mask bits set to 0). Subnetting means borrowing host bits to create more, smaller networks. You must be able to do it quickly and without a calculator.
Binary and masks

Each octet has eight bits worth 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 from left to right. To convert 172 to binary, subtract the largest values that fit: 172 = 128 + 32 + 8 + 4, so 172 = 10101100. To convert back, add the values of the bits set to 1. A mask is always a run of 1s followed by 0s, so only nine values are possible in any octet.

items.definition: The number of mask bits set to 1, written after a slash: /26 = 255.255.255.192.
All host bits set to 0. Identifies the subnet; it cannot be assigned to an interface.
All host bits set to 1. Reaches every host in the subnet; not assignable.
2^h - 2, where h is the number of host bits. A /26 has 6 host bits: 64 - 2 = 62 hosts.
2^s, where s is the number of bits borrowed from the original host part.
A /31 (RFC 3021) has two addresses, both usable, for point-to-point links. A /32 identifies a single host (loopbacks, host routes).

course_blocks.text: Classful addressing still shows up in questions about default masks: Class A is 1 to 126 in the first octet (/8), Class B 128 to 191 (/16), Class C 192 to 223 (/24), Class D 224 to 239 is multicast, Class E 240 to 255 is reserved. 127.0.0.0/8 is reserved for loopback (127.0.0.1).
The block-size (magic number) method

items.title: Find the interesting octet
items.body: It is the octet where the mask is neither 255 nor 0. For /20 (255.255.240.0) it is the third octet; for /27 (255.255.255.224) it is the fourth.

items.title: Compute the block size
items.body: Block size = 256 - mask value in that octet. 256 - 240 = 16; 256 - 224 = 32. Subnets start at multiples of this number in the interesting octet.

items.title: Find the network address
items.body: Take the largest multiple of the block size that is less than or equal to the address value in the interesting octet. Octets to the left stay the same, octets to the right become 0.

items.title: Find the broadcast address
items.body: Next subnet minus one: add the block size to the network value, subtract 1, and set the octets to the right to 255.

items.title: Derive the host range
items.body: First host = network + 1; last host = broadcast - 1. Usable hosts = 2^h - 2.

course_blocks.title: Worked example 1: 192.168.10.77/27
course_blocks.body: Mask /27 = 255.255.255.224, so the interesting octet is the fourth. Block size = 256 - 224 = 32, giving subnets .0, .32, .64, .96, .128... The largest multiple of 32 not above 77 is 64. Network: **192.168.10.64**. Next subnet is .96, so broadcast: **192.168.10.95**. Usable range: **192.168.10.65 to 192.168.10.94**, that is 2^5 - 2 = **30 hosts**.

course_blocks.title: Worked example 2: 172.16.45.200/20
course_blocks.body: Mask /20 = 255.255.240.0, so the interesting octet is the third. Block size = 256 - 240 = 16: subnets at 172.16.0.0, .16.0, .32.0, .48.0... The value 45 falls between 32 and 48. Network: **172.16.32.0**. Broadcast: 48 - 1 = 47 in the third octet and 255 in the fourth, so **172.16.47.255**. Usable range: **172.16.32.1 to 172.16.47.254**. Host bits = 32 - 20 = 12, so 2^12 - 2 = **4094 hosts**.

course_blocks.title: Worked example 3: choosing a mask from requirements
course_blocks.body: A LAN needs 50 hosts. Find the smallest h with 2^h - 2 >= 50: 2^5 - 2 = 30 is too small, 2^6 - 2 = 62 works. Keep 6 host bits, so the prefix is 32 - 6 = **/26** (255.255.255.192). Another case: you must split 10.20.0.0/16 into at least 100 subnets of equal size. 2^6 = 64 is too few, 2^7 = 128 is enough, so borrow 7 bits: **/23** (255.255.254.0), with 2^9 - 2 = 510 hosts per subnet.

course_blocks.text: VLSM design

Variable Length Subnet Masking (VLSM) uses different prefix lengths inside the same major network so that each subnet is sized to its need. The rule is simple: **allocate the largest subnets first**, each one starting on a boundary that is a multiple of its own block size, then fill the remaining space with smaller subnets. This avoids overlaps and wasted addresses.

course_blocks.title: VLSM example: 192.168.50.0/24
course_blocks.body: Requirements: LAN A 100 hosts, LAN B 50 hosts, LAN C 25 hosts, and three router-to-router links (2 hosts each). Sorted from largest to smallest: LAN A needs 7 host bits (126 hosts), so **192.168.50.0/25**, hosts .1 to .126, broadcast .127. LAN B needs 6 host bits (62 hosts), so **192.168.50.128/26**, hosts .129 to .190, broadcast .191. LAN C needs 5 host bits (30 hosts), so **192.168.50.192/27**, hosts .193 to .222, broadcast .223. Each link uses a /30 (2 hosts): **192.168.50.224/30** (.225 and .226), **192.168.50.228/30** (.229 and .230), **192.168.50.232/30** (.233 and .234). The space from .236 to .255 stays free for growth.

course_blocks.text: Configuration and verification

On a Cisco router, an interface gets its IPv4 address with `ip address <address> <mask>` in interface configuration mode; IOS expects the dotted-decimal mask, not the /prefix. Router interfaces are shut down by default, so `no shutdown` is needed. Below, R1 receives the first usable address of LAN A and of the first link from the VLSM plan.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# description LAN-A
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.128
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# description LINK-TO-R2
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.50.225 255.255.255.252
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end

R1# show ip interface brief
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     192.168.50.1    YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     192.168.50.225  YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down

R1# show ip route connected
      192.168.50.0/24 is variably subnetted, 4 subnets, 3 masks
C        192.168.50.0/25 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        192.168.50.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        192.168.50.224/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        192.168.50.225/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1

course_blocks.text: In `show ip interface brief`, check the address, the method (`manual` for a static address, `DHCP` when learned) and both Status and Protocol columns: you want up/up. The routing table confirms the mask: each configured interface adds a **C** (connected) route for its subnet and an **L** (local) /32 route for the interface address itself. The line *variably subnetted* tells you VLSM is in use. `show running-config interface g0/0` and `show ip interface g0/0` (line *Internet address is 192.168.50.1/25*) also display the mask.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: IOS refuses to put the network or broadcast address of a subnet on an interface, and refuses an address that overlaps a subnet already configured on another interface. Watch for answer options that use .0 or .127 with a /25, or a host and gateway that are in different subnets (for example 192.168.50.130/25 with gateway 192.168.50.1).

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Block size = 256 - mask value in the interesting octet; networks start at its multiples.
Broadcast = next network - 1; usable hosts = 2^h - 2 (except /31 point-to-point and /32).
VLSM: allocate the largest subnets first, each on its own block boundary.
Configure with `ip address <ip> <dotted mask>` plus `no shutdown`.
Verify with `show ip interface brief` (up/up) and `show ip route connected` (C and L routes).

course_blocks.text: 1.7 Describe private IPv4 addressing

The IPv4 address space ran out years ago. RFC 1918 reserves three ranges that any organisation may use internally without asking anyone. These private addresses are not routed on the public internet: ISPs drop them. To reach the internet, hosts with private addresses go through NAT (usually PAT) on the edge router or firewall, which replaces the private source address with a public one.

items: **Benefits**: saves public addresses, lets every company reuse the same ranges, hides the internal addressing plan.
**Limits**: requires NAT to reach the internet, overlaps appear when two companies merge or connect through a VPN, and NAT complicates some protocols and end-to-end tracing.

**Other special ranges** not to confuse with RFC 1918: 127.0.0.0/8 loopback, 169.254.0.0/16 link-local (APIPA, used by a client that got no DHCP answer), 100.64.0.0/10 shared address space for carrier-grade NAT (RFC 6598).

course_blocks.title: Private or public?
course_blocks.body: 172.20.5.1: private (between 172.16 and 172.31). 172.32.0.1: **public**, just outside the /12. 192.169.1.1: public. 10.200.3.4: private. 169.254.10.20: not RFC 1918, it is APIPA, a sign that DHCP failed on the client.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: The private Class B range is 172.16.0.0/12, so it stops at 172.31.255.255: 172.32.x.x and 172.15.x.x are public. 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local (APIPA), not an RFC 1918 private range.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Private addresses are not routed on the internet; NAT/PAT translates them at the edge.
169.254.0.0/16 (APIPA) means the host did not get a DHCP lease.

course_blocks.text: 1.8 Configure and verify IPv6 addressing and prefix

An IPv6 address is 128 bits long, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits (called hextets or quartets) separated by colons. Each hex digit is 4 bits (a nibble), each hextet 16 bits. IPv6 has no broadcast and no need for NAT to save addresses, and the standard subnet size for a LAN is a **/64**: 64 bits of prefix and 64 bits of interface ID.
Abbreviation rules

items.title: Rule 1: drop leading zeros
items.body: In each hextet you may remove the zeros on the left: 0DB8 becomes DB8, 0042 becomes 42, 0000 becomes 0. Zeros on the right must stay (ABC0 stays ABC0).

items.title: Rule 2: replace one run of zero hextets with ::
items.body: One contiguous run of all-zero hextets can be replaced by a double colon. It may appear **only once** per address, otherwise the address would be ambiguous.

items.title: Recommended form (RFC 5952)
items.body: Use :: on the longest run of zeros; if two runs are equal, compress the first one; do not use :: for a single zero hextet; write hex letters in lowercase. IOS displays addresses in uppercase, which is equally valid.

course_blocks.title: Abbreviating and expanding
course_blocks.body: 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0000:FF00:0042:8329 becomes **2001:db8::ff00:42:8329**. 2001:0DB8:0000:0001:0000:0000:0000:0001 has two zero runs (one hextet, then three): compress the longer one, **2001:db8:0:1::1**. To expand FE80::1, count the hextets you see (2) and insert 8 - 2 = 6 hextets of zeros: FE80:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.

course_blocks.text: Prefix and subnetting

The prefix length works exactly like an IPv4 mask but is always written as /n. To find the prefix of 2001:db8:acad:10:1234:5678:9abc:def0/64, keep the first 64 bits (the first four hextets) and set the rest to zero: **2001:db8:acad:10::/64**. A typical enterprise receives a /48 from its provider: the next 16 bits (the fourth hextet) are the **subnet ID**, which gives 65,536 /64 subnets, and the last 64 bits are the interface ID.

When the prefix does not end on a hextet boundary, work on the nibble or the bits. For 2001:db8:acad:4c7::1/56, a /56 keeps 3 full hextets (48 bits) plus the first 8 bits of the fourth hextet. 04c7 has its first two hex digits 04 kept and c7 set to 0, so the prefix is **2001:db8:acad:400::/56**.
Configuration on IOS

A Cisco router does not forward IPv6 packets until you enable `ipv6 unicast-routing` globally; this command also makes it send Router Advertisements (RAs) and join the all-routers group FF02::2. Each interface can then receive one or more IPv6 addresses. Configuring any IPv6 address on an interface automatically creates a link-local address; `ipv6 enable` creates the link-local address alone.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:10::1/64
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:20::/64 eui-64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# end

rows.label: `ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:10::1/64`
values: Static global unicast address, interface ID typed manually.

rows.label: `ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:20::/64 eui-64`
values: You give the /64 prefix, IOS builds the interface ID from the MAC with modified EUI-64.

rows.label: `ipv6 address fe80::1 link-local`
values: Replaces the automatic link-local address with an easy-to-read one.

rows.label: `ipv6 enable`
values: Enables IPv6 with only an automatic link-local address.

rows.label: `ipv6 address autoconfig`
values: The interface learns its prefix from an RA (SLAAC), like a host.

rows.label: `ipv6 address dhcp`
values: The interface requests its address from a DHCPv6 server.

course_blocks.content:
R1# show ipv6 interface brief
GigabitEthernet0/0     [up/up]
    FE80::2C1:64FF:FE12:3401
    2001:DB8:ACAD:10::1
GigabitEthernet0/1     [up/up]
    FE80::1
    2001:DB8:ACAD:20:2C1:64FF:FE12:3402
GigabitEthernet0/2     [administratively down/down]
    unassigned

R1# show ipv6 route connected
C   2001:DB8:ACAD:10::/64 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0, directly connected
L   2001:DB8:ACAD:10::1/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/0, receive
C   2001:DB8:ACAD:20::/64 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/1, directly connected
L   2001:DB8:ACAD:20:2C1:64FF:FE12:3402/128 [0/0]
     via GigabitEthernet0/1, receive

course_blocks.text: `show ipv6 interface brief` lists, for each interface, its state and every IPv6 address: the link-local (FE80::) first, then the global ones. On G0/0 the link-local was generated automatically from the MAC 00c1.6412.3401; on G0/1 it is the manual FE80::1, and the global address ends with the EUI-64 interface ID built from MAC 00c1.6412.3402. In the routing table, each prefix gives a **C** route and each address an **L** /128 route. `show ipv6 interface g0/0` adds details, including the multicast groups the interface joined (see 1.9).

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Without `ipv6 unicast-routing`, interfaces still get IPv6 addresses and can ping their neighbours, but the router does not route IPv6 between interfaces nor send RAs, so SLAAC hosts get no prefix or default gateway. Also, :: may appear only once: 2001:db8::1::5 is invalid.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: 128 bits, 8 hextets; drop leading zeros and replace one run of zero hextets with :: (once).
LAN subnets are /64; a /48 site leaves 16 bits of subnet ID.
`ipv6 unicast-routing` is required for the router to route IPv6 and send RAs.
`ipv6 address <prefix>/64 eui-64` builds the interface ID from the MAC; `link-local` sets a manual FE80 address.
Verify with `show ipv6 interface brief`, `show ipv6 interface` and `show ipv6 route` (C and L /128).

course_blocks.text: 1.9 Describe IPv6 address types

IPv6 defines three kinds of destinations: **unicast** (one interface), **anycast** (the nearest of several interfaces sharing the same address) and **multicast** (all interfaces that joined a group). There is no broadcast: functions that used broadcast in IPv4, such as ARP, now use multicast. An interface normally has several IPv6 addresses at the same time: at least a link-local, often a global unicast, and several multicast group memberships.
Unicast: global, unique local and link-local

rows.label: Global unicast (GUA)
values: Globally unique, routed on the internet

rows.label: Unique local (ULA)
values: Routed inside the organisation, not on the internet

rows.label: Link-local (LLA)
values: Valid only on the local link, never routed

items: **Global unicast**: structure usually 48 bits of global routing prefix (from the provider), 16 bits of subnet ID, 64 bits of interface ID. 2001:db8::/32 is reserved for documentation, which is why examples use it.
**Unique local**: FD followed by a 40-bit randomly generated Global ID, then a 16-bit subnet ID and the interface ID. The random Global ID makes collisions unlikely if two companies merge.

**Link-local**: created automatically on every IPv6-enabled interface. Used by Neighbor Discovery, as the source of Router Advertisements, and as the next hop in routing protocols (OSPFv3, EIGRP for IPv6). The same link-local address can be reused on every interface of a router because it only matters on its own link.
**Special addresses**: :: (unspecified, /128, used as a source before an address is obtained) and ::1 (loopback, /128).

course_blocks.text: Anycast

An anycast address is a normal unicast address configured on several devices. Routing delivers each packet to the **nearest** one, according to the routing metric. It is used for redundant services such as DNS resolvers: clients use one address and automatically reach the closest working server. There is no special anycast prefix; on IOS you mark the address with the `anycast` keyword, for example `ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:99::53/64 anycast`, so the router does not flag it as a duplicate.
Multicast

Multicast addresses start with **FF** (FF00::/8). The fourth hex digit gives the scope: FF02 is link-local (never forwarded by routers), FF05 site-local, FF0E global. The well-known link-local groups below appear in exam questions.

rows.label: FF02::1
values: All nodes on the link (closest thing to a broadcast)

rows.label: FF02::5 / FF02::6
values: All OSPFv3 routers / OSPFv3 DR and BDR

rows.label: FF02::1:2
values: All DHCPv6 servers and relay agents

course_blocks.text: The **solicited-node multicast** address replaces the ARP broadcast. For every unicast address it owns, an interface joins FF02::1:FF00:0/104 followed by the **last 24 bits** (last 6 hex digits) of that address. A device that wants the MAC address of 2001:db8:acad:10::1 sends its Neighbor Solicitation to FF02::1:FF00:1 instead of disturbing every host on the link: only hosts whose address ends the same way listen to that group.

course_blocks.content:
R1# show ipv6 interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  IPv6 is enabled, link-local address is FE80::2C1:64FF:FE12:3401
  No Virtual link-local address(es):
  Global unicast address(es):
    2001:DB8:ACAD:10::1, subnet is 2001:DB8:ACAD:10::/64
  Joined group address(es):
    FF02::1
    FF02::2
    FF02::1:FF00:1
    FF02::1:FF12:3401
  MTU is 1500 bytes
  ICMP error messages limited to one every 100 milliseconds
  ICMP redirects are enabled
  ND DAD is enabled, number of DAD attempts: 1
  ND reachable time is 30000 milliseconds
  ND advertised reachable time is 0 (unspecified)
  ND router advertisements are sent every 200 seconds

course_blocks.text: Read the joined groups: FF02::1 (all nodes), FF02::2 (all routers, present because `ipv6 unicast-routing` is on), FF02::1:FF00:1 (solicited-node of the global address ending in ::1) and FF02::1:FF12:3401 (solicited-node of the link-local address ending in 12:3401).
Modified EUI-64

Modified EUI-64 builds a 64-bit interface ID from a 48-bit MAC address, so a device can create a unique address without manual input. It is used by `ipv6 address ... eui-64`, by automatic link-local addresses on Cisco routers, and by SLAAC on hosts that do not use random identifiers (Windows uses random interface IDs by default for privacy).

items.title: Split the MAC in two
items.body: Separate the 24-bit OUI from the 24-bit device part: 3C5A.B412.3456 becomes 3C5AB4 | 123456.

items.title: Insert FFFE in the middle
items.body: 3C5AB4 FFFE 123456 gives 64 bits: 3C5A:B4FF:FE12:3456.

items.title: Flip the 7th bit
items.body: The 7th bit from the left of the first byte is the Universal/Local (U/L) bit. 3C = 0011 1100; flipping the 7th bit gives 0011 1110 = 3E. In practice the second hex digit changes: 0 and 2, 1 and 3, 4 and 6, 5 and 7, 8 and A, 9 and B, C and E, D and F swap.

items.title: Append to the prefix
items.body: Interface ID 3E5A:B4FF:FE12:3456. With prefix 2001:db8:acad:20::/64, the address is 2001:db8:acad:20:3e5a:b4ff:fe12:3456; the link-local is fe80::3e5a:b4ff:fe12:3456.

course_blocks.title: Exercise: EUI-64 from MAC 00c1.6412.3402
course_blocks.body: Split: 00C164 | 123402. Insert FFFE: 00C1:64FF:FE12:3402. First byte 00 = 0000 0000, flip the 7th bit: 0000 0010 = 02. Interface ID: **02C1:64FF:FE12:3402**, displayed by IOS as 2C1:64FF:FE12:3402 because leading zeros are dropped. With `ipv6 address 2001:db8:acad:20::/64 eui-64`, R1's G0/1 gets **2001:DB8:ACAD:20:2C1:64FF:FE12:3402**, exactly what `show ipv6 interface brief` showed in 1.8. Its solicited-node group is FF02::1:FF12:3402.

items.definition: Stateless Address Autoconfiguration: a host learns the /64 prefix and default gateway from a Router Advertisement and builds its own interface ID (EUI-64 or random).
Neighbor Discovery Protocol (ICMPv6): Router Solicitation/Advertisement (RS/RA), Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement (NS/NA, the ARP replacement) and Duplicate Address Detection (DAD).
Seventh bit of a MAC address: 0 means universally administered (burned-in), 1 locally administered. EUI-64 inverts it.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: FE80::/10 is link-local, FC00::/7 (FD in practice) is unique local, FF00::/8 is multicast and 2000::/3 is global. In EUI-64, the bit flipped is the 7th, so the change happens in the second hex digit of the address, and FFFE (not FFFF) is inserted. The solicited-node address uses the last 24 bits, not the last 32.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Unicast types: global 2000::/3, unique local FC00::/7 (FD), link-local FE80::/10 (always present, never routed).
Anycast = same unicast address on several devices; the nearest one receives the packet.
Multicast FF00::/8: FF02::1 all nodes, FF02::2 all routers; no broadcast in IPv6.
Solicited-node = FF02::1:FF + last 24 bits of the unicast address; used by NDP instead of ARP.
Modified EUI-64: split the MAC, insert FFFE, flip the 7th bit.

course_blocks.text: 1.10 Verify IP parameters for Client OS (Windows, Mac OS, Linux)

When a user cannot reach anything, the first job is to check four values on the client: **IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers**. The address and the gateway must be in the same subnet, the gateway must answer, and DNS must resolve names. Each operating system has its own commands to display these values.

rows.label: Renew a DHCP lease
values: System Settings or `sudo ipconfig set en0 DHCP`

course_blocks.text: On Linux, `ip addr` gives the prefix length directly (/25), the broadcast address (`brd`), the MAC (`link/ether`) and every IPv6 address with its scope; `dynamic` means it was learned (DHCP or SLAAC). This host built its IPv6 interface ID with EUI-64 (3c becomes 3e, ff:fe in the middle). The default gateway is in `ip route` on the line starting with `default via`. On macOS, `networksetup -getinfo` shows the address, mask and router (gateway) of a network service, while `ifconfig en0` shows the mask in hex (for example 0xffffff80 = 255.255.255.128).

course_blocks.title: Troubleshooting from the client output
course_blocks.body: Case 1: `ipconfig` shows 169.254.33.7 with mask 255.255.0.0 and no gateway. The client got no DHCP answer (APIPA): check the cable, the access VLAN, the DHCP server or the `ip helper-address` relay. Case 2: address 192.168.50.140/25 with gateway 192.168.50.1: the host is in 192.168.50.128/25 and the gateway in 192.168.50.0/25, so off-subnet traffic fails; fix the address or the mask. Case 3: pinging 8.8.8.8 works but names do not resolve: the DNS server entry is wrong or unreachable.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: `ipconfig` alone does not show the MAC address, the DHCP server or (in most cases) the DNS servers: you need `ipconfig /all`. On Linux and macOS the command is `ifconfig` or `ip`, not `ipconfig` (macOS does have an `ipconfig` utility, but with different options).

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Always check IP address, mask, default gateway and DNS, and that address and gateway share a subnet.
Windows: `ipconfig`, `ipconfig /all`, `/release`, `/renew`, `route print`.
Linux: `ip addr`, `ip route`, `ip neigh` (older `ifconfig`, `route`).
macOS: `ifconfig`, `networksetup -getinfo`, `netstat -rn`.
A 169.254.x.x address means DHCP failed.

course_blocks.text: 1.11 Describe wireless principles

Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11) carries frames over radio waves instead of cables. The medium is shared and half duplex: only one device can transmit on a channel at a time, so stations use **CSMA/CA** (collision avoidance), because a radio cannot listen for collisions while it transmits. Understanding channels, RF behaviour, network names and encryption explains most wireless problems.
RF basics

items.definition: Frequency is the number of cycles per second (Hz). Higher frequency means shorter wavelength and less range through obstacles: 5 GHz and 6 GHz cover less distance than 2.4 GHz at the same power.
Amplitude is the signal strength. Power is expressed in dBm (0 dBm = 1 mW; +3 dB doubles, -3 dB halves). RSSI is the received signal strength, for example -65 dBm is good, -85 dBm is weak.
Signal-to-noise ratio: the gap in dB between the received signal and the background noise. A higher SNR allows higher data rates.

Absorption (walls, water, people weaken the signal), reflection (metal surfaces bounce it), refraction (it bends through materials of different density), diffraction (it bends around obstacles), scattering (rough surfaces spread it), plus free-space path loss with distance.

course_blocks.text: Nonoverlapping channels

In the **2.4 GHz** band, channels are numbered 1 to 13 in Europe (1 to 11 in North America) and spaced only 5 MHz apart, while each transmission is about 20 to 22 MHz wide. Neighbouring channels therefore overlap, and only **channels 1, 6 and 11** can be used side by side without interfering. Adjacent APs should use different channels from this set. The **5 GHz** band offers many more nonoverlapping 20 MHz channels (around twenty or more, depending on the country), which can be bonded into 40, 80 or 160 MHz channels for more throughput. Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6 GHz band with even more channels.
SSID, BSSID and service sets

items.definition: Service Set Identifier: the human-readable network name (up to 32 characters) that clients see and select. One AP can broadcast several SSIDs, usually each mapped to a different VLAN.
The MAC address of the AP radio (or of each SSID on that radio). It uniquely identifies one BSS, even when many APs share the same SSID.
Basic Service Set: one AP and its associated clients. The Basic Service Area is the physical coverage cell of that AP.
Extended Service Set: several APs connected by a wired distribution system and advertising the same SSID, so clients can roam between cells. Cells should overlap by about 10 to 15 percent.
Independent BSS (ad hoc): clients talk directly to each other without an AP.

course_blocks.text: Encryption overview

rows.label: WPA3
values: AES-CCMP (128-bit) as baseline, AES-GCMP-256 in 192-bit Enterprise mode (Cisco courses summarise this as GCMP); SAE instead of PSK; PMF required

course_blocks.text: Every WPA generation has two authentication modes: **Personal** (one pre-shared passphrase for everyone, or SAE in WPA3) and **Enterprise** (802.1X with a RADIUS server, each user authenticated individually). Domain 5 (objective 5.9) goes deeper into these protocols.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: The nonoverlapping 2.4 GHz channels are 1, 6 and 11, not 1, 5, 9 or 1, 7, 13. The SSID is the network name, the BSSID is a MAC address. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP, while TKIP belongs to the original WPA.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Wi-Fi is half duplex and uses CSMA/CA.
2.4 GHz: only channels 1, 6, 11 do not overlap; 5 GHz offers many more channels but shorter range.
SSID = network name; BSSID = AP radio MAC; ESS = several APs with one SSID for roaming.
RF: absorption, reflection, refraction, diffraction, scattering; measure in dBm, RSSI, SNR.
WEP and WPA/TKIP are obsolete; WPA2 = AES-CCMP; WPA3 = SAE + PMF.

course_blocks.text: 1.12 Explain virtualization fundamentals (server virtualization, containers, and VRFs)

Virtualization runs several logical instances on one physical resource. For servers, it lets one physical host run many isolated machines, which improves hardware use and makes it fast to create, move or restore a server. For networks, it lets one router keep several separate routing tables.
Server virtualization and hypervisors

A **hypervisor** shares the physical CPU, memory, storage and network cards between **virtual machines (VMs)**. Each VM has its own guest operating system and virtual hardware (vCPU, vRAM, vNIC). VMs on the same host connect to a **virtual switch** (vSwitch) inside the hypervisor, which can tag VLANs; the host's physical NICs then act as uplinks, usually configured as 802.1Q trunks on the physical switch.

rows.label: Runs on
values: A normal host OS (Windows, macOS, Linux)

rows.label: Examples
values: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, KVM, Xen
Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation and Fusion

course_blocks.text: Containers

A **container** packages an application with its libraries and dependencies but **shares the kernel of the host OS** instead of carrying a full guest OS. Containers are therefore much lighter than VMs (megabytes instead of gigabytes), start in seconds and run identically on a laptop, a server or a cloud. Docker is the common container engine; Kubernetes orchestrates many containers across many hosts (scheduling, scaling, restart on failure).
VRFs

A **VRF** (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) instance is a separate routing table inside one router. Each interface (or subinterface) belongs to one VRF, and packets received in a VRF are routed only with that VRF's table. Two customers or departments can therefore use **overlapping IP addresses** on the same router without seeing each other. Using VRFs without MPLS is called **VRF-Lite**; service providers combine VRFs with MPLS to build MPLS VPNs.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# vrf definition CUST-A
R1(config-vrf)# address-family ipv4
R1(config-vrf-af)# exit-address-family
R1(config-vrf)# exit
R1(config)# vrf definition CUST-B
R1(config-vrf)# address-family ipv4
R1(config-vrf-af)# exit-address-family
R1(config-vrf)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# vrf forwarding CUST-A
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# vrf forwarding CUST-B
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# end

course_blocks.text: Both interfaces carry 10.1.1.1/24, which would be refused in the global table but is accepted here because each lives in its own VRF. `show ip route vrf CUST-A` displays only that VRF's table, `show vrf` lists the VRFs and their interfaces, and tests must also name the VRF (`ping vrf CUST-A 10.1.1.10`). Note that moving an interface into a VRF with `vrf forwarding` removes its existing IP address, so the address is configured afterwards. Older IOS versions use `ip vrf` and `ip vrf forwarding` for the same purpose.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM); VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are type 2. Containers do not include a guest OS: they share the host kernel. A VRF virtualizes the routing table (Layer 3), whereas a VLAN virtualizes the Layer 2 broadcast domain.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Hypervisors run VMs; type 1 = bare-metal, type 2 = on top of a host OS.
VMs connect to a vSwitch; host uplinks are usually 802.1Q trunks.
Containers share the host kernel: lighter and faster than VMs; Docker runs them, Kubernetes orchestrates them.
A VRF is a separate routing table on one router, allowing overlapping addresses; VRF-Lite = VRFs without MPLS.

course_blocks.text: 1.13 Describe switching concepts

A Layer 2 switch makes one decision per frame: through which port(s) should it leave? It bases that decision on its **MAC address table** (also called the CAM table), which it builds by itself from the traffic it sees. Three actions are possible: **forward** out a single port, **flood** out all ports of the VLAN except the incoming one, or **filter** (drop) the frame.
MAC learning and aging

**Learning uses the source MAC address.** When a frame arrives, the switch records its source MAC, the incoming port and the VLAN. If the MAC was already known on another port (the device moved), the entry is updated. Each dynamic entry has an aging timer, reset every time a frame from that MAC is seen; if the MAC stays silent for **300 seconds** (default), the entry is removed. This keeps the table small and accurate when devices are unplugged or moved.
Frame switching and flooding

**Forwarding uses the destination MAC address.** If the destination is a known unicast MAC on another port, the frame goes out that port only. If it is known on the same port it arrived on, the switch filters (drops) it. If the destination is a **broadcast** (FFFF.FFFF.FFFF), a **multicast** (without IGMP snooping), or an **unknown unicast** (not in the table), the switch floods the frame out every port in the same VLAN except the incoming port. Flooding is normal and temporary: the reply from the destination teaches the switch where that MAC lives.

course_blocks.code:
graph TD
  A[Frame received on a port] --> B[Learn or refresh source MAC, port and VLAN]
  B --> C{Destination MAC type}
  C -->|Broadcast or multicast| F[Flood out all ports in the VLAN except the incoming port]
  C -->|Unicast| D{Destination in MAC table?}
  D -->|No: unknown unicast| F
  D -->|Yes, same port as incoming| G[Filter: drop the frame]
  D -->|Yes, other port| H[Forward out that port only]
course_blocks.caption: Switch decision: learn from the source, forward based on the destination.

rows.label: Store-and-forward
values: The whole frame, then checks the FCS
Drops corrupted frames; slightly more latency. Default on most Cisco Catalyst switches.

rows.label: Cut-through
values: Only the destination MAC (first 6 bytes of the frame)
Lowest latency, but forwards corrupted frames.

rows.label: Fragment-free
values: Filters most collision fragments (runts); a middle ground.

course_blocks.text: The MAC address table on IOS

course_blocks.content:
SW1# show mac address-table dynamic
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------

Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
  10    3c5a.b412.3456    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
  10    3c5a.b412.3457    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
  10    00c1.6412.3401    DYNAMIC     Gi0/24
  20    3c5a.b412.3458    DYNAMIC     Gi0/3
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 4

SW1# show mac address-table aging-time
Global Aging Time:  300
Vlan    Aging Time
----    ----------

course_blocks.text: Each line gives the VLAN, the MAC address, how it was learned (DYNAMIC or STATIC) and the port. Several MACs on one port, such as Gi0/24 towards a router or another switch, is normal for an uplink. Useful commands: `show mac address-table address 3c5a.b412.3456`, `show mac address-table interface Gi0/1`, `show mac address-table count`, `clear mac address-table dynamic`. To change the aging timer use `mac address-table aging-time <seconds>`; to pin a MAC to a port use `mac address-table static 3c5a.b412.3456 vlan 10 interface GigabitEthernet0/1`.

course_blocks.title: Walk-through with an empty table
course_blocks.body: PC-A (Gi0/1) sends a frame to PC-B (Gi0/2), both in VLAN 10, and the table is empty. 1) The switch learns PC-A's MAC on Gi0/1. 2) PC-B's MAC is unknown, so the frame is flooded out every VLAN 10 port except Gi0/1; PC-C in VLAN 20 never sees it. 3) PC-B replies: the switch learns PC-B on Gi0/2 and, since PC-A is known, forwards the reply out Gi0/1 only. 4) From now on, traffic between them is forwarded, not flooded. If PC-A then stays silent for 300 seconds, its entry ages out and the next frame towards it is flooded again.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Switches learn from the **source** MAC and forward on the **destination** MAC; questions often swap the two. Flooding never sends the frame back out the port it came in on and never leaves its VLAN. The default aging time is 300 seconds (5 minutes), not the ARP cache timeout of a router (4 hours by default).

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Learn from the source MAC (MAC, port, VLAN); forward based on the destination MAC.
Dynamic entries age out after 300 seconds of silence by default.
Unknown unicast, broadcast and multicast are flooded within the VLAN, except out the incoming port.
Store-and-forward checks the FCS; cut-through reads only the destination MAC; fragment-free reads 64 bytes.
Verify with `show mac address-table` (dynamic, address, interface, count, aging-time).

course_blocks.text: 2.0 Network Access (20%)

This domain is about everything that happens between an end device and the first router: VLANs and trunks that segment a switched network, discovery protocols, EtherChannel bundles, Rapid PVST+ that keeps the Layer 2 topology loop-free, and the wireless side (architectures, AP modes, WLC connections and the WLC GUI), plus how you reach a device to manage it. Expect questions that show you `show` output (`show vlan brief`, `show interfaces trunk`, `show etherchannel summary`, `show spanning-tree`) and ask what is wrong or which port does what, as well as configuration questions where one keyword changes everything (`add` in an allowed list, `active` versus `on`). The heaviest weight is on VLANs, trunks and spanning tree: master those first, then make sure you can read a WLC screen without hesitation.
2.1 Configure and verify VLANs (normal range) spanning multiple switches

A VLAN (Virtual LAN) is a broadcast domain created inside a switch by software. Without VLANs, every port of a switch belongs to the same broadcast domain: an ARP request from the accounting PC reaches the guest laptops too. With VLANs, you group ports by function (Sales, Engineering, Voice, Guests) regardless of where users physically sit, and a frame in one VLAN is never switched into another VLAN. To move traffic between VLANs you need a Layer 3 device (router or multilayer switch). Each VLAN normally maps to one IP subnet.

VLAN IDs are 12-bit values. The **normal range** is 1 to 1005 and is stored in the `vlan.dat` file in flash (not in the startup-config). The **extended range** is 1006 to 4094. IDs 0 and 4095 are reserved and never usable. The CCNA objective focuses on the normal range.

items.definition: A switch port that belongs to a single data VLAN and sends and receives untagged frames. Used for end devices.
A second VLAN configured on an access port for an IP phone. The phone tags its voice frames with 802.1Q, while the PC behind it stays untagged in the data VLAN.
VLAN 1. Every port is in VLAN 1 out of the box. It cannot be deleted or renamed.
Switched Virtual Interface (`interface vlan X`): a logical Layer 3 interface of a switch inside a VLAN, used for management or for inter-VLAN routing.
Inter-VLAN routing with one physical router interface split into 802.1Q subinterfaces, one per VLAN, over a trunk.
Flash file holding the normal-range VLAN database. Erasing the startup-config alone does not delete VLANs.

course_blocks.text: 2.1.a Access ports (data and voice)

Configuration has two parts: create the VLAN (optionally with a name) in global configuration, then assign ports to it. `switchport mode access` turns DTP off and forces the port to be an access port; `switchport access vlan` chooses the data VLAN; `switchport voice vlan` adds the voice VLAN for a phone. The switch advertises the voice VLAN ID to Cisco phones through CDP (or LLDP-MED for other vendors), so the phone knows which tag to use.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# vlan 10
SW1(config-vlan)# name SALES
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
SW1(config-vlan)# name VOICE
SW1(config-vlan)# vlan 30
SW1(config-vlan)# name ENG
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport voice vlan 20
SW1(config-if-range)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/3
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 30
SW1(config-if)# end

course_blocks.text: Verify with `show vlan brief`, which lists each VLAN, its name, its status and its **access** ports. A port with a voice VLAN appears in both its data VLAN and its voice VLAN. For the details of one port, `show interfaces gi0/1 switchport` shows the administrative and operational mode, the access VLAN and the voice VLAN.

course_blocks.content:
SW1# show vlan brief

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports

1    default                          active    Gi0/4, Gi0/5, Gi0/6, Gi0/7
                                                Gi0/8, Gi0/9, Gi0/10, Gi0/11
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2
20   VOICE                            active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2
30   ENG                              active    Gi0/3
1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
1003 token-ring-default               act/unsup
1004 fddinet-default                  act/unsup

SW1# show interfaces gigabitethernet0/1 switchport

Switchport: Enabled
Administrative Mode: static access
Operational Mode: static access
Administrative Trunking Encapsulation: dot1q
Negotiation of Trunking: Off
