course_blocks.text: What to read: Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 are in VLAN 10 for data and VLAN 20 for voice; Gi0/12 is missing from the list because it is the trunk configured in 2.2 (trunk ports are never listed in `show vlan brief`); VLANs 1002 to 1005 are the legacy FDDI and Token Ring VLANs, always present, shown as `act/unsup`, and they cannot be deleted. `Negotiation of Trunking: Off` confirms that `switchport mode access` disabled DTP.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: If you assign a port to a VLAN that does not exist yet (`switchport access vlan 40`), IOS creates VLAN 40 automatically with the name VLAN0040. The exception is a switch in VTP client mode: it cannot create VLANs, so the port stays inactive until the VLAN is learned from a VTP server. Also remember: a port missing from `show vlan brief` is not necessarily shut down, it is often a trunk. And a deleted VLAN leaves its access ports inactive until you recreate the VLAN or move them.

course_blocks.text: 2.1.b Default VLAN

VLAN 1 is special: all ports start in it, it is the default native VLAN on trunks, and switches send control traffic such as CDP, VTP, DTP and PAgP in VLAN 1. It cannot be deleted or renamed, and neither can VLANs 1002 to 1005. Because every unconfigured port lands in VLAN 1, it is a security best practice to avoid using it for users or management: put management in a dedicated VLAN (for example an SVI in VLAN 99), move unused ports to an unused "parking" VLAN and shut them down, and change the native VLAN on trunks.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# vlan 999
SW1(config-vlan)# name PARKING
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet0/8 - 11
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 999
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown

course_blocks.text: 2.1.c InterVLAN connectivity

Hosts in different VLANs are in different subnets, so they send inter-VLAN traffic to their default gateway. Two designs are on the exam. **Router-on-a-stick**: one router interface connected to a switch trunk, split into subinterfaces; each subinterface has `encapsulation dot1q <vlan>` and the gateway IP of that VLAN. It is cheap but all inter-VLAN traffic crosses one link twice (in and out). **Multilayer switch with SVIs**: one `interface vlan X` per VLAN, each with the gateway IP, and `ip routing` enabled globally. Routing happens in hardware inside the switch, which is faster and is the usual campus design.

course_blocks.caption: Router-on-a-stick: one trunk link carries VLANs 10 and 20 to the router subinterfaces.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.10
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 10
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 20
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# interface gigabitethernet0/0.99
R1(config-subif)# encapsulation dot1q 99 native
R1(config-subif)# ip address 192.168.99.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-subif)# exit

SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99

course_blocks.text: Read this configuration carefully: the physical interface needs `no shutdown` (subinterfaces inherit its state), each subinterface number is only a label (matching it to the VLAN is a good habit, not a rule), and the `encapsulation dot1q` VLAN ID is what really matters. The `native` keyword tells the router that VLAN 99 is untagged, matching the switch native VLAN. The switch port must be a static trunk because a router does not negotiate DTP.

course_blocks.content:
DSW1(config)# ip routing
DSW1(config)# interface vlan 10
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# interface vlan 20
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# interface vlan 30
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0
DSW1(config-if)# no shutdown
DSW1(config-if)# end

DSW1# show ip interface brief | include Vlan
Vlan10                 192.168.10.1    YES manual up                    up
Vlan20                 192.168.20.1    YES manual up                    up
Vlan30                 192.168.30.1    YES manual down                  down

DSW1# show ip route connected
      192.168.10.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        192.168.10.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan10
L        192.168.10.1/32 is directly connected, Vlan10
      192.168.20.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected, Vlan20
L        192.168.20.1/32 is directly connected, Vlan20

course_blocks.text: An SVI is up/up only if the VLAN exists in the VLAN database, at least one access or trunk port carrying that VLAN is up and forwarding (this is called autostate), and the SVI is not administratively shut down. Here Vlan30 is down/down: VLAN 30 has no active port on DSW1, so its subnet is missing from the routing table. On a multilayer switch, a physical port can also become a routed port with `no switchport` and receive an IP address directly, for example on an uplink to a router.

rows.label: Performance
values: Limited by one link, traffic hairpins

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Forgetting `ip routing` on a multilayer switch is a classic: SVIs are up/up and each host can ping its own gateway, but hosts in different VLANs cannot reach each other. Another classic: on router-on-a-stick, a host's default gateway must be the IP of the subinterface of its own VLAN, and the switch port toward the router must be a trunk, not an access port.

course_blocks.title: Troubleshooting exercise: VLAN 20 cannot reach VLAN 10
course_blocks.body: PC-A (192.168.10.11/24, gateway 192.168.10.1) cannot ping PC-B (192.168.20.11/24, gateway 192.168.20.1). R1 has `interface gi0/0.20` with `encapsulation dot1q 2` and IP 192.168.20.1. Question: what is wrong? Answer: the subinterface tags VLAN 2 instead of VLAN 20, so frames from VLAN 20 arriving tagged 20 are not accepted by any subinterface, and replies leave tagged 2. PC-B cannot even ping its gateway. Fix: `encapsulation dot1q 20` under Gi0/0.20.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Normal range VLANs are 1 to 1005, stored in `vlan.dat`; VLAN 1 and VLANs 1002 to 1005 cannot be deleted.
Access port: `switchport mode access` + `switchport access vlan X`; add `switchport voice vlan Y` for an IP phone (voice tagged, PC untagged).
`show vlan brief` lists access ports only; trunk ports never appear in it.
Router-on-a-stick: subinterfaces with `encapsulation dot1q X` (add `native` for the native VLAN) over a static trunk.
Multilayer switch: one SVI per VLAN plus `ip routing`; an SVI needs an active port in its VLAN to be up/up.

course_blocks.text: 2.2 Configure and verify interswitch connectivity

When the same VLANs exist on several switches, you could run one cable per VLAN between them, but that does not scale. A **trunk** carries many VLANs over one link: each frame is marked with its VLAN so the receiving switch puts it back in the right VLAN. Trunks connect switches to switches, switches to routers (router-on-a-stick), and switches to servers, hypervisors, autonomous APs or FlexConnect APs.

items.definition: A port that carries traffic for multiple VLANs, tagging frames with their VLAN ID (except the native VLAN).
The standard trunking protocol. It inserts a 4-byte tag inside the Ethernet frame.
Inter-Switch Link, Cisco's old proprietary trunking protocol that encapsulated the whole frame. Obsolete and absent from most current switches.
Dynamic Trunking Protocol, Cisco proprietary, used to negotiate whether a link becomes a trunk.
The VLAN whose frames cross an 802.1Q trunk untagged. VLAN 1 by default. Must match on both ends.
The VLANs permitted on a trunk. All VLANs (1 to 4094) by default.

course_blocks.text: 2.2.a Trunk ports

A port can become a trunk statically (`switchport mode trunk`) or dynamically through DTP. DTP modes are: `access` (never trunks), `trunk` (always trunks and still sends DTP), `dynamic desirable` (actively asks to trunk), and `dynamic auto` (trunks only if the other side asks). The default mode on most current Catalyst access switches is `dynamic auto`, so two switches cabled together with default settings stay in access mode. `switchport nonegotiate` stops DTP frames entirely; it is accepted only on a port in `access` or `trunk` mode, and the neighbor must then be configured statically as a trunk too.

On switches that also support ISL (for example older Catalyst 3560 or 3750), the encapsulation defaults to `negotiate` and `switchport mode trunk` is rejected until you set `switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q`. Switches that only support 802.1Q (2960, Catalyst 9000) do not have or do not need that command. Best practice: configure trunks statically, disable DTP with `switchport nonegotiate`, and set every user port to `switchport mode access` so an attacker cannot negotiate a trunk.

The allowed VLAN list controls which VLANs may cross the trunk. `switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99` **replaces** the list; `add 30` and `remove 20` modify it; `all`, `none` and `except` are also available. Restricting the list limits broadcast flooding and the reach of a VLAN.

802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag between the source MAC address field and the EtherType/Length field. The original frame is not encapsulated, it is modified, so the switch recalculates the FCS. The tag contains: **TPID** (16 bits, value 0x8100, which identifies a tagged frame), **PCP** (3 bits, the 802.1p Class of Service used for QoS, for example 5 for voice), **DEI** (1 bit, formerly CFI, drop eligible indicator) and **VID** (12 bits, the VLAN ID, hence 4096 values with 0 and 4095 reserved). A tagged frame can be up to 1522 bytes instead of 1518.

course_blocks.content:
Untagged: | Dest MAC | Src MAC | EtherType | Payload | FCS |
Tagged:   | Dest MAC | Src MAC | TPID 0x8100 | PCP(3) DEI(1) VID(12) | EtherType | Payload | FCS* |
                                  <------------- 802.1Q tag, 4 bytes ------------->   * recalculated

course_blocks.text: 2.2.c Native VLAN

On an 802.1Q trunk, frames from the native VLAN are sent untagged, and any untagged frame received is placed in the native VLAN. The default native VLAN is 1. Both ends must agree: if SW1 uses native VLAN 99 and SW2 uses native VLAN 1, untagged frames leaving SW1 from VLAN 99 land in VLAN 1 on SW2. Traffic leaks between VLANs, and CDP reports it with a `%CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH` message. Per-VLAN spanning tree also detects the inconsistency and blocks the affected VLANs on that port. The trunk itself stays up, which makes this fault easy to miss.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# vlan 99
SW1(config-vlan)# name NATIVE
SW1(config-vlan)# exit
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/12
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,99
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
SW1(config-if)# end

SW1# show interfaces trunk

Port        Mode             Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/12      on               802.1q         trunking      99

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/12      10,20,30,99

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/12      10,20,30,99

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/12      10,20,30,99

course_blocks.text: How to read it: **Mode** `on` means the trunk is configured statically (a negotiated trunk shows `desirable` or `auto`); **Status** must be `trunking`; **Native vlan** must match the neighbor. The second section is the configured allowed list; the third removes VLANs that do not exist on this switch; the fourth removes VLANs that are blocked by STP (or pruned by VTP) on this port. A VLAN in the second list but not in the fourth is allowed but not forwarding: check STP or whether the VLAN exists. Only ports that are actually trunking appear in this command.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: `switchport trunk allowed vlan 30` on a trunk that already allows 10, 20 and 99 leaves **only** VLAN 30: the other VLANs are cut immediately. To append, use `switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30`. Also: two switches left at the default `dynamic auto` do not form a trunk, and a native VLAN mismatch does not bring the trunk down.

course_blocks.title: Read the symptoms
course_blocks.body: SW2 logs `%CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH: Native VLAN mismatch discovered on GigabitEthernet0/12 (1), with SW1 GigabitEthernet0/12 (99).` and users in VLAN 99 behind SW1 cannot reach the VLAN 99 SVI on SW2. Question: fix? Answer: the trunk on SW2 still uses native VLAN 1. Configure `switchport trunk native vlan 99` on SW2 Gi0/12 so both ends agree, then confirm with `show interfaces trunk` on both switches. As a hardening option, `vlan dot1q tag native` (global) makes the switch tag even native VLAN frames.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: 802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag (TPID 0x8100, PCP 3 bits, DEI 1 bit, VID 12 bits) and the FCS is recalculated.
DTP: auto + auto = access; desirable with auto, desirable or trunk = trunk; `switchport nonegotiate` disables DTP.
Native VLAN = untagged, VLAN 1 by default, must match on both ends; a mismatch leaks traffic and CDP logs it.
Use `switchport trunk allowed vlan add X` to append; without `add` the list is replaced.
`show interfaces trunk`: mode, status, native VLAN, allowed, active, and forwarding VLANs per trunk.

course_blocks.text: 2.3 Configure and verify Layer 2 discovery protocols (Cisco Discovery Protocol and LLDP)

CDP and LLDP let directly connected devices announce themselves: hostname, model, interface, IP address, capabilities. They work at Layer 2, so they reveal a neighbor even when IP is misconfigured, which makes them the first tool to draw or check a topology. They only see **directly connected** neighbors: a device two hops away is not shown. CDP is Cisco proprietary and enabled by default on Cisco devices. LLDP is the IEEE 802.1AB standard, works between vendors, and is disabled by default on most Cisco IOS devices.

SW1(config-if)# no lldp transmit

The **Holdtime** counts down and is reset each time an advertisement arrives; when it reaches zero the neighbor is removed. The summary output does not show IP addresses: use `show cdp neighbors detail` (or `show cdp entry R1`) and `show lldp neighbors detail`, which add the management IP address, the software version, the native VLAN and duplex (CDP), and the system description. `show cdp` displays the global timers and `show cdp interface` the per-interface state.

course_blocks.title: Security note
course_blocks.body: Everything CDP and LLDP reveal (model, IOS version, IP address, VLANs) is also useful to an attacker. Disable them on ports facing the Internet, other organizations or untrusted users, and keep them on infrastructure links and on ports with IP phones (which use CDP or LLDP-MED to learn the voice VLAN).

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: LLDP is off by default on Cisco IOS: `lldp run` is needed before any LLDP neighbor appears, and per interface transmit and receive are two separate commands. Do not swap the timers: CDP is 60/180 seconds, LLDP is 30/120 seconds. And neither protocol shows a device that is not directly connected.

course_blocks.title: Map the topology from one command
course_blocks.body: From the `show cdp neighbors` output above, without logging into any other device you can write: SW1 Gi0/24 connects to R1 Gi0/0/0 (an ISR4331 router), SW1 Gi0/12 connects to SW2 Gi0/12 (a 2960X switch), and SW1 Gi0/1 has a Cisco IP phone. To find R1's IP address for an SSH session, run `show cdp entry R1` and read the `IP address` line.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: CDP: Cisco, on by default, 60 s timer, 180 s holdtime; `cdp run` globally, `cdp enable` per interface.
LLDP: IEEE 802.1AB, off by default, 30 s timer, 120 s holdtime; `lldp run`, then `lldp transmit` / `lldp receive` per interface.
Local Intrfce = your port; Port ID = the neighbor's port.
`detail` or `entry` outputs add IP address, software version and more.
Only directly connected neighbors are seen; disable both protocols on untrusted edges.

course_blocks.text: 2.4 Configure and verify (Layer 2/Layer 3) EtherChannel (LACP)

If you connect two switches with two parallel links, spanning tree blocks one of them to avoid a loop: you pay for two links and use one. **EtherChannel** bundles up to 8 active physical links into one logical interface called a **port-channel**. STP sees a single link, so all members forward; if one member fails, traffic moves to the others without an STP recalculation. Traffic is not split packet by packet: the switch hashes fields of each frame (MAC addresses, IP addresses or ports, set with `port-channel load-balance`) and always sends a given flow over the same member, which keeps packets in order.

items.definition: The logical interface (`interface port-channel 1`) that represents the bundle. Configuration applied to it is applied to the members.
Link Aggregation Control Protocol, IEEE 802.3ad (now 802.1AX), open standard. Modes `active` and `passive`.
Port Aggregation Protocol, Cisco proprietary. Modes `desirable` and `auto`.
`channel-group X mode on`: the bundle is forced with no negotiation protocol at all.
A bundle of routed ports (`no switchport`) with the IP address on the port-channel interface.

course_blocks.text: PAgP follows the same logic: `desirable` + `desirable` or `desirable` + `auto` form a bundle, `auto` + `auto` does not. LACP and PAgP cannot be mixed on the same bundle, and `on` only works with `on` on the other side. LACP is preferred because it is standard and it detects misconfiguration; `on` is risky because a wrong cabling or a mismatched neighbor can create a loop or black-hole traffic without any warning. LACP can also hold up to 8 additional links in hot-standby (flag H) that take over if an active member fails.

Members must be consistent to join the bundle: same speed and duplex, same switchport mode (all access or all trunk), same access VLAN, same native VLAN and allowed VLAN list on trunks, and for Layer 3 all members must be routed ports with no IP address of their own. A member that does not match is suspended (flag `s`) or stays stand-alone (flag `I`). The simplest way to stay consistent is to configure the members together with `interface range`, then apply Layer 2 or Layer 3 settings on the port-channel interface.

course_blocks.content:
! Layer 2 EtherChannel (trunk) between DSW1 and DSW2
DSW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1 - 2
DSW1(config-if-range)# channel-protocol lacp
DSW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
DSW1(config-if-range)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface port-channel 1
DSW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
DSW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
DSW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30,99
DSW1(config-if)# exit

! Layer 3 EtherChannel (routed) toward the core
DSW1(config)# ip routing
DSW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/3 - 4
DSW1(config-if-range)# no switchport
DSW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 2 mode active
DSW1(config-if-range)# exit
DSW1(config)# interface port-channel 2
DSW1(config-if)# no switchport
DSW1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.252
DSW1(config-if)# end

course_blocks.text: The lines starting with `!` are comments in IOS. `channel-protocol lacp` is optional (the mode `active` already implies LACP) but documents your intent. For Layer 3, `no switchport` goes on the members **before** `channel-group`, so the port-channel is created as a routed interface; the IP address is configured only on the port-channel. The other switch needs a matching configuration with `active` or `passive`.

items.title: Read the port-channel flags
items.body: `SU` = Layer 2 and in use (healthy L2 bundle); `RU` = Layer 3 and in use (healthy routed bundle); `SD` or `RD` = the bundle is down.

items.title: Read the member flags
items.body: `P` = bundled, the normal state; `I` = stand-alone, the neighbor did not negotiate (for example both sides `passive`, or the neighbor not configured); `s` = suspended, usually a configuration mismatch; `D` = down; `H` = hot-standby.

items.title: Check the protocol column
items.body: `LACP`, `PAgP`, or a dash for mode `on`. Both ends must use the same protocol.

items.title: Dig deeper if needed
items.body: `show etherchannel port-channel`, `show lacp neighbor`, `show interfaces port-channel 1` and `show etherchannel load-balance` give details on members, LACP partners, bandwidth and the hash method.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: `passive` + `passive` (LACP) and `auto` + `auto` (PAgP) never form a bundle: at least one side must initiate. `on` does not negotiate, so `on` on one side and `active` on the other fails. Also, an EtherChannel does not give one flow the sum of the bandwidth: a single file transfer still uses one member link.

course_blocks.title: Why is Po3 down?
course_blocks.body: In the output above, Po3 shows `(SD)` and its members `(I)`. DSW1 has `channel-group 3 mode passive` on Gi1/0/5 and Gi1/0/6. DSW2 has the same configuration. Question: what is wrong? Answer: two passive LACP ends wait for each other, so no LACPDU exchange starts and both ports stay stand-alone. Change one side to `channel-group 3 mode active`; the members should change to `(P)` and Po3 to `(SU)`.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: EtherChannel bundles up to 8 active links into one port-channel; STP sees one link and all members forward.
LACP (IEEE): active/passive; PAgP (Cisco): desirable/auto; `on`: static, only with `on`.
passive + passive and auto + auto fail; at least one side must be active or desirable.
Members need identical speed, duplex, mode and VLAN settings; L3 needs `no switchport` and the IP on the port-channel.
`show etherchannel summary`: SU = L2 OK, RU = L3 OK, P = bundled, I = stand-alone, s = suspended.

course_blocks.text: 2.5 Interpret basic operations of Rapid PVST+ Spanning Tree Protocol

Redundant links between switches are good for availability but deadly at Layer 2: Ethernet frames have no TTL, so a broadcast caught in a loop circulates forever, multiplies (broadcast storm), and MAC tables flap as the same source MAC is learned on different ports. Spanning Tree Protocol builds a loop-free tree by electing a root bridge and putting redundant ports in a discarding state; if an active link fails, a discarding port takes over.

Several versions exist. The original IEEE 802.1D converges in 30 to 50 seconds. **RSTP** (IEEE 802.1w, now part of 802.1D-2004) converges in a few seconds or less. Cisco runs one spanning-tree instance per VLAN: **PVST+** is per-VLAN 802.1D, and **Rapid PVST+** is per-VLAN RSTP, the version in the CCNA objective. Because each VLAN has its own instance, you can make SW1 root for some VLANs and SW2 root for others to use both uplinks. Enable it with `spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst` (many Catalyst switches default to PVST+, newer IOS XE models often to Rapid PVST+).

items.definition: 8 bytes: priority (4 bits, a multiple of 4096) + extended system ID (12 bits, the VLAN number) + switch MAC address (48 bits). Lowest wins.
The switch with the lowest BID in a VLAN. All its ports are designated ports.
Sum of the costs of the ports a frame enters on its way to the root, counted on each receiving port.
Bridge Protocol Data Unit, the STP message. Sent every 2 seconds (hello time) by designated ports.
An RSTP port connected to an end device, configured with PortFast; it goes straight to forwarding.
A BPDU advertising a better (lower) root BID or a better path than the one currently known.

course_blocks.text: 2.5.a Root port, root bridge (primary/secondary), and other port names

The default priority is 32768. Because the VLAN number is added through the extended system ID, the priority shown for VLAN 10 is 32768 + 10 = 32778. The configurable part must be a multiple of 4096 (0, 4096, 8192 ... 61440). When all switches keep the default priority, the one with the lowest MAC address wins, which is often the oldest switch in the network: a good reason to choose the root deliberately.

items.title: Elect the root bridge
items.body: Every switch starts by claiming to be root. When it receives a superior BPDU it stops and relays the better one. The lowest BID wins: lowest priority first, then lowest MAC address.

items.title: Choose one root port on each non-root switch
items.body: The port with the lowest root path cost. Tie-breakers, in order: lowest neighbor (sender) BID, lowest neighbor port priority, lowest neighbor port number.

items.title: Choose one designated port on each segment
items.body: On each link, the port of the switch with the lowest root path cost becomes designated. Tie: lowest BID of the switch, then lowest port ID. All ports of the root bridge are designated.

items.title: Block everything else
items.body: Any remaining port becomes an alternate port (or a backup port) in the discarding state.

course_blocks.text: The short costs are the ones used on the exam and the default on most Catalyst IOS switches (`spanning-tree pathcost method` changes it). You can override a port cost with `spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 10` or a port priority (default 128, multiples of 16) with `spanning-tree vlan 10 port-priority 64`. To choose the root, set the priority directly with `spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096`, or use the macros: `spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary` sets 24576, or 4096 below the current root priority if that is already lower; `spanning-tree vlan 10 root secondary` sets 28672, so this switch takes over if the primary fails. The macro is calculated once and written in the running-config as a plain `priority` command.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW1(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary
SW2(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
SW2(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root secondary
SW3(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst

course_blocks.text: How to read it: `protocol rstp` confirms Rapid PVST+ (PVST+ would show `ieee`). **Root ID** is the root bridge (SW1, priority 24576 + 10); **Bridge ID** is the local switch. If both blocks show the same address, you are on the root bridge (and the output says `This bridge is the root`). `Cost 4` is SW3's root path cost through `Port 1`, its root port. In the port table, Gi0/2 is the alternate port: SW2 and SW3 both have cost 4 to the root on that link, and SW2 has the lower BID (28682 versus 32778), so SW2's port is designated and SW3's port discards. IOS displays the discarding state as `BLK`. Gi0/3 is an access port with PortFast (`Edge`), cost 19 because it runs at 100 Mbps.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Root port tie-breakers compare the **neighbor's** BID and the **neighbor's** port ID, not the local ones. Also: the root bridge has no root port; a priority like 30000 is rejected because it is not a multiple of 4096; and the priority displayed includes the VLAN number (32778 for VLAN 10 is still the default 32768).

course_blocks.text: 2.5.b Port states and roles

RSTP separates the **role** of a port (its job in the topology) from its **state** (what it does with frames). It has only three states: **discarding** (drops data frames, does not learn MACs), **learning** (still drops data but learns MAC addresses), **forwarding** (normal operation). 802.1D's disabled, blocking and listening states all map to discarding. Convergence is fast because, on point-to-point links (full duplex), switches use a proposal/agreement handshake instead of waiting for timers, and an alternate port can become root port immediately when the root port fails. RSTP considers a neighbor lost after 3 missed hellos (6 seconds) instead of the 20-second max age of 802.1D.

rows.label: Root port
values: Best path to the root on a non-root switch, one per switch

rows.label: Designated port
values: Best port toward the root on a segment, one per segment

rows.label: Alternate port
values: Backup path to the root, receives a better BPDU from another switch; replaces the root port

rows.label: Backup port
values: Backup of a designated port of the same switch on a shared segment (hub); rare

rows.label: Disabled
values: Administratively down port, no STP role

rows.label: Timers
values: Hello 2 s, forward delay 15 s, max age 20 s
Hello 2 s; neighbor lost after 3 missed hellos

course_blocks.text: 2.5.c PortFast

A port connected to a PC, printer or server does not create a loop, so waiting for STP before forwarding only delays DHCP and logins. **PortFast** makes the port an edge port that goes to forwarding immediately when the link comes up. Enable it per interface with `spanning-tree portfast`, or for all access ports at once with `spanning-tree portfast default`. For a trunk to a server or hypervisor, use `spanning-tree portfast trunk`. If an edge port receives a BPDU, it loses its edge status and behaves as a normal STP port, which is why PortFast is usually paired with BPDU guard. Newer IOS XE releases display the same feature as `spanning-tree portfast edge`.
2.5.d Root guard, loop guard, BPDU filter, and BPDU guard

rows.label: BPDU filter
values: Rarely; edges where STP must be silent
Interface: no BPDU sent or processed (STP off on the port); global: port loses PortFast

rows.label: Root guard
values: Designated ports toward switches that must never become root
Root-inconsistent (discarding), recovers when superior BPDUs stop

rows.label: Loop guard
values: Loop-inconsistent (discarding) instead of forwarding, recovers when BPDUs return

course_blocks.content:
SW3(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/3
SW3(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW3(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW3(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
SW3(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
SW3(config-if)# exit
SW3(config)# spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
SW3(config)# errdisable recovery cause bpduguard
SW3(config)# errdisable recovery interval 300

SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree guard root

SW2(config)# interface gigabitethernet0/1
SW2(config-if)# spanning-tree guard loop

%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port Gi0/3 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Gi0/3, putting Gi0/3 in err-disable state

course_blocks.text: `spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default` enables BPDU guard on every PortFast port. An err-disabled port stays down until you enter `shutdown` then `no shutdown`, or until errdisable recovery brings it back (300 seconds by default once the cause is enabled). Root guard and loop guard never err-disable a port: they keep it discarding and recover automatically. Global equivalents exist: `spanning-tree portfast bpdufilter default` and `spanning-tree loopguard default`. Root guard and loop guard cannot be combined on the same port.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: BPDU guard shuts the port (err-disabled); root guard and loop guard only block it (inconsistent state) and recover on their own. BPDU filter configured on an interface silently disables STP on that port, which can create a loop: it is not a protection feature. Do not confuse root guard (superior BPDUs arrive where they should not) with loop guard (expected BPDUs stop arriving).

course_blocks.title: Predict the root and the ports
course_blocks.body: Three switches in a triangle with 1 Gbps links, VLAN 20, all default priorities. MACs: SWA 0050.0000.0003, SWB 0050.0000.0001, SWC 0050.0000.0002. Question: root, root ports, blocked port? Answer: all priorities are 32788 (32768 + 20), so the lowest MAC wins: SWB is root. SWA and SWC each reach SWB directly at cost 4, so their ports toward SWB are root ports. On the SWA to SWC link both have cost 4, so the lower BID wins the designated role: SWC (MAC ...0002) has the designated port and SWA's port becomes alternate (discarding). If you want SWA to be root for VLAN 20, configure `spanning-tree vlan 20 root primary` on SWA.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: BID = priority (multiple of 4096, default 32768) + VLAN ID + MAC; lowest BID is root.
Root port: lowest cost, then neighbor BID, neighbor port priority, neighbor port number; designated port: one per segment.
Short costs: 10 Mbps 100, 100 Mbps 19, 1 Gbps 4, 10 Gbps 2. `root primary` = 24576, `root secondary` = 28672.
RSTP states: discarding, learning, forwarding; roles: root, designated, alternate, backup; IOS shows discarding as BLK.
PortFast = immediate forwarding on edge ports; BPDU guard err-disables; root guard and loop guard block then self-recover.

course_blocks.text: 2.6 Describe Cisco Wireless Architectures and AP modes

An access point (AP) bridges 802.11 wireless frames to Ethernet. The question is where the intelligence lives. In an **autonomous** architecture, each AP is a standalone device with its own configuration (SSIDs, VLANs, security, RF settings), managed one by one through its CLI or GUI. It works for a few APs, but consistent settings, roaming and RF tuning become painful as the network grows. In a **lightweight** (controller-based) architecture, APs are managed by a **Wireless LAN Controller (WLC)**: you configure WLANs once on the WLC, and hundreds of APs download their settings from it. In a **cloud-based** architecture (Cisco Meraki), APs are managed from a web dashboard hosted in the cloud, while user traffic stays on the local network.

Lightweight APs use **split-MAC**: the 802.11 MAC functions are divided. The AP keeps the real-time functions (sending beacons, answering probe requests, acknowledging frames, encrypting and decrypting, queuing and prioritizing frames, transmitting on the radio). The WLC handles the management functions (authentication, association and roaming, security and QoS policy, Radio Resource Management for channels and power, and management of all APs). AP and WLC communicate with **CAPWAP** (Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points, RFC 5415), which builds two tunnels over UDP: a **control** tunnel on UDP 5246, always encrypted with DTLS, and a **data** tunnel on UDP 5247 that carries client traffic (encryption optional, off by default). Because the tunnels are IP-based, the WLC can be in the same building or in a remote data center.

course_blocks.code:
graph LR
  C[Wireless client] -->|802.11| AP[Lightweight AP local mode]
  AP -->|CAPWAP control UDP 5246 DTLS| WLC[WLC]
  AP -->|CAPWAP data UDP 5247| WLC
  WLC -->|802.1Q trunk, client VLANs| SW[Distribution switch]
course_blocks.caption: Local mode: client traffic is tunneled in CAPWAP to the WLC, which drops it into the right VLAN.

rows.label: Client data path
values: Tunneled to the WLC (local mode) or switched locally (FlexConnect)
Local; only management goes to the cloud

rows.label: Fits
values: Many distributed sites, small IT teams

course_blocks.text: Controllers can be deployed in several ways: a dedicated appliance in a central location (centralized or unified), a controller running as a virtual machine in a private or public cloud (Catalyst 9800-CL), a controller embedded in a Catalyst 9000 switch, or a controller embedded in an AP (Mobility Express, now Embedded Wireless Controller on Catalyst APs) for small sites.

items.definition: Default mode. The AP serves clients and tunnels all their traffic to the WLC through CAPWAP. Between client frames it briefly scans other channels for RRM and rogue detection.
For branch offices across a WAN. The AP can switch client traffic locally onto a VLAN and can keep serving clients and authenticating them locally if the link to the WLC goes down.
No client service. The AP scans all channels full time for rogue devices, intrusion detection (wIPS) and location tracking.
The AP captures all 802.11 frames on one channel and forwards them to a remote PC running a protocol analyzer such as Wireshark.
Radios are off. The AP listens on the wired network and compares MAC addresses seen there (ARP) with the list of rogue clients and APs heard over the air, to find rogues plugged into the LAN.

Spectrum Expert Connect: the AP becomes a dedicated spectrum analyzer on all channels and sends the data to remote spectrum analysis software, to identify non-Wi-Fi interference (microwave ovens, Bluetooth, cameras).
The AP builds wireless links between APs: point-to-point or point-to-multipoint bridges between buildings, or a mesh where a root AP (wired) relays traffic for mesh APs that have no cable.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Monitor, sniffer, rogue detector and SE-Connect modes do **not** serve clients. Only local, FlexConnect and (with some limits) bridge/mesh do. Do not mix up the CAPWAP ports: 5246 is control (DTLS-encrypted), 5247 is data. And split-MAC puts encryption and beacons on the AP, not on the WLC.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Autonomous = standalone APs; lightweight = APs managed by a WLC; cloud = Meraki dashboard, data stays local.
Split-MAC: real-time functions on the AP, management functions on the WLC.
CAPWAP: UDP 5246 control (DTLS), UDP 5247 data.
Local mode tunnels client traffic to the WLC; FlexConnect can switch it locally and survive a WAN outage.
Monitor, sniffer, rogue detector and SE-Connect are dedicated modes with no client service.

course_blocks.text: 2.7 Describe physical infrastructure connections of WLAN components (AP, WLC, access/trunk ports, and LAG)

The switch port type depends on what crosses the cable. A **lightweight AP in local mode** sends everything (its own management and all client traffic) inside CAPWAP, addressed from a single IP in one VLAN: the switch port is an **access port** in the AP management VLAN. A **FlexConnect AP with local switching** puts client traffic directly onto several VLANs: the port is a **trunk**, with the native VLAN set to the AP management VLAN (the AP sends its own traffic untagged) and the client VLANs tagged. An **autonomous AP** with several SSIDs mapped to VLANs also needs a trunk. Most APs are powered by the switch through PoE (802.3af up to 15.4 W, 802.3at PoE+ up to 30 W, 802.3bt for more), so check the power budget of the switch.

An AireOS WLC (such as the 3504, 5520 or 8540) has several physical ports. The **service port** is an out-of-band management port for initial setup and recovery; it does not carry client or CAPWAP traffic and connects to an access port. The **distribution system ports** carry all normal traffic (CAPWAP from APs, client data, management) and connect to switch **trunks** because the WLC maps WLANs to several VLANs. There is also a console port and, on models that support high availability, a **redundancy port** linking two WLCs in an SSO pair. On top of the ports, the WLC uses logical interfaces: the **management interface** (CAPWAP and administration), the **virtual interface** (a non-routed address used for DHCP relay and web authentication redirects), the service-port interface, and **dynamic interfaces**, each mapped to a client VLAN.

To use several distribution ports together, enable **LAG** (Link Aggregation) on the WLC. All distribution ports then form a single bundle; if one link fails, traffic continues on the others. An AireOS WLC does not negotiate with LACP or PAgP, so the switch side must be an EtherChannel in static mode: `channel-group X mode on`. Enabling or disabling LAG on AireOS requires a reboot, and the WLC supports only one LAG. The Catalyst 9800 runs IOS XE and offers the usual EtherChannel options including LACP, but the static `mode on` rule for AireOS is the one to know.

course_blocks.content:
! WLC distribution ports, LAG enabled on the WLC
SW1(config)# interface range gigabitethernet1/0/1 - 2
SW1(config-if-range)# description WLC-DISTRIBUTION
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,100
SW1(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode on
SW1(config-if-range)# exit

! Lightweight AP in local mode
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/10
SW1(config-if)# description AP-LOCAL-MODE
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 100
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast

! FlexConnect AP with local switching
SW1(config)# interface gigabitethernet1/0/11
SW1(config-if)# description AP-FLEXCONNECT
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 100
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,100
SW1(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast trunk

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: A WLC LAG on AireOS needs `channel-group X mode on` on the switch: `active`, `passive`, `desirable` and `auto` will not form the bundle. A local-mode AP goes on an access port, not a trunk; a FlexConnect AP doing local switching needs a trunk whose native VLAN is the AP management VLAN.

course_blocks.title: Choose the port type
course_blocks.body: A branch office has two FlexConnect APs that switch the Staff (VLAN 10) and Guest (VLAN 20) WLANs locally; the APs get their IP address in VLAN 100. Headquarters has a WLC with four distribution ports and 50 local-mode APs in VLAN 200. Question: switch configuration? Answer: branch AP ports are trunks with native VLAN 100 and allowed VLANs 10, 20, 100. Headquarters AP ports are access ports in VLAN 200. The four WLC distribution ports form one LAG: a trunk EtherChannel with `channel-group 1 mode on`, allowing the management VLAN and every VLAN mapped to a dynamic interface.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Local-mode lightweight AP: access port in the AP management VLAN.
FlexConnect (local switching) and autonomous APs: trunk, native VLAN = AP management VLAN.
WLC distribution ports connect to trunks; the service port is out-of-band management on an access port.
AireOS LAG: all distribution ports in one bundle, switch side `channel-group X mode on`, no LACP or PAgP.

course_blocks.text: 2.8 Describe network device management access (Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, console, TACACS+/RADIUS, and cloud managed)

There are two families of management access. **Out-of-band** access uses a path separate from user traffic: the console port, or a dedicated management network. It still works when the production network is broken. **In-band** access goes through the production network to an IP address on the device (an SVI, a loopback or an interface): Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, SNMP. It is convenient but disappears if the device loses IP connectivity.

items.definition: Physical serial access (RJ-45 or USB console port) with a terminal emulator. Default settings: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control. Configured under `line con 0`.
Remote CLI over TCP port 23. Everything, including the password, travels in clear text.
Secure Shell, remote CLI over TCP port 22 with encryption and strong authentication. Use version 2. Needs a hostname, a domain name, RSA keys and a local user or AAA.
Virtual terminal lines that accept Telnet and SSH sessions (`line vty 0 4` or `0 15`). `transport input ssh` refuses Telnet.
Web GUI on TCP 80 (clear text) or TCP 443 (TLS-encrypted). `ip http server` and `ip http secure-server` enable them; WLCs are normally managed over HTTPS.
Devices (for example Cisco Meraki) open an outbound secure connection to a vendor cloud and are configured and monitored from a web dashboard; user traffic does not go through the cloud.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# hostname R1
R1(config)# ip domain-name example.local
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
R1(config)# ip ssh version 2
R1(config)# username admin secret Str0ng!Pass
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
R1(config-line)# exit
R1(config)# no ip http server
R1(config)# ip http secure-server
R1(config)# ip http authentication local

course_blocks.text: This configuration allows only SSH on the VTY lines, disables the clear-text web server and keeps HTTPS with local authentication. Objective 4.8 details the SSH configuration step by step. With many devices, local usernames on each device become hard to manage: a central **AAA** server (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) such as Cisco ISE stores the accounts, and devices query it with TACACS+ or RADIUS. Keep a local user as a fallback: with `aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local`, the local database is used only if no TACACS+ server answers, not when a server rejects the password.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# tacacs server ISE1
R1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.1.1.10
R1(config-server-tacacs)# key T4c$SharedKey
R1(config-server-tacacs)# exit
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Telnet (TCP 23) and HTTP (TCP 80) send credentials in clear text; SSH (TCP 22) and HTTPS (TCP 443) encrypt them. TACACS+ uses TCP and encrypts the whole body; RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password. Cloud management means the management plane is in the cloud, not that user data transits through it.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Console = out-of-band, physical, 9600 8N1; works without IP.
Telnet TCP 23 and HTTP TCP 80 are clear text; prefer SSHv2 TCP 22 and HTTPS TCP 443.
`transport input ssh` on VTY lines blocks Telnet; `login local` uses the local user database.
TACACS+: TCP 49, full encryption, separate AAA, device admin. RADIUS: UDP 1812/1813, password only, network access.
Cloud-managed devices are configured from a vendor dashboard; data traffic stays local.

course_blocks.text: 2.9 Interpret the wireless LAN GUI configuration for client connectivity, such as WLAN creation, security settings, QoS profiles, and advanced settings

On the exam you may see screenshots of a WLC GUI and must say what a setting does or why clients cannot connect. The reference here is the AireOS WLC (Cisco 3504, 5520, 8540), whose GUI has a top menu: Monitor, WLANs, Controller, Wireless, Security, Management, Commands. A **WLAN** ties together an SSID (the network name clients see), a security policy, a QoS level and a VLAN (through an interface). Before creating the WLAN, the VLAN must exist on the controller as a **dynamic interface** (Controller > Interfaces > New: name, VLAN ID, IP address, mask, gateway, physical port and DHCP server), and the switch trunk toward the WLC must allow that VLAN.

items.title: Create the WLAN
items.body: WLANs > Create New > Go. Choose Type `WLAN`, a **Profile Name** (internal name used by the WLC), the **SSID** (broadcast name, up to 32 characters) and the **WLAN ID** (a number that identifies the WLAN; IDs 1 to 16 are added to the default AP group automatically). Click Apply.

items.title: General tab
items.body: Check **Status: Enabled** (a new WLAN is not active until you do), choose the **Radio Policy** (all bands or a single band), select the **Interface/Interface Group** that maps the WLAN to its VLAN, and decide whether to **Broadcast SSID**.

items.title: Security tab
items.body: Sub-tabs: **Layer 2** (Layer 2 Security such as WPA+WPA2, WPA2 policy with AES encryption, Authentication Key Management `802.1X` or `PSK` with the pre-shared key), **Layer 3** (web authentication or passthrough for guest portals) and **AAA Servers** (which RADIUS servers to use for 802.1X). The default for a new WLAN is WPA2 with AES and 802.1X.

items.title: QoS tab
items.body: Choose the **Quality of Service** profile (Platinum, Gold, Silver, Bronze; Silver by default) and the **WMM Policy** (Disabled, Allowed, Required).

items.title: Advanced tab, then save
items.body: Adjust options such as AAA override, session timeout, client exclusion, maximum clients, DHCP address assignment, FlexConnect local switching. Click **Apply**, then **Save Configuration** so the change survives a reboot.

items.definition: Lets the RADIUS server (for example ISE) return per-user attributes that override the WLAN settings, such as the VLAN, QoS profile or ACL. Disabled by default.
Maximum time a client session lasts before the client must reauthenticate, in seconds (1800 seconds is a common default for 802.1X WLANs).
Clients must obtain their IP address through DHCP; a client with a static IP address is not allowed to pass traffic. Often paired with DHCP server override.
Temporarily blocks clients that repeatedly fail authentication or association.
Limits the number of clients on the WLAN; 0 means no limit.
Lets FlexConnect APs switch this WLAN's traffic locally instead of tunneling it to the WLC.

course_blocks.text: The **Catalyst 9800** (IOS XE) splits the same information into reusable building blocks. The **WLAN profile** holds the SSID and security; the **policy profile** holds the VLAN, QoS, ACLs, session timeout and AAA override; a **policy tag** links WLAN profiles to policy profiles; and the policy tag, a **site tag** and an **RF tag** are assigned to the APs. In its GUI, WLANs are under Configuration > Tags & Profiles > WLANs. The concepts are the same as on AireOS, only the place where you set them changes: on a 9800 the VLAN is not on the WLAN but in the policy profile.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Profile Name and SSID are different fields: the profile name is internal, the SSID is what clients see. A WLAN left with Status unchecked is not broadcast. Changing the QoS profile does not change security, and Silver (not Gold) is the default. On the 9800, look for the VLAN in the policy profile, not in the WLAN.

course_blocks.title: Read the screen
course_blocks.body: A WLAN edit page shows: General tab, Profile Name `CORP`, SSID `Corp-WiFi`, Status `Enabled`, Interface `staff` (VLAN 10). Security > Layer 2: WPA+WPA2, WPA2 Policy checked, AES checked, Auth Key Mgmt `802.1X`. QoS: `Platinum (voice)`. Advanced: Allow AAA Override checked, DHCP Addr. Assignment Required checked. Questions and answers: Which name do users choose on their laptop? `Corp-WiFi`. Do users type a shared password? No, they authenticate individually with 802.1X against a RADIUS server. Why might a user land in VLAN 30 instead of VLAN 10? AAA override is on, so ISE returned VLAN 30 for that user. Why can a laptop with a static IP not reach anything? DHCP address assignment is required. Is Platinum a good choice for a data WLAN? Not ideal: it is meant for voice, Silver fits general data.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: A WLAN = Profile Name (internal) + SSID (broadcast) + WLAN ID; enable it in the General tab.
The interface (dynamic interface) chosen in the General tab maps the WLAN to its VLAN.
Security tab: Layer 2 (WPA2/WPA3, 802.1X or PSK), Layer 3 (web auth), AAA servers.
QoS profiles: Platinum voice, Gold video, Silver best effort (default), Bronze background.
Advanced: AAA override, session timeout, DHCP address assignment, client limits; Catalyst 9800 uses WLAN profile, policy profile and tags.

course_blocks.text: 3.0 IP Connectivity (25%)

This domain is about how a router moves packets between networks: how it reads its routing table, how it picks one route when several match, how you give it routes by hand (static routing), how it learns them automatically with OSPF, and how hosts keep a working default gateway when a router fails (FHRP). At 25% it is the heaviest domain of the exam, and it is tested both with theory questions and with outputs to interpret: a `show ip route`, a `show ip ospf neighbor`, a configuration with one wrong line. What matters most: reading the routing table fluently, the forwarding decision order (longest prefix, then administrative distance, then metric), the static route syntax in IPv4 and IPv6, and the OSPF adjacency rules and DR/BDR election.
3.1 Interpret the components of routing table

The routing table (the RIB, Routing Information Base) is the list of destinations a router knows and, for each one, where to send the packet next. Every IP packet that arrives is compared to this table. If no entry matches and there is no default route, the packet is dropped. Before you can troubleshoot anything in routing, you must be able to read each column of `show ip route` without thinking.

Here is the full table of a router R1 used in a lab. It deliberately mixes several sources (connected, static, OSPF, EIGRP, RIP, BGP) so that you see every code at least once; a real router rarely runs all of them at the same time.

course_blocks.text: 3.1.a Routing protocol code
The letter at the start of each line says **where the route comes from**. The legend at the top of the output lists them all, but the exam expects you to know the common ones by heart.

rows.label: C
values: Connected network: an interface that is up/up with an IP address

rows.label: L
values: Local route: the router's own interface address, always /32 (/128 in IPv6)

rows.label: O
values: OSPF route inside the area (O IA between areas, O E1/E2 external)

rows.label: D
values: EIGRP internal route (D EX is external EIGRP)
Candidate default: this route can be used as the default route

course_blocks.text: The `*` is not a source but a flag added to a code: `S*` is a static default route, `O*E2` is a default route learned through OSPF (for example from a neighbor that runs `default-information originate`).
3.1.b Prefix and 3.1.c Network mask

The **prefix** is the network address of the destination (`10.2.2.0`), and the **mask** is written in prefix-length notation right after it (`/24`). Together they define the range of addresses the route covers: `10.2.2.0/24` covers 10.2.2.0 to 10.2.2.255. The longer the mask, the more specific the route.

IOS groups subnets under their **classful parent network**. The line `10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 9 subnets, 4 masks` is not a route: it is a header that says 'below are 9 subnets of the class A network 10.0.0.0, using 4 different mask lengths' (here /16, /24, /30 and /32). If all the subnets had the same mask, the header would read `10.0.0.0/24 is subnetted, 3 subnets`. A route whose mask equals the classful mask (such as `172.16.0.0/16` or `198.51.100.0/24`) is printed alone, without a header.
3.1.d Next hop

`via 10.1.12.2` is the **next hop**: the IP address of the neighbor router to which R1 hands the packet. It must be reachable, usually on a connected subnet (10.1.12.2 is in 10.1.12.0/30, connected on Gi0/1). The **outgoing interface** at the end of the line (`GigabitEthernet0/1`) is the interface R1 uses to reach that next hop. Connected routes have no next hop: they say `is directly connected, <interface>`.

Some routes show only `via <next hop>` with no interface, like `S 172.16.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.1.12.2`. The router then performs a **recursive lookup**: it looks up 10.1.12.2 in the table, finds the connected route 10.1.12.0/30 on Gi0/1, and sends the packet there.
3.1.e Administrative distance and 3.1.f Metric

The numbers in brackets are `[AD/metric]`. In `[110/2]`, **110 is the administrative distance** (how much the router trusts the source, here OSPF) and **2 is the metric** (the cost of the path as computed by that protocol, here the OSPF cost). Lower is better for both. AD is used to choose between different sources for the same prefix; metric is used to choose between paths from the same source.

Each protocol has its own metric unit, so metrics are never compared across protocols: OSPF uses a cost based on bandwidth (`[110/2]`), EIGRP a composite of bandwidth and delay (`[90/3072]`), RIP a hop count (`[120/2]` means 2 routers away). Static routes show `[1/0]`. Connected and local routes do not show brackets at all; their AD is 0.

After the next hop, dynamic routes show a **timer** (`00:12:45`, `01:02:03`, `2d03h`): how long ago the route was learned or last refreshed. For RIP, which re-advertises every 30 seconds, the value stays under 30 seconds when all is well; a RIP age climbing well past that is a sign that updates are no longer arriving. Static and connected routes have no timer.
3.1.g Gateway of last resort

`Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0` means a default route is installed: any packet that matches no more specific route goes to 203.0.113.1. The default route itself appears as `S* 0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1`. If no default route exists, the line reads `Gateway of last resort is not set`, and packets with an unknown destination are dropped (the router sends an ICMP destination unreachable back).

items.definition: The list of best routes the router has selected, one or more per prefix, displayed by `show ip route`.
The destination network address and the number of network bits in its mask (/24 = 255.255.255.0).
The IP address of the neighbor router that receives the packet next.
Trustworthiness of a route source, 0 to 255, lower is preferred; 255 means never used.
Protocol-specific cost of a path, used to compare routes learned from the same protocol.
A /32 host route for the router's own interface address, used to deliver packets addressed to the router itself.
The next hop of the default route (0.0.0.0/0), used when nothing more specific matches.

course_blocks.text: The IPv6 routing table

`show ipv6 route` carries the same information with a slightly different layout: each route takes two lines, the brackets `[AD/metric]` are shown for every entry (connected and local show `[0/0]`), and next hops are often **link-local addresses** (FE80::...) because IPv6 routing protocols use them to talk to neighbors. There is no 'Gateway of last resort' line in IPv6: the default route is simply `::/0`.

course_blocks.text: 3.2 Determine how a router makes a forwarding decision by default

Two different moments must not be confused. **Building the table**: when several sources offer a route to exactly the same prefix and length, the router keeps the one with the lowest AD, and inside one protocol the one with the lowest metric. **Forwarding a packet**: the router compares the destination address with all the routes in the table and uses the **most specific match**, whatever its AD or metric. Most exam mistakes come from mixing these two steps.

course_blocks.code:
graph TD
  A["Packet arrives, destination IP read"] --> B["Find all routes whose prefix contains the destination"]
  B --> C{"Any match?"}
  C -->|No, no default route| D["Drop packet, send ICMP unreachable"]
  C -->|Yes| E["Keep the match with the longest prefix length"]
  E --> F["Forward to its next hop or exit interface"]
  G["Several sources offer the SAME prefix and length"] --> H["Lowest AD wins the place in the table"]
  H --> I["Same protocol: lowest metric wins, equal metrics give ECMP"]
course_blocks.caption: Forwarding uses longest prefix match; AD and metric only decide which route for a given prefix enters the table.

course_blocks.text: 3.2.a Longest prefix match

A route matches a destination when the first N bits of the destination equal the first N bits of the prefix, N being the prefix length. Several routes can match at once (a /8, a /16, a /24 and the default /0). The router picks the one with the **largest N**, because it describes the destination most precisely. The default route `0.0.0.0/0` matches everything with zero bits, so it is always the last choice.

3.2.b Administrative distance

When two sources know the **same prefix with the same length**, for example OSPF and EIGRP both learn 172.20.0.0/16, the router cannot install both from different protocols. It compares their administrative distance and installs only the lower one. The other route stays in its protocol's database and comes back if the winner disappears.

values: Also 1 when it points to an exit interface

course_blocks.title: Same prefix, two protocols
course_blocks.body: R2 learns 172.20.0.0/16 from OSPF with cost 2 and from EIGRP with metric 2 816 000. The metrics are not comparable. AD decides: EIGRP 90 beats OSPF 110, so the table shows `D 172.20.0.0/16 [90/2816000]`. If R2 also learned 172.20.5.0/24 through OSPF, that /24 would be installed too (different prefix length), and a packet to 172.20.5.9 would follow OSPF because of the longest prefix match.

course_blocks.text: AD is local to the router and can be changed: on a static route by adding a number at the end of the command (this is how a floating static route is built, see 3.3), or for a protocol with the `distance` command under the routing process. Changing it only affects that router's choice.
3.2.c Routing protocol metric

Inside one routing protocol, when several paths lead to the same prefix, the protocol keeps the path with the **lowest metric**: lowest total OSPF cost, lowest EIGRP composite metric, fewest RIP hops. Only that best path is offered to the routing table.

If two or more paths have exactly the same best metric, the router installs all of them and shares traffic between them: this is **ECMP** (Equal-Cost Multi-Path). On IOS, OSPF and EIGRP install up to 4 equal paths by default, adjustable with `maximum-paths` under the routing process. In the table, an ECMP route shows several `via` lines under the same prefix. EIGRP can also do unequal-cost load balancing with the `variance` command, which OSPF cannot.

course_blocks.text: 3.3 Configure and verify IPv4 and IPv6 static routing

A static route is a route you type by hand. It costs no CPU or bandwidth, it is predictable and secure (nothing is advertised), but it does not adapt: if the topology changes, you must edit it yourself. Static routes are ideal for small networks, for stub sites that have a single exit, for a default route toward an Internet provider, and as a backup for a dynamic protocol.

The lab topology for this section: R1 has a LAN on Gi0/0 (192.168.1.0/24), a link to R2 on Gi0/1 (10.0.12.0/30, R2 = 10.0.12.2), a link to R3 on Gi0/2 (10.0.13.0/30, R3 = 10.0.13.2) and an Internet link on Gi0/3 (203.0.113.0/30, ISP = 203.0.113.1). R2's LAN is 192.168.2.0/24.
IPv4 static route syntax: next hop, exit interface, or both

The command is `ip route <network> <mask> {next-hop | exit-interface [next-hop]} [AD]`. The network must be the real network address for that mask; if you type host bits (for example `ip route 192.168.2.1 255.255.255.0 ...`), IOS refuses it with `%Inconsistent address and mask`. There are three ways to say where packets go, and they behave differently.

rows.label: Next hop only
values: Recursive lookup: the router looks up 10.0.12.2 in its table to find the exit interface. Recommended default choice.

rows.label: Exit interface only
values: The destination is treated as if it were on the link. Fine on point-to-point serial links, risky on Ethernet (see below).

rows.label: Fully specified (both)
values: No recursive lookup, and the router ARPs only for the next hop. The most precise form on Ethernet.

course_blocks.text: **Why exit-interface-only is a problem on Ethernet.** With `ip route 192.168.3.0 255.255.255.0 GigabitEthernet0/2`, R1 believes every address in 192.168.3.0/24 is reachable directly on Gi0/2. To send a packet to 192.168.3.25, it sends an ARP request for 192.168.3.25 itself, not for R3. That only works if R3 answers on behalf of the remote host, which is **proxy ARP** (enabled by default on IOS interfaces, but often disabled for security). Without proxy ARP the route is in the table but traffic fails; with it, R1 fills its ARP cache with one entry per remote destination. On a point-to-point link (serial HDLC or PPP) there is only one possible neighbor, so no ARP is needed and the exit-interface form is perfectly fine.

A static route is installed only if it is usable: with a next hop, that address must be reachable through the table; with an exit interface, the interface must be up/up. If the interface goes down, the route disappears from the table automatically (and comes back when it returns). This behavior is what makes floating static routes work.
3.3.a to 3.3.d: the four kinds of static route

items.definition: Matches every destination: `0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0` in IPv4, `::/0` in IPv6. Used as a last resort, typically toward the ISP. Creates the gateway of last resort.
Points to a whole subnet, for example 192.168.2.0/24. The most common static route.
Points to a single address: mask 255.255.255.255 (/32) in IPv4, /128 in IPv6. Being the longest possible prefix, it overrides any network route for that address.
A backup static route configured with an AD higher than the primary route, so it stays out of the table until the primary disappears.

course_blocks.title: Watching the floating route take over
course_blocks.body: The Internet link fails and Gi0/3 goes down. The connected route 203.0.113.0/30 disappears, so the next hop 203.0.113.1 is no longer reachable and the primary default route is removed. The floating route can now enter the table: `show ip route` displays `Gateway of last resort is 10.0.13.2 to network 0.0.0.0` and `S* 0.0.0.0/0 [10/0] via 10.0.13.2`. When Gi0/3 comes back up, the AD 1 route returns and pushes the floating route out again. Note the limit: if the ISP fails further away while Gi0/3 stays up, R1 sees nothing and keeps the primary route (tracking the path, for example with IP SLA, goes beyond the CCNA).

course_blocks.text: A floating static route is also the usual way to back up a dynamic protocol: to back up an OSPF route (AD 110), give the static route an AD above 110, for example `ip route 192.168.50.0 255.255.255.0 10.0.13.2 115`. If you forget the AD, the static route (AD 1) wins immediately and OSPF's route is never used.
IPv6 static routes

IPv6 static routes follow the same logic with the command `ipv6 route <prefix>/<length> {next-hop | exit-interface [next-hop]} [AD]`. Before anything else, the router must be enabled for IPv6 routing with `ipv6 unicast-routing` in global configuration: without it, the router does not forward IPv6 packets between interfaces and does not send Router Advertisements.

The next hop can be the neighbor's global unicast address or its **link-local address**. A link-local address (FE80::/10) exists on every link, so FE80::3 alone is ambiguous: the router cannot know on which interface it lives. That is why a link-local next hop **must** be combined with the exit interface. As in IPv4, avoid exit-interface-only routes on Ethernet and give a next hop.

R1(config)# ipv6 route ::/0 GigabitEthernet0/2 FE80::3 10
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:DB8:2::/64 2001:DB8:12::2
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:DB8:2::50/128 2001:DB8:13::2
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:DB8:3::/64 GigabitEthernet0/2 FE80::3

course_blocks.text: 3.4 Configure and verify single area OSPFv2

OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is an open-standard **link-state** interior routing protocol. OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) carries IPv4 routes; OSPFv3 is its IPv6 version. On the CCNA you must configure OSPFv2 in a **single area** (area 0, the backbone), form neighbor adjacencies, understand the DR/BDR election on Ethernet, change a link to point-to-point, and choose the router ID. It is the dynamic protocol you will meet most often in the exam.
How link-state routing works

A distance-vector protocol such as RIP only tells its neighbors 'I can reach network X at distance Y'. A link-state protocol does something different: every router describes **its own links** (its interfaces, their subnets and costs, its neighbors) in a small record called an **LSA** (Link-State Advertisement) and floods it to all routers of the area. Each router stores all the LSAs it receives in its **LSDB** (Link-State Database). Inside one area, every router ends up with the same LSDB: the same map of the network.

From that map, each router runs the **SPF algorithm** (Dijkstra) with itself as the root, computes the lowest-cost path to every subnet, and offers those best paths to the routing table. In a single area you mainly see two LSA types: **Type 1 (Router LSA)**, sent by every router to describe its links, and **Type 2 (Network LSA)**, sent by the DR to describe a multi-access segment and the routers attached to it.

items.definition: Link-State Advertisement: a piece of topology information (a router's links, a segment) flooded through the area.
Link-State Database: all the LSAs of the area; identical on every router of the area once synchronized.
Algorithm each router runs on its LSDB to compute the lowest-cost path to every destination.
The central OSPF area; in a single-area design, every interface is in area 0.
A 32-bit number written like an IPv4 address that uniquely identifies the router in OSPF.
Type 1 Hello, 2 DBD (Database Description), 3 LSR (Link-State Request), 4 LSU (Link-State Update), 5 LSAck. Carried directly in IP, protocol number 89.
Multicast addresses: AllSPFRouters (all OSPF routers, used for Hellos) and AllDRouters (only the DR and BDR listen).

course_blocks.text: Basic configuration: router ospf, network and interface commands

OSPF runs as a process started with `router ospf <process-id>`. The process ID (1 to 65535) is **locally significant**: two neighbors can use different process IDs and still become neighbors. Then you tell OSPF which interfaces take part, in one of two ways.

items: **`network <address> <wildcard> area <id>`** under the process: every interface whose IP address matches the address/wildcard pair is enabled for OSPF in that area. The wildcard is an inverted mask (0 = must match, 1 = any value). The command does not advertise 'the network you typed': it selects interfaces, and OSPF then advertises each selected interface's real subnet and mask.

**`ip ospf <process-id> area <id>`** in interface configuration: enables OSPF directly on that interface. Clearer and less error-prone; it takes precedence over a `network` statement for that interface.

**`passive-interface <interface>`** under the process: the interface's subnet is still advertised, but no Hellos are sent or accepted on it, so no neighbor can form there. Use it on LAN interfaces where only hosts live. `passive-interface default` makes all interfaces passive, then `no passive-interface <interface>` re-enables the ones toward routers.

course_blocks.title: Which interfaces does a network statement match?
course_blocks.body: R1 has Gi0/0 10.1.123.1/24, Gi0/1 10.1.14.1/30, Gi0/2 10.1.1.1/24 and Gi0/3 203.0.113.2/30. `network 10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0` matches any address starting with 10.1: Gi0/0, Gi0/1 and Gi0/2, not Gi0/3. `network 10.1.14.1 0.0.0.0 area 0` matches exactly one address: only Gi0/1. `network 0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255 area 0` matches every interface, including the Internet link, which is usually not what you want.
