A **VPN** (virtual private network) creates a private, protected path across an untrusted network such as the internet. **IPsec** is a framework of open standards that secures IP packets at Layer 3. It provides **confidentiality** (encryption, for example AES), **integrity** (hashing, for example SHA-256), **authentication** of the peers (pre-shared keys or certificates) and **anti-replay** protection. IPsec is used in two designs: **site-to-site**, which links whole networks, and **remote access**, which connects an individual user.

items.definition: The protocol that authenticates the peers and negotiates the keys and parameters (security associations). Uses UDP 500, and UDP 4500 when NAT traversal is needed. IKEv2 is the current version.
The agreed set of parameters (algorithms, keys, lifetime) used to protect traffic in one direction between two peers.
IP protocol 50. Encrypts and authenticates the payload. The protocol used in practice.
IP protocol 51. Integrity and authentication only, **no encryption**. Breaks with NAT because it also protects the outer IP header.
Wraps ESP inside UDP 4500 so it can cross devices that perform NAT/PAT.

course_blocks.code:
graph LR
  LAN1[HQ LAN 10.1.0.0/16] --> R1[HQ router]
  R1 ==>|IPsec tunnel with ESP| R2[Branch router]
  R1 -.-> NET((Internet))
  NET -.-> R2
  R2 --> LAN2[Branch LAN 10.2.0.0/16]
  PC[Remote laptop with VPN client] ==>|Remote access VPN, IPsec or TLS| FW[HQ VPN headend]
  FW --> LAN1
course_blocks.caption: Site-to-site VPN between two routers, and a remote access VPN from a laptop to a headend.

course_blocks.text: How an IPsec tunnel is built

items.title: Interesting traffic
items.body: A packet that matches the VPN policy (for example 10.1.0.0/16 to 10.2.0.0/16) triggers the negotiation if no tunnel exists yet.

items.title: IKE phase 1 (IKE SA)
items.body: The peers agree on algorithms, run a Diffie-Hellman exchange to create shared keys, and authenticate each other with a pre-shared key or certificates. This builds a secure management channel.

items.title: IKE phase 2 (IPsec SAs)
items.body: Inside that channel, the peers negotiate the IPsec SAs (ESP, encryption and hash algorithms, lifetimes) that will protect user data. IKEv2 uses different names: phase 1 is done by the IKE_SA_INIT and IKE_AUTH exchanges, the first IPsec SA (a CHILD_SA) is created during IKE_AUTH, and further CHILD_SAs use CREATE_CHILD_SA.

items.title: Data transfer
items.body: User packets are encrypted with ESP and sent through the tunnel.

items.title: Rekey or teardown
items.body: SAs expire after their lifetime and are renegotiated, or the tunnel closes when no longer used.

course_blocks.text: ESP vs AH, tunnel vs transport mode

rows.label: Integrity and authentication
values: Yes (including most of the outer IP header)

course_blocks.text: IPsec also has two **modes**. In **tunnel mode**, the whole original packet (header included) is encrypted and placed behind a new IP header whose addresses are the two VPN gateways; this is the normal mode for site-to-site VPNs, because it hides the internal addresses. In **transport mode**, the original IP header is kept and only the payload is protected; it is used between two end hosts, or when another tunnel (such as GRE) already provides the outer header.
GRE over IPsec

Classic IPsec tunnels carry only unicast IP traffic, so routing protocols that rely on multicast (OSPF, EIGRP) cannot run through them. **GRE** (IP protocol 47) can carry multicast and other protocols but has no security. **GRE over IPsec** combines both: routers build a GRE tunnel interface and run their routing protocol over it, and IPsec encrypts the GRE packets, often in transport mode. DMVPN builds on the same idea to create many branch tunnels dynamically.
Remote access VPNs: IPsec and TLS

A remote access VPN connects one user, usually from a laptop or phone, to the company network. The user runs a **VPN client** (for example Cisco Secure Client, formerly AnyConnect) that builds the tunnel to a headend such as a firewall or router. The tunnel can use **IPsec (IKEv2)** or **SSL/TLS** (TCP 443, often with DTLS over UDP 443 for performance). TLS VPNs are popular because port 443 crosses almost any firewall or hotel network. A **clientless** TLS VPN needs only a web browser but gives access only to web-based resources.

rows.label: Connects
values: Two or more networks (HQ and branches)
One user device to a network

rows.label: Tunnel endpoints
values: Routers or firewalls on each site
VPN client software and a headend

rows.label: Users see the VPN?
values: Yes, the user starts the client

rows.label: Typical protocols
values: IPsec (often tunnel mode), GRE over IPsec, DMVPN

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: AH provides **no encryption**: if a question asks which IPsec protocol gives confidentiality, the answer is ESP. Do not confuse IKE (UDP 500/4500, key negotiation) with ESP (IP protocol 50, not a TCP or UDP port). And in a site-to-site VPN the end hosts need no VPN software: the gateways do all the work.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: IPsec provides confidentiality, integrity, peer authentication and anti-replay at Layer 3.
IKE negotiates keys over UDP 500, or UDP 4500 with NAT traversal; ESP is IP protocol 50, AH is 51 and does not encrypt.
Tunnel mode adds a new IP header (site-to-site); transport mode keeps the original header (host to host, GRE over IPsec).
GRE over IPsec lets routing protocols and multicast cross an encrypted tunnel.
Remote access VPNs use a client with IPsec IKEv2 or TLS (TCP 443); site-to-site VPNs are transparent to hosts.

course_blocks.text: 5.6 Configure and verify access control lists

An **access control list (ACL)** is an ordered list of permit and deny statements that a router uses to classify packets. Applied to an interface, it filters traffic in one direction. ACLs are also used to select traffic for other features (NAT, QoS, vty access, route filtering), but on the CCNA they mainly appear as **packet filters**. To master them you need three skills: write the right matching criteria (wildcard masks), put the lines in the right order, and apply the ACL on the right interface and direction.

items.definition: One line of an ACL: a permit or deny action plus matching conditions.
A 32-bit mask where a 0 bit means 'this bit must match' and a 1 bit means 'ignore this bit'.
An invisible `deny any` (or `deny ip any any`) at the end of every ACL.
Inbound ACLs check packets as they arrive on the interface, before routing; outbound ACLs check packets about to leave it, after routing.
The position of each ACE (10, 20, 30... by default), used to insert or delete lines.

course_blocks.text: Standard, extended, numbered and named ACLs

rows.label: Matches on
values: Protocol, source and destination addresses, source and destination ports, ICMP type, and more

rows.label: Placement rule
values: As close as possible to the **destination**
As close as possible to the **source**

rows.label: Typical use
values: vty access (`access-class`), NAT, simple source filtering
Precise traffic filtering (allow web, block Telnet...)

course_blocks.text: **Named** ACLs work exactly like numbered ones, but a descriptive name (such as `ENG-TO-SERVERS`) replaces the number, and they are configured in a sub-mode where each line gets a sequence number you can edit. On current IOS you can also enter that sub-mode for a numbered ACL (`ip access-list standard 10`), so editing by sequence number works for both.
Wildcard masks

A wildcard mask looks like an inverted subnet mask, and for a whole subnet it is exactly that: **0 = must match, 1 = don't care**. The keyword `host 10.1.1.1` is a shortcut for `10.1.1.1 0.0.0.0` (match one address), and `any` is a shortcut for `0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255` (match everything). In a standard numbered ACL, an address with no wildcard (`access-list 10 permit 10.1.1.1`) is treated as a host.

items.title: Start from the subnet mask
items.body: Write the mask of the network you want to match. Example: 192.168.10.64/26, mask 255.255.255.192.

items.title: Write the ACE with the network address
For a range, use block size minus one
items.body: To match 172.16.32.0 to 172.16.47.255, the third octet spans 16 values (32 to 47), so that octet of the wildcard is 15: **172.16.32.0 0.0.15.255**. This only works when the range size is a power of 2 and starts on a multiple of it.

course_blocks.text: Processing order and the implicit deny

course_blocks.caption: An ACL is read top-down and stops at the first match; a packet that matches nothing is dropped.

course_blocks.text: Three consequences follow. First, **put specific lines before general ones**: a `deny 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255` placed after `permit any` is never reached. Second, every ACL needs **at least one permit**, otherwise the implicit deny drops everything. Third, the implicit deny has no hit counter in `show access-lists`; add an explicit `deny ip any any log` at the end if you want to count or log dropped packets. Also note that an interface accepts **one ACL per direction per protocol** (one IPv4 in, one IPv4 out), and an outbound ACL does not filter packets generated by the router itself.
Example 1: standard numbered ACL

Topology for the examples: R1 has the Sales LAN 192.168.10.0/24 on G0/0 and the Engineering LAN 192.168.20.0/24 on G0/1, and connects to R2. R2 has the server LAN 10.0.0.0/24 on G0/0, with a web server at 10.0.0.10. Goal: Sales must not reach the server LAN; everyone else may. A standard ACL only sees the source, so it goes **near the destination**, outbound on R2 G0/0. Placed on R1, it would also block Sales from every other destination.

course_blocks.content:
R2(config)# access-list 10 remark Block Sales from the server LAN
R2(config)# access-list 10 deny 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config)# access-list 10 permit any
R2(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R2(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out

course_blocks.text: Example 2: extended named ACL

Goal: Engineering may reach the web server 10.0.0.10 on HTTP (TCP 80) and HTTPS (TCP 443) and ping it, but nothing else on the server LAN; all other traffic stays allowed. An extended ACL can match the destination, so it goes **near the source**, inbound on R1 G0/1, which drops unwanted packets before they cross the WAN. The extended syntax is: action, protocol, source and wildcard, optional source port, destination and wildcard, optional destination port (`eq`, `neq`, `lt`, `gt`, `range`).

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# ip access-list extended ENG-TO-SERVERS
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.10 eq www
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.10 eq 443
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit icmp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.10 echo
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 log
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group ENG-TO-SERVERS in

course_blocks.text: Editing a named ACL with sequence numbers

The lines above received sequence numbers 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50. A new requirement allows SSH (TCP 22) to the server: it must sit **before** the deny at 40, so insert it as 35. To delete a line, type `no` followed by its number. `ip access-list resequence` renumbers the list (start at 10, step 10) when the gaps run out. With the old numbered syntax (`access-list 101 ...` in global mode), new lines are always added at the end, and `no access-list 101` deletes the **whole** ACL.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# ip access-list extended ENG-TO-SERVERS
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 35 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.10 eq 22
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 30
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# ip access-list resequence ENG-TO-SERVERS 10 10

course_blocks.text: Example 3: securing vty lines with access-class

To limit who can open SSH or Telnet sessions **to the router itself**, apply a standard ACL to the vty lines with `access-class ... in`, not to an interface with `ip access-group`. It filters on the source address of the management session, whatever interface it arrives on. Apply it to all vty lines (0 to 15 on most devices), or attackers simply use a line you forgot.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# ip access-list standard MGMT-HOSTS
R1(config-std-nacl)# permit 192.168.99.0 0.0.0.15
R1(config-std-nacl)# deny any log
R1(config-std-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# line vty 0 15
R1(config-line)# access-class MGMT-HOSTS in

course_blocks.text: Verification

course_blocks.content:
R1# show access-lists
Standard IP access list MGMT-HOSTS
    10 permit 192.168.99.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.15 (6 matches)
    20 deny   any log (2 matches)
Extended IP access list ENG-TO-SERVERS
    10 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.10 eq www (152 matches)
    20 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.10 eq 443 (1310 matches)
    30 permit tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.0.0.10 eq 22 (24 matches)
    40 deny ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255 log (12 matches)
    50 permit ip any any (8734 matches)

R1# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/1 | include access list
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is ENG-TO-SERVERS

R1# clear access-list counters ENG-TO-SERVERS

course_blocks.text: `show access-lists` lists every ACL with its sequence numbers and a **match counter** per line: a line stuck at zero is either useless or shadowed by an earlier line, and an unexpected counter rising on a deny line explains why users complain. Notice that the resequence turned 35 into 30 and that the deleted ping line is gone. `show ip interface` confirms which ACL is applied and in which direction (`show running-config` shows the `ip access-group` command too). `clear access-list counters` resets the counters before a test.

course_blocks.title: Find the bug
course_blocks.body: An admin wants to block host 192.168.10.50 and allow the rest of 192.168.10.0/24, and writes: `access-list 20 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255` then `access-list 20 deny host 192.168.10.50`, applied outbound toward the servers. Host .50 still gets through. Why? The first line already matches .50 and permits it; the deny is never reached. Fix: put the `deny host 192.168.10.50` first, then the permit for the subnet. With a named or sequence-numbered ACL you can simply insert the deny as line 5.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Watch for: a **subnet mask** written where a wildcard is expected (`192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0` matches almost nothing useful); an ACL with only deny lines (the implicit deny then blocks everything); a standard ACL placed near the source (it blocks too much); `access-class` versus `ip access-group` (lines versus interfaces); and the direction: `in` is traffic entering the interface from the attached link, `out` is traffic leaving toward that link.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Standard ACLs (1-99, 1300-1999) match source only and go near the destination; extended ACLs (100-199, 2000-2699) go near the source.
Wildcard = 255.255.255.255 minus the subnet mask; `host` = 0.0.0.0, `any` = 255.255.255.255.
Top-down, first match wins, implicit deny at the end: specific lines first, at least one permit.
Apply with `ip access-group NAME in|out` on an interface, or `access-class NAME in` on vty lines; one ACL per interface, direction and protocol.
Edit named ACLs by sequence number; verify with `show access-lists` (hit counters) and `show ip interface`.

course_blocks.text: 5.7 Configure and verify Layer 2 security features (DHCP snooping, dynamic ARP inspection, and port security)

Access switches trust whatever a connected device says by default: any PC can answer DHCP requests, send fake ARP replies or flood the MAC table. Three Catalyst features close these holes and build on each other. **DHCP snooping** stops rogue DHCP servers and records who received which address. **Dynamic ARP inspection (DAI)** uses that record to drop forged ARP messages. **Port security** limits which and how many MAC addresses may use a port.
DHCP snooping

Once enabled, every port is **untrusted** by default. On an untrusted port the switch drops **DHCP server messages** (OFFER, ACK, NAK), so a rogue server plugged into a user port cannot hand out addresses or a fake gateway. You mark as **trusted** only the ports that lead to the real DHCP server: usually the uplinks. The switch also watches the exchanges and builds the **binding table**: client MAC, leased IP, lease time, VLAN and port. It can additionally **rate-limit** DHCP packets on untrusted ports to stop starvation attacks (a client requesting thousands of leases with fake MACs); a port that exceeds the limit is err-disabled.

course_blocks.code:
graph LR
  DS[Legitimate DHCP server] --- R1[Router / relay]
  R1 --- G01[SW1 Gi0/1: TRUSTED]
  G01 --- SW1((SW1))
  SW1 --- F01[Fa0/1: untrusted]
  F01 --- PC[User PC]
  SW1 --- F05[Fa0/5: untrusted]
  F05 --- ROGUE[Rogue DHCP server]
  ROGUE -. OFFER dropped .-> F05
course_blocks.caption: Only the trusted uplink may carry DHCP server messages; offers from the rogue server are dropped.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10,20
SW1(config)# no ip dhcp snooping information option
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# description Uplink toward the DHCP server
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range FastEthernet0/1 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15

SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
Switch DHCP snooping is enabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
10,20
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
10,20
Insertion of option 82 is disabled
Verification of hwaddr field is enabled
Interface                  Trusted    Allow option    Rate limit (pps)
-----------------------    -------    ------------    ----------------
GigabitEthernet0/1         yes        yes             unlimited
FastEthernet0/1            no         no              15
FastEthernet0/5            no         no              15

SW1# show ip dhcp snooping binding
MacAddress          IpAddress        Lease(sec)  Type           VLAN  Interface
------------------  ---------------  ----------  -------------  ----  --------------------
00:50:56:A1:12:34   192.168.10.21    86120       dhcp-snooping   10    FastEthernet0/1
00:50:56:A1:56:78   192.168.20.33    85977       dhcp-snooping   20    FastEthernet0/9
Total number of bindings: 2

course_blocks.text: Check three things: the feature is enabled **and** operational on the right VLANs (both commands, global and per VLAN, are required); only the uplink shows `Trusted yes`; and the binding table fills up as clients get addresses. An empty binding table usually means the uplink is not trusted, so the real server's offers are being dropped too.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap: option 82
course_blocks.body: By default the switch inserts DHCP **option 82** (relay agent information) into client requests. When the DHCP server is an IOS router reached without a real relay, it may drop these requests and clients get no address. The usual fix on the access switch is `no ip dhcp snooping information option`, which is why it appears in the configuration above.

course_blocks.text: Dynamic ARP inspection (DAI)

ARP has no authentication, so an attacker can send gratuitous ARP replies saying 'the gateway's IP is at my MAC' and become a man-in-the-middle. DAI intercepts every ARP message on **untrusted** ports and checks the sender IP and MAC against the **DHCP snooping binding table**; mismatches are dropped and logged. That is why DAI depends on DHCP snooping. Hosts with **static IP addresses** have no binding, so you allow them with an **ARP ACL**. Uplinks to other switches and routers are set as **trusted**, so their ARP traffic is not checked. Untrusted ports are rate-limited to **15 ARP packets per second** by default; above that, the port is err-disabled. The optional `validate` command adds checks on source MAC, destination MAC and IP addresses.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 10,20
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip
SW1(config)# arp access-list STATIC-HOSTS
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# permit ip host 192.168.10.5 mac host 0011.2233.4455
SW1(config-arp-nacl)# exit
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection filter STATIC-HOSTS vlan 10
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip arp inspection trust

SW1# show ip arp inspection interfaces
 Interface        Trust State     Rate (pps)    Burst Interval
 ---------------  -----------     ----------    --------------
 Gi0/1            Trusted               None               N/A
 Fa0/1            Untrusted               15                 1
 Fa0/5            Untrusted               15                 1

SW1# show ip arp inspection vlan 10
Source Mac Validation      : Enabled
Destination Mac Validation : Enabled
IP Address Validation      : Enabled

 Vlan     Configuration    Operation   ACL Match          Static ACL
 ----     -------------    ---------   ---------          ----------
   10     Enabled          Active      STATIC-HOSTS       No

SW1# show ip arp inspection statistics vlan 10
 Vlan      Forwarded        Dropped     DHCP Drops      ACL Drops
 ----      ---------        -------     ----------      ---------
   10           1342             27             27              0

course_blocks.text: The uplink is trusted with no rate limit, user ports are untrusted at the default 15 pps, DAI is `Active` on VLAN 10 with the ARP ACL attached, and 27 ARP packets were dropped because they did not match any DHCP binding: a sign of spoofing, or of a static host you forgot to add to the ARP ACL.
Port security

Port security limits the source MAC addresses allowed on an access port. It stops MAC flooding attacks (filling the MAC table so the switch floods traffic like a hub) and unauthorized devices such as a personal switch under a desk. Defaults once enabled: **maximum 1 MAC**, violation mode **shutdown**, no aging. Secure addresses can be static (typed by hand), dynamic (learned, lost on reboot) or **sticky** (learned and written into the running configuration, kept after a reboot if you save the config). The port must be a **static access** (or trunk) port: on a dynamic (DTP auto/desirable) port the command is rejected.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# interface FastEthernet0/5
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security maximum 2
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security mac-address sticky
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security violation restrict
SW1(config-if)# exit
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation
SW1(config)# errdisable recovery interval 300

SW1# show port-security interface FastEthernet0/5
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-up
Violation Mode             : Restrict
Aging Time                 : 0 mins
Aging Type                 : Absolute
SecureStatic Address Aging : Disabled
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 2
Total MAC Addresses        : 2
Configured MAC Addresses   : 0
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 2
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0050.56a1.9abc:10
Security Violation Count   : 3

SW1# show running-config interface FastEthernet0/5 | include sticky
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky 0050.56a1.1234
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky 0050.56a1.5678

SW1# show interfaces status err-disabled
Port      Name               Status       Reason               Err-disabled Vlans
Fa0/7                        err-disabled psecure-violation

course_blocks.text: On Fa0/5 the two allowed MACs were learned as sticky and appear in the running configuration; a third device tried to send frames; in restrict mode each dropped frame increments the counter (here **3 violations**), but the port stays `Secure-up`. On Fa0/7, which uses the default shutdown mode, a violation put the port in **err-disabled**; `show port-security interface Fa0/7` would show `Port Status: Secure-shutdown`.

items.title: Find the cause
items.body: Use `show interfaces status err-disabled` or `show port-security` to see which port and which reason (psecure-violation, dhcp-rate-limit, arp-inspection...).

items.title: Remove the offending device
items.body: Otherwise the port fails again as soon as it comes back up.

items.title: Recover manually
items.body: Enter the interface and type `shutdown` then `no shutdown`.

items.title: Or recover automatically
items.body: `errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation` brings the port back after `errdisable recovery interval` seconds (300 by default).

course_blocks.title: Design exercise
course_blocks.body: Each office desk has an IP phone with a PC plugged behind it, on access port Fa0/10 (data VLAN 10, voice VLAN 110). The security policy says: only those two devices, learned automatically, kept after reboot, and keep the phone working if a stranger plugs in. Answer: `switchport port-security`, `maximum 2` (phone and PC), `mac-address sticky`, and `violation restrict` (or `protect` if no logging is wanted) so a violation does not cut the phone, then save the configuration so the sticky addresses survive a reload. Add DHCP snooping and DAI on VLANs 10 and 110 with the uplink trusted.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Classic mistakes: enabling DAI without DHCP snooping (all dynamic hosts' ARP is then dropped, since there are no bindings); forgetting to trust the uplink (legitimate DHCP offers and ARP from the router are blocked); configuring `switchport port-security maximum` without the plain `switchport port-security` command (the feature stays off); and mixing up **protect** (silent) and **restrict** (logs and counts). Sticky MACs are only in the running-config until you save.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: DHCP snooping: all ports untrusted by default, server messages dropped on untrusted ports, binding table built from DHCP exchanges, optional rate limit.
DAI checks ARP on untrusted ports against the snooping bindings; static hosts need an ARP ACL; default limit 15 pps.
Port security defaults: max 1 MAC, violation shutdown; sticky learns MACs into the running-config.
Protect drops silently, restrict drops and logs and counts, shutdown err-disables the port.
Recover err-disabled ports with shutdown / no shutdown or `errdisable recovery` (300 s default).

course_blocks.text: 5.8 Compare authentication, authorization, and accounting concepts

**AAA** answers three questions in order. **Authentication**: who are you? (prove your identity with a username and password, a certificate, a token). **Authorization**: what are you allowed to do? (privilege level, which commands, which VLAN or network access). **Accounting**: what did you do? (login and logout times, commands entered, data used), recorded for audits and troubleshooting. Instead of keeping user accounts on every device, a network uses a central AAA server such as Cisco ISE, which speaks **RADIUS** and **TACACS+**.

items.definition: Verifying the identity of a user or device.
Deciding which resources and actions the authenticated identity may use.
Recording what the user did and when, for auditing and billing.
An ordered list of AAA sources to try (for example TACACS+ group, then the local database).

rows.label: AAA functions
values: Authentication and authorization combined; accounting separate

rows.label: Command authorization
values: Yes, each CLI command can be checked

rows.label: Origin
values: Cisco-developed, now documented in an informational RFC

rows.label: Typical use
values: Device administration: admins logging into routers and switches

course_blocks.text: The example enables AAA, defines a TACACS+ server for administrator logins on the vty lines with the local database as backup, records every level 15 command, and also shows how a RADIUS server is declared. Create the local user **before** `aaa new-model`, so you never lock yourself out. The `local` method is used only if the server **does not answer**: if the server answers and rejects the password, the login fails and the local database is not tried.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# username fallback privilege 15 algorithm-type scrypt secret Fallb4ck-Only!
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# tacacs server TAC-1
R1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.0.0.50
R1(config-server-tacacs)# key T4cacs-Shared-Key
R1(config-server-tacacs)# exit
R1(config)# radius server RAD-1
R1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.0.0.51 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
R1(config-radius-server)# key R4dius-Shared-Key
R1(config-radius-server)# exit
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-AUTH group tacacs+ local
R1(config)# aaa authorization exec VTY-AUTH group tacacs+ local
R1(config)# aaa accounting commands 15 default start-stop group tacacs+
R1(config)# line vty 0 15
R1(config-line)# login authentication VTY-AUTH
R1(config-line)# authorization exec VTY-AUTH

course_blocks.title: Classify each action
course_blocks.body: An engineer types her username and password: **authentication**. The server answers that she gets privilege level 15 but may not use `reload`: **authorization**. The server logs that she ran `configure terminal` at 14:02 and logged out at 14:20: **accounting**. A company that wants per-command control and a full audit of admin sessions chooses **TACACS+**; for Wi-Fi users authenticated with 802.1X it uses **RADIUS**.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: RADIUS uses **UDP** and encrypts **only the password**; TACACS+ uses **TCP 49** and encrypts the **whole payload**. RADIUS combines authentication and authorization, TACACS+ separates all three. A question about 'separate authorization of each command entered by an administrator' points to TACACS+.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Authentication = who you are, authorization = what you may do, accounting = what you did.
RADIUS: open standard, UDP 1812/1813, encrypts only the password, combines authN and authZ, used for network access.
TACACS+: Cisco, TCP 49, encrypts the whole payload, separates the three A's, used for device administration.
`aaa new-model` enables AAA; method lists define the order (server group, then local).
The local fallback is used only when the server does not respond, not when it rejects the user.

course_blocks.text: 5.9 Describe wireless security protocols (WPA, WPA2, and WPA3)

Radio waves cross walls, so anyone nearby can capture Wi-Fi frames. Wireless security must therefore **authenticate** clients and **encrypt** traffic. The original WEP did both badly and is broken. The Wi-Fi Alliance then certified three generations: **WPA**, **WPA2** and **WPA3**. Each comes in two flavors: **Personal**, where everyone shares a passphrase, and **Enterprise**, where each user authenticates individually with **802.1X/EAP** against a RADIUS server.

items.definition: Temporal Key Integrity Protocol: WPA's stopgap encryption, still based on RC4 so it could run on WEP hardware. Deprecated.
Counter Mode with CBC-MAC Protocol: AES-based encryption and integrity, mandatory in WPA2.
Galois/Counter Mode Protocol: a stronger and more efficient AES mode; GCMP-256 is used by WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode.
Simultaneous Authentication of Equals: the WPA3-Personal handshake that replaces PSK key derivation, resists offline dictionary attacks and provides forward secrecy.
Protected Management Frames: protects deauthentication and disassociation frames against forgery. Optional in WPA2, mandatory in WPA3.
Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (Wi-Fi Enhanced Open): encrypts open networks without a password, but does not authenticate users.

rows.label: Encryption
values: CCMP with AES-128 (TKIP only for backward compatibility)

course_blocks.text: In **Personal** mode (WPA2-PSK), the passphrase and the SSID produce the master key, and the client and AP prove they know it in the **4-way handshake**, which then derives fresh session keys. An attacker who captures that handshake can try passwords offline, which is why short passphrases are dangerous; SAE in WPA3 removes this weakness. In **Enterprise** mode, 802.1X uses three roles: the **supplicant** (client), the **authenticator** (AP or WLC) and the **authentication server** (RADIUS). The EAP method (PEAP, EAP-TLS, EAP-FAST...) carries the credentials, each user gets unique keys, and an employee who leaves is simply disabled on the server.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Match encryption to generation: **TKIP = WPA**, **CCMP/AES = WPA2**, **SAE + mandatory PMF = WPA3**. 'Personal' versus 'Enterprise' is about **authentication** (shared key versus 802.1X with RADIUS), not about the strength of encryption. OWE encrypts an open network but does not authenticate anyone.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: WPA used TKIP (RC4) and is obsolete; WPA2 (802.11i) uses CCMP with AES; WPA3 adds SAE, GCMP-256 for 192-bit Enterprise and mandatory PMF.
Personal = shared passphrase (PSK or SAE); Enterprise = 802.1X/EAP with a RADIUS server and per-user keys.
802.1X roles: supplicant, authenticator, authentication server.
A captured WPA2-PSK handshake allows offline guessing; SAE prevents it and adds forward secrecy.
OWE (Enhanced Open) encrypts open networks without authentication.

course_blocks.text: 5.10 Configure and verify WLAN within the GUI using WPA2 PSK

On the exam, wireless configuration is done in the **GUI of a wireless LAN controller (WLC)**, typically the classic AireOS interface. A WLAN ties an **SSID** to a **dynamic interface** (and so to a VLAN) and to a security policy. Before you start, the dynamic interface for the user VLAN should exist (Controller > Interfaces), with its VLAN, IP address and DHCP server. The steps below create a WPA2-Personal WLAN with AES and a pre-shared key.

items.title: Create the WLAN
items.body: Open the **WLANs** tab, choose **Create New** in the drop-down menu and click **Go**. Set Type to WLAN, enter a **Profile Name** (for example STAFF), the **SSID** clients will see, and an **ID**, then click **Apply**.

items.title: General tab
items.body: On the edit page, check **Status: Enabled** (a new WLAN is disabled until you do), select the **Interface/Interface Group** that maps the WLAN to the right VLAN, keep **Broadcast SSID** checked, and choose the radio policy (all bands, or 2.4 or 5 GHz only).

items.title: Security > Layer 2
items.body: Open **Security**, then **Layer 2**. Set **Layer 2 Security** to **WPA+WPA2**. In the WPA+WPA2 parameters, check **WPA2 Policy**, check **AES** as WPA2 encryption, and leave WPA Policy and TKIP unchecked.

items.title: Authentication Key Management
items.body: Under **Authentication Key Management**, uncheck **802.1X** (the default) and enable **PSK**. Set **PSK Format** to **ASCII** and type the passphrase: **8 to 63 characters** (or exactly 64 hexadecimal characters with the HEX format).

items.title: Check the other tabs and apply
items.body: Leave **Layer 3** security at None, adjust QoS and Advanced settings if needed, click **Apply** and confirm. Save the configuration (Save Configuration at the top of the page) so it survives a reboot.

items.title: Verify
items.body: The **WLANs** list should show the WLAN with Admin Status **Enabled** and Security Policies **[WPA2][Auth(PSK)]**. Connect a client, then open **Monitor > Clients** to see its MAC address, AP, WLAN/SSID, IP address and status (Associated, policy RUN).

course_blocks.text: The same checks exist on the AireOS command line, which is handy to confirm what the GUI shows.

course_blocks.content:
(Cisco Controller) >show wlan summary

Number of WLANs.................................. 1

WLAN ID  WLAN Profile Name / SSID               Status    Interface Name
-------  -------------------------------------  --------  --------------------
1        STAFF / STAFF                          Enabled   staff-vlan10

(Cisco Controller) >show client summary

Number of Clients................................ 1

MAC Address       AP Name           Slot Status        WLAN  Auth Protocol
----------------- ----------------- ---- ------------- ----- ---- ----------------
a4:5e:60:12:34:56 AP-FLOOR1          1   Associated     1    Yes  802.11ac(5 GHz)

course_blocks.text: Note: the Catalyst 9800 controller

On a Catalyst 9800 (IOS XE), the WLAN is created under **Configuration > Tags & Profiles > WLANs > + Add**. The General tab holds the profile name, SSID, WLAN ID, status and broadcast setting; the **Security > Layer2** tab offers WPA2 policy, AES (CCMP128) encryption, **PSK** as Auth Key Mgmt and the pre-shared key format and value. Click **Apply to Device**. The big difference: the VLAN is not set in the WLAN. A **policy profile** holds the VLAN, and a **policy tag** maps the WLAN to that policy profile; the tag is then assigned to the access points. Clients appear under **Monitoring > Wireless > Clients**. The equivalent CLI looks like this:

course_blocks.content:
WLC9800(config)# wlan STAFF 1 STAFF
WLC9800(config-wlan)# no security wpa akm dot1x
WLC9800(config-wlan)# security wpa akm psk
WLC9800(config-wlan)# security wpa psk set-key ascii 0 Correct-Horse-Battery-42
WLC9800(config-wlan)# no shutdown

course_blocks.title: Troubleshooting case
course_blocks.body: Users see the SSID STAFF but every connection fails, and the WLAN list shows [WPA2][Auth(802.1X)]. Cause: in Authentication Key Management, 802.1X was left enabled and PSK was never selected, so the controller expects a RADIUS login that the clients cannot provide. Fix: uncheck 802.1X, enable PSK, enter the ASCII key, Apply. Another case: the SSID is not visible at all. Check that Status is Enabled on the General tab and that Broadcast SSID is checked.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: A new AireOS WLAN defaults to **WPA2 with 802.1X**, not PSK: you must switch Auth Key Management to PSK. The ASCII passphrase is **8 to 63** characters (64 only in HEX). The interface chosen on the General tab decides the clients' VLAN and subnet. And the WLAN does nothing until **Status: Enabled** is checked.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: AireOS path: WLANs > Create New > Go, then profile name, SSID, ID, Apply.
General tab: Status Enabled, interface (VLAN), Broadcast SSID.
Security > Layer 2: WPA+WPA2, WPA2 Policy with AES, Auth Key Mgmt PSK instead of 802.1X, ASCII key of 8 to 63 characters.
Verify in the WLANs list ([WPA2][Auth(PSK)]) and Monitor > Clients, or with `show wlan summary` and `show client summary`.
On the 9800, the WLAN profile holds security, the policy profile holds the VLAN, and the policy tag links them to the APs.

course_blocks.text: 6.0 Automation and Programmability (10%)

This domain moves from configuring one device at a time to managing the network as a system through software. It covers why automation matters, how controller-based and software-defined networks differ from traditional ones, the role of AI and machine learning in operations, REST APIs, configuration management tools such as Ansible and Terraform, and how to read JSON. The exam does not ask you to write programs: it checks that you **recognize** concepts, vocabulary and data formats. Expect questions that compare two approaches (traditional vs controller-based, northbound vs southbound, Ansible vs Terraform, PUT vs PATCH) and questions that show a JSON snippet or an HTTP exchange and ask you to interpret it.
6.1 Explain how automation impacts network management

In a traditional network, an engineer connects to each router or switch over SSH and types commands. That works for ten devices. With five hundred devices, the same change takes days, every engineer types it slightly differently, and a single typo (a wrong VLAN number, a missing `no shutdown`) can cause an outage. Network automation replaces repetitive manual work with software that applies a defined configuration, collects data and checks results, the same way every time.

The key idea is that the desired state of the network is described once, in a template, a playbook or a controller policy, and software takes care of pushing it to every device. The configuration becomes data that can be stored in version control (Git), reviewed before it is applied and rolled back if needed.

items: **Consistency**: every device receives the same standard configuration, built from the same template.
**Speed and agility**: a change that took days by hand is deployed to hundreds of devices in minutes, so new sites and services come online faster.
**Fewer human errors**: no retyping, so no typos; changes can be validated (syntax, pre-checks, post-checks) before and after deployment.
**Scale**: the effort to configure 1,000 devices is close to the effort to configure 10, because the tool does the repetition.
**Less configuration drift**: automation can compare the running configuration with the intended one and report or correct differences.
**Compliance and auditing**: you can prove that every device follows the security baseline (SSH only, NTP, logging, banners) and keep a history of who changed what.
**Operational cost**: engineers spend less time on repetitive tasks and more on design and troubleshooting.

items.definition: Using software to configure, manage, test and operate network devices with little or no manual intervention.
The gradual divergence between a device's actual configuration and the intended standard, usually caused by one-off manual changes.
The configuration the network should have, described in templates, playbooks or controller policies.
Managing infrastructure through machine-readable definition files kept under version control, instead of manual commands.
Checking that devices meet a defined policy (security, regulatory or internal standard) and reporting exceptions.

rows.label: Time per change
values: Grows with the number of devices

rows.label: Error risk
values: Low once the template is tested

course_blocks.title: Rotating an SNMP community on 300 switches
course_blocks.body: A security audit requires replacing an old SNMP community string on 300 access switches. Manually, at about 3 minutes per switch, that is 15 hours of repetitive typing, with a real chance of skipping a switch or mistyping the new string. With an automation tool, the engineer updates one variable, runs the job against the inventory of 300 switches, and gets a report listing any device that failed. A second run in check mode confirms that no switch still has the old string: the change is faster, consistent and provable for the auditor.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Automation does not remove the need for networking knowledge, and it does not make errors impossible: a wrong template is applied everywhere, very quickly. That is why automated changes are tested in a lab or in check mode first. Also, automation reduces configuration drift, it does not "increase flexibility for manual changes": manual one-off changes are exactly what causes drift.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Automation applies a defined intended state to many devices through software instead of manual CLI.
Main benefits: consistency, speed, fewer human errors, scale, compliance and lower operating cost.
Configuration drift is the gap between actual and intended configuration; automation detects and corrects it.
Configurations become versioned data (Infrastructure as Code), which gives an audit trail and easy rollback.
A bad template spreads fast: test automated changes before deploying them.

course_blocks.text: 6.2 Compare traditional networks with controller-based networking

In a **traditional network**, every router and switch is an independent box. Each one runs its own control plane: it exchanges OSPF or STP messages with its neighbors and computes its own forwarding decisions. This is a **distributed control plane**. Management is also distributed: an engineer configures each device separately through the CLI (box-by-box), and the overall policy exists only as the sum of hundreds of individual configurations.

In a **controller-based network**, a software controller has a network-wide view. The administrator expresses what the network should do (for example "guests can reach the Internet but not the servers"), and the controller translates that intent into device configurations and pushes them through southbound APIs. Depending on the solution, the controller centralizes management and policy only, or also takes over part or all of the control plane decisions. The data plane stays on the devices, which keep forwarding traffic at hardware speed.

rows.label: Control plane
values: Distributed: each device decides on its own
Centralized (logically) in the controller, fully or partly

rows.label: Configuration method
values: Policy defined once in the controller GUI or API

rows.label: Network view
values: Each device sees only itself and its neighbors
Global, end-to-end view in one place

rows.label: Consistency
values: Prone to drift and human error

rows.label: Programmability
values: Northbound REST API for scripts and applications

rows.label: Troubleshooting
values: Device by device, with show commands
Centralized assurance, telemetry and path analysis

items.definition: Each device runs its own control protocols and builds its own tables, as in a classic OSPF or STP network.
Software (often on a server or appliance) that holds a network-wide view, stores policy and programs the devices. Examples: Cisco Catalyst Center, Cisco APIC, a WLC for access points.
Approach where the administrator states the business intent and the system translates, deploys and continuously verifies it.
One place (the controller) from which the whole network is configured and monitored.

course_blocks.title: Adding a new VLAN to 40 branch switches
course_blocks.body: Traditional way: open 40 SSH sessions, type `vlan 30` and `name VOICE`, add the VLAN to every trunk, then verify each switch with `show vlan brief` and `show interfaces trunk`. Controller-based way: create the VLAN or the segment once in the controller, select the 40 sites, and let the controller provision every switch and report success or failure for each one. The result is the same VLAN everywhere, deployed in minutes, with a central record of the change.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: A controller does not forward user traffic. The data plane remains on the switches and routers; if the controller becomes unreachable, devices keep forwarding with the configuration they already have (you just lose central management and new changes). Also remember that "centralized" means logically centralized: controllers are usually deployed as clusters for redundancy.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Traditional networks: distributed control plane and box-by-box CLI management.
Controller-based networks: a central controller with a global view translates policy into device configurations.
The data plane always stays on the devices; the controller is not in the traffic path.
Controller benefits: consistency, speed, central visibility, programmability through APIs.

course_blocks.text: 6.3 Describe controller-based, software defined architecture (overlay, underlay, and fabric)

Software-Defined Networking (SDN) is an architecture in which the logic that decides how the network behaves is moved, at least partly, into software running on a controller, and the network is programmed through APIs. To understand it, you need three building blocks: the planes of a network device, the overlay/underlay/fabric model, and the APIs that connect applications, controller and devices.
6.3.a Separation of control plane and data plane

Every network device performs three kinds of work, called planes. The **data plane** (forwarding plane) moves packets from an input interface to an output interface: it encapsulates and de-encapsulates frames, looks up the MAC or routing table, applies ACLs and NAT, and forwards. The **control plane** builds the tables that the data plane uses: routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP), STP, ARP, CDP/LLDP. The **management plane** is how humans and tools access and monitor the device: SSH, Telnet, SNMP, syslog, NTP, the web GUI and APIs.

In a traditional device, all three planes live in the same box and the control plane is distributed across all devices. SDN separates them: the control plane (or the policy and management logic) can be centralized in a controller, while the data plane stays distributed on the devices, usually implemented in specialized hardware (ASICs) for speed. Separating the planes lets the controller compute decisions with a global view and program many devices consistently.

rows.label: Data plane
values: Forwards user traffic using existing tables
Frame switching, IP forwarding, ACL filtering, NAT, encapsulation

rows.label: Control plane
values: Decides where traffic should go and builds the tables
OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, STP, ARP, CDP/LLDP

rows.label: Management plane
values: Lets admins and tools configure and monitor the device
SSH, Telnet, SNMP, syslog, NTP, HTTPS GUI, NETCONF/RESTCONF

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Classify a protocol by what it does, not by where it runs. OSPF and STP messages are control plane. SSH and SNMP are management plane. Forwarding a packet according to the routing table, or dropping it because of an ACL, is data plane. In SDN, it is the control plane that is centralized; the data plane is never moved into the controller.

course_blocks.text: Overlay, underlay and fabric

Modern controller-based campus and data center networks are built in two layers. The **underlay** is the physical network: switches, routers and links, with a simple, stable routed design whose only job is IP reachability between the network devices. The **overlay** is a set of virtual networks built on top of the underlay with tunnels: user traffic is encapsulated at the edge, carried across the underlay, and de-encapsulated at the destination edge. The underlay does not need to know about users, VLANs or groups; the overlay does not care about the physical path.

The **fabric** is the combination of underlay and overlay managed as one system, usually by a controller. Seen from the outside, the fabric behaves like one big switch: endpoints can connect anywhere and keep the same policy, and the controller handles the details.

items.definition: The physical network (devices and links) and its routing protocol, providing IP connectivity between fabric nodes.
Logical/virtual networks created with tunnels on top of the underlay to carry user traffic and segment it.
Underlay plus overlay, automated and managed as a single system by a controller.
Wrapping the original frame or packet in an outer header so it can cross the underlay; VXLAN is a common example.

course_blocks.text: **Cisco SD-Access** is Cisco's campus fabric, managed by Cisco Catalyst Center. At a high level, it uses:

items: An **underlay** of routed links between switches (Layer 3 access); when the controller automates the underlay it uses IS-IS as the routing protocol.
An **overlay** whose data plane is **VXLAN** encapsulation between fabric switches.
**LISP** as the overlay control plane: a control plane node keeps track of where each endpoint is connected.
**Cisco TrustSec** Security Group Tags (SGTs) as the policy plane, so access rules follow groups of users and devices rather than IP addresses.
Node roles such as **edge nodes** (where endpoints connect), **border nodes** (exit to outside networks) and **control plane nodes**.

course_blocks.text: The controller and Cisco Catalyst Center

The SDN controller sits between applications and devices. Upward, it exposes a **northbound API** so scripts, IT service management tools or custom applications can ask for information or request changes. Downward, it uses **southbound APIs** and protocols to read device state and push configuration. **Cisco Catalyst Center** (formerly Cisco DNA Center) is Cisco's controller for enterprise campus and branch networks: it provides design (sites, IP pools), policy, automated provisioning (including SD-Access fabrics and software image management), and assurance (health scores and telemetry-based troubleshooting). It offers a REST-based northbound API (the Intent API) and talks to devices with protocols such as SSH/CLI, NETCONF and SNMP.

graph TD A["Applications and scripts
(Python, ITSM, Ansible)"] -->|"Northbound API (REST, JSON)"| C["SDN controller
(e.g. Cisco Catalyst Center)
global view, policy, control logic"] C -->|"Southbound APIs
(NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, SSH/CLI, SNMP)"| D1["Switch
data plane"] C -->|"Southbound APIs"| D2["Router
