course_blocks.caption: SDN layers: applications talk to the controller through the northbound API; the controller programs devices through southbound APIs; devices keep the data plane.

course_blocks.text: 6.3.b Northbound and Southbound APIs

An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for one piece of software to talk to another. The direction is named from the controller's point of view, drawn in the middle of the diagram: **northbound** goes up to applications, **southbound** goes down to network devices. Northbound APIs on modern controllers are almost always REST APIs exchanging JSON over HTTPS. Southbound interfaces vary with the controller and the device.

items.definition: Open standard (Open Networking Foundation) that lets a controller program the flow tables of switches directly; the classic "pure SDN" southbound protocol, used for example by OpenDaylight.
IETF protocol (RFC 6241) to read and change configuration using YANG data models and XML-encoded messages, carried over SSH (TCP port 830).
IETF protocol (RFC 8040) that exposes the same YANG models through a REST-style HTTPS interface, with JSON or XML data.
Cisco-developed policy protocol used by Cisco ACI: the APIC controller sends policy, and the devices decide how to implement it.
The controller logs in like an engineer and sends IOS commands; works with devices that have no modern API.
Simple Network Management Protocol, mainly used southbound to poll device state and receive traps (UDP 161 and 162).
Data modeling language (RFC 7950) that describes the structure of configuration and state data; used by NETCONF and RESTCONF.

rows.label: Typical technology
values: NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, SSH/CLI, SNMP

rows.label: Data format
values: XML (NETCONF), JSON/XML (RESTCONF), CLI text, binary messages (OpenFlow)

rows.label: Example use
values: A script asks Catalyst Center for the list of devices
Catalyst Center pushes a VLAN to a switch

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Northbound and southbound are always relative to the controller. A REST API exposed by the controller to your Python script is northbound, even though your script "sends commands down". NETCONF and OpenFlow are southbound. RESTCONF is listed as a southbound protocol in the SDN architecture (controller to device), but it is also an API that a script can call directly on a router, with no controller involved.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Three planes: data (forwards traffic), control (builds tables: OSPF, STP, ARP), management (SSH, SNMP, APIs).
SDN centralizes control logic in a controller; the data plane stays on the devices.
Underlay = physical IP network; overlay = virtual networks in tunnels (VXLAN); fabric = both, managed as one system.
SD-Access: IS-IS underlay (when automated), VXLAN data plane, LISP control plane, TrustSec SGT policy, managed by Catalyst Center.
Northbound = apps to controller (REST/JSON); southbound = controller to devices (NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow, OpFlex, SSH, SNMP).

course_blocks.text: 6.4 Explain AI (generative and predictive) and machine learning in network operations

Networks produce huge amounts of data: interface counters, syslog messages, flow records, wireless client statistics, streaming telemetry. No human can watch all of it. **Machine learning (ML)** is the branch of artificial intelligence in which a system learns patterns from data instead of following rules written by hand. In network operations, ML and AI are used to find what is abnormal, anticipate problems, and help engineers understand and fix them faster.

items.definition: Broad field of systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence, such as recognizing patterns or producing language.
Subset of AI where models learn from historical data to classify, detect or predict, without explicit rules for every case.
AI that analyzes past and current data to forecast or flag events: anomalies, failures, capacity exhaustion.
AI that creates new content (text, configurations, summaries, code) from a prompt, usually based on large language models (LLMs).
The learned normal behavior of a metric (for example usual traffic on a link at 9 a.m. on a Monday), used to spot deviations.
A confident but wrong or invented answer produced by a generative model, such as a command that does not exist.

rows.label: Main goal
values: Detect, classify and forecast from data
Produce new content in natural language or code

rows.label: Typical input
values: Telemetry, counters, logs, flows over time
A question or instruction (prompt), plus context

rows.label: Typical output
values: Alert, score, forecast, probable root cause
Explanation, summary, draft configuration or script

rows.label: Network examples
values: Anomaly detection, baselining, capacity prediction, failure prediction

rows.label: Main risk
values: False positives/negatives if data is poor

items: **Anomaly detection**: the model learns what is normal and raises an alert when, for example, DHCP failures or interface errors jump far above the baseline, even if no fixed threshold was configured.
**Baselining**: thresholds adapt to time of day and day of week instead of one static value for every hour.
**Capacity prediction**: trends in link utilization or address pool usage are extrapolated to warn weeks before a WAN link or DHCP scope is exhausted.
**Assisted troubleshooting**: correlating events from many devices to suggest the probable root cause and the next checks to run.

**Natural-language assistants**: an engineer asks "why are users on floor 3 failing to connect?" and a generative AI assistant summarizes relevant data, explains it, or drafts a configuration change for review.

course_blocks.title: From an alert to a fix
course_blocks.body: Monday 9:10 a.m., the assurance platform reports that Wi-Fi onboarding failures in one building are four times higher than the usual Monday-morning baseline (predictive ML, anomaly detection). The engineer asks the assistant to summarize the issue in plain language; it correlates the failures with a RADIUS server that stopped responding (assisted troubleshooting). The assistant drafts the commands to check reachability of the RADIUS server; the engineer reviews them, confirms they are valid on the device's IOS version, and runs them. The AI saved time, but the human made the decision.

course_blocks.title: Limits of AI in operations
course_blocks.body: **Hallucinations**: generative AI can produce commands, features or values that look right but do not exist. **Data quality**: models are only as good as the data they learn from; missing telemetry, wrong time stamps or a baseline learned during an outage give misleading results. **Context and security**: sending configurations or logs to an external AI service can expose sensitive data. **Human validation**: AI output is a suggestion; changes must still be reviewed, tested and approved by an engineer.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Do not mix the two families. Forecasting that a link will be saturated next month, or flagging unusual traffic, is **predictive** AI/ML. Answering a question in natural language or writing a draft configuration is **generative** AI. Machine learning is a subset of AI, not a separate field opposed to it.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Machine learning learns patterns from data; it is a subset of AI.
Predictive AI: anomaly detection, dynamic baselines, capacity and failure prediction.
Generative AI: natural-language assistants, summaries, draft configurations and troubleshooting guidance.
Limits: hallucinations, dependence on data quality, data privacy; a human must validate every change.

course_blocks.text: 6.5 Describe characteristics of REST-based APIs (authentication types, CRUD, HTTP verbs, and data encoding)

REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for APIs, built on HTTP. A REST API exposes **resources** (a device, an interface, a VLAN, a user) at addresses called URIs. A client acts on those resources with standard HTTP methods and receives a representation of the resource, usually in JSON. Because REST reuses HTTP, any language or tool that can send an HTTP request (Python, Postman, curl, Ansible) can use it, which is why controllers such as Catalyst Center expose REST northbound APIs.
REST constraints

items: **Client/server**: the client (script, application) and the server (controller, device) are separate; the client only knows the API, not how the server stores data.
**Stateless**: each request carries everything the server needs (including authentication); the server keeps no session memory between requests.
**Cacheable**: responses state whether they can be cached, so clients or proxies can reuse a response instead of asking again.
**Uniform interface**: resources are identified by URIs and manipulated with the same standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) and representations (JSON, XML).
**Layered system**: the client does not know whether it talks to the server directly or through a load balancer or proxy.
**Code on demand** (optional): the server may send executable code to the client; rarely relevant for network APIs.

course_blocks.text: URI structure

A URI identifies the resource. It is made of a **scheme** (`https`), an **authority** (host name or IP address, optionally a port), a **path** that names the resource, and an optional **query** string after `?` that filters or modifies the request with `key=value` pairs separated by `&`. In the example below, the path asks for the network-device resource and the query filters on one hostname.

course_blocks.content:
https://controller.example.com:443/api/v1/network-device?hostname=SW1
|___|   |________________________||____________________| |__________|
scheme  authority (host:port)     path (resource)        query

course_blocks.text: CRUD and HTTP verbs
CRUD lists the four basic operations on data: **Create, Read, Update, Delete**. REST maps them to HTTP methods (verbs). You must know this mapping by heart.

rows.label: Create
values: Creates a new resource; the server usually assigns its ID
Add a new device to the controller inventory

rows.label: Read
values: List all devices or read one interface

rows.label: Update (replace)
values: Replaces the whole resource with the data sent (can also create it at a known URI)
Replace the full configuration of an interface

rows.label: Update (modify)
values: Changes only the fields sent; the rest is kept
Change only the description of an interface

rows.label: Delete
values: Remove a device from the inventory

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Create is **POST**, not PUT. Both PUT and PATCH are Update: PUT replaces the entire resource (fields you omit can be removed or reset), PATCH changes only what you send. GET must not change anything on the server. Also, PUT and DELETE are idempotent (sending the same request twice gives the same result), while POST is not: two POSTs can create two resources.

course_blocks.text: HTTP status codes

Every response starts with a three-digit status code. The first digit gives the family: **2xx** success, **3xx** redirection, **4xx** client error (the request is wrong), **5xx** server error (the request may be fine but the server failed).

values: Successful GET (or PUT/PATCH) with data in the body
Successful POST: a new resource was created
Success with an empty body, common after DELETE or PATCH
Malformed request, for example invalid JSON or a missing field
Missing, wrong or expired credentials or token
Authenticated, but not allowed to perform this action
The URI or resource does not exist
Unexpected failure on the server side

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: **401** means "I do not know who you are" (authentication failed). **403** means "I know who you are, but you are not allowed" (authorization failed). A typo in the URI gives **404**, while invalid JSON in the body gives **400**.

course_blocks.text: Headers and authentication

items.definition: Header that states the format of the body being sent, for example `application/json` or `application/xml`.
Header in which the client states the format it wants in the response, for example `application/json`.
Header that carries the credentials, for example `Basic <base64>` or `Bearer <token>`.

rows.label: Basic authentication
values: Username and password joined as `user:password`, Base64-encoded, sent in the `Authorization: Basic` header
Base64 is encoding, not encryption: always use HTTPS. Often used once to obtain a token

rows.label: Bearer token
values: The client first authenticates, receives a token, then sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on each request
Tokens expire; the password is not sent every time. Some APIs use a custom header, such as `X-Auth-Token` in Catalyst Center

rows.label: API key
values: A long, pre-generated secret string sent in a header or query parameter
Identifies an application rather than a user; must be kept secret and rotated

rows.label: OAuth 2.0
values: Authorization framework: an authorization server issues an access token to an application, with a limited scope
Lets a user grant access without sharing their password with the application

course_blocks.text: Data encoding: JSON, XML and YAML

The body of a request or response is structured data. REST APIs most often use JSON; XML is common with NETCONF and older APIs; YAML is rarely used on the wire but is the format of Ansible playbooks and many configuration files. The same data, an interface named GigabitEthernet1 that is enabled, looks like this in each format:

rows.label: JSON
values: Curly braces, square brackets, double-quoted keys, colons and commas

rows.label: XML
values: Opening and closing tags, like HTML

rows.label: YAML
values: `name: GigabitEthernet1` and `enabled: true` on two lines
Indentation with spaces, `key: value`, list items start with `-`, file may start with `---`

course_blocks.text: Example: a REST request and its response

Here a script reads the configuration of one interface on an IOS XE router through RESTCONF, a REST-style API. It is a GET (Read), over HTTPS, asking for JSON with the `Accept` header and authenticating with Basic authentication.

course_blocks.content:
GET /restconf/data/ietf-interfaces:interfaces/interface=GigabitEthernet1 HTTP/1.1
Host: 10.10.10.1
Accept: application/yang-data+json
Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46Q2lzY28xMjM=

course_blocks.text: How to read it: the status line `200 OK` says the GET succeeded. `Content-Type` confirms the body is JSON (the `yang-data+json` media type is the JSON form used by RESTCONF). The interface is enabled (`true`, a boolean), its description is a string, and its IPv4 address sits inside an array, because an interface can have several addresses. If the token or password were wrong, you would get `401` and no data; if the interface name were misspelled in the URI, `404`.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: REST: client/server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface (URIs plus standard HTTP methods), over HTTP(S).
CRUD mapping: Create = POST, Read = GET, Update = PUT (replace) or PATCH (partial), Delete = DELETE.
Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error.
Headers: Content-Type (format sent), Accept (format wanted), Authorization (credentials).
Authentication: Basic (Base64, needs HTTPS), bearer token, API key, OAuth 2.0; encoding: JSON (most common), XML, YAML.

course_blocks.text: 6.6 Recognize the capabilities of configuration management mechanisms such as Ansible and Terraform

Configuration management tools turn the intended state of the infrastructure into files that software applies to devices. For the CCNA you need to recognize each tool's model: how it connects to devices, whether it needs an agent, whether it pushes or pulls, which language its files use, and how it knows what to change.
Ansible

Ansible (Red Hat, written in Python) is **agentless**: nothing is installed on the managed devices. A control node connects to them, typically over **SSH** for network devices (NETCONF and HTTPS APIs are also possible), and **pushes** the changes. Tasks are written in **playbooks** in **YAML**, the list of target devices is the **inventory**, and the work is done by **modules** such as `cisco.ios.ios_command` (run show commands) and `cisco.ios.ios_config` (apply configuration lines). Most modules are **idempotent**: if the device is already in the desired state, running the playbook again changes nothing and reports `ok` instead of `changed`.

items.definition: The machine where Ansible is installed and from which playbooks are run.
File (INI or YAML) listing managed hosts, their groups and variables such as addresses and connection type.
YAML file with one or more plays; each play maps a group of hosts to an ordered list of tasks.
Unit of work called by a task, for example `ios_config`, `ios_command`, `ios_vlans`.
Property that applying the same operation several times gives the same result as applying it once.

course_blocks.text: A minimal inventory with two access switches, then a playbook that creates VLAN 10 and displays the VLAN table:

course_blocks.content:
[access_switches]
sw1 ansible_host=10.0.0.11
sw2 ansible_host=10.0.0.12

[access_switches:vars]
ansible_network_os=cisco.ios.ios
ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli

---
- name: Standard VLANs on access switches
  hosts: access_switches
  gather_facts: false

  tasks:
    - name: Create VLAN 10
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        parents: vlan 10
        lines:
          - name USERS

    - name: Show the VLAN table
      cisco.ios.ios_command:
        commands:
          - show vlan brief
      register: vlan_output

course_blocks.text: Reading it: `hosts` points to the inventory group, so both switches are configured in parallel. `ios_config` enters `vlan 10` (the parent) and applies `name USERS` only if that line is missing, which makes the task idempotent. `ios_command` runs a show command and stores the result in a variable. The `network_cli` connection means Ansible opens an SSH session and talks CLI to the switch.
Terraform

Terraform (HashiCorp) is an Infrastructure as Code tool that is fully **declarative**: you describe the end state you want, not the steps to reach it. Files are written in **HCL** (HashiCorp Configuration Language). **Providers** are plugins that translate HCL resources into API calls for a platform: public clouds, VMware, Cisco platforms such as IOS XE, ACI, Meraki or Catalyst Center. Terraform keeps a **state file** (`terraform.tfstate`) recording what it has created, and compares it with the configuration and the real infrastructure to compute the changes. Terraform is agentless and talks to the target APIs.

items.title: terraform init
items.body: Prepares the working directory and downloads the providers declared in the configuration.

items.title: terraform plan
items.body: Compares the desired configuration with the state and shows what would be created, changed or destroyed, without touching anything.

items.title: terraform apply
items.body: Executes the plan after confirmation, then updates the state file.

items.title: terraform destroy
items.body: Removes the resources managed by this configuration.

course_blocks.text: Puppet and Chef, for contrast

Puppet and Chef are older configuration management tools built mainly for servers. Both are traditionally **agent-based** and use a **pull** model: an agent installed on each managed node periodically contacts a central server (Puppet server, Chef Infra Server), downloads its configuration and applies it. Puppet uses manifests written in its own declarative language; Chef uses recipes and cookbooks written in a Ruby-based language. Requiring an agent is a problem for many network devices, which is one reason Ansible became the most common choice for network automation.

rows.label: Model
values: Pull: agents fetch from the server

rows.label: Style
values: Mostly procedural (ordered tasks), with idempotent modules

rows.label: Tracks state
values: No state file; checks the device each run
Server keeps node reports and catalogs

rows.label: Typical strength
values: Day-to-day configuration of existing network devices
Keeping large server fleets in a defined state

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Match each tool to its keywords: Ansible = agentless, SSH, push, YAML playbooks, inventory, modules. Terraform = declarative, HCL, providers, state file, plan/apply. Puppet and Chef = agent-based, pull. A classic distractor says "Ansible requires an agent on each router" or "Ansible playbooks are written in JSON": both are false.

course_blocks.title: Choosing the tool
course_blocks.body: A team must (1) push a new NTP and logging baseline to 200 existing IOS XE switches and (2) create cloud networks and virtual routers for a new branch. For (1), Ansible fits naturally: agentless SSH access, an inventory of the 200 switches and an idempotent playbook that can be rerun to fix drift. For (2), Terraform fits: the resources are declared in HCL, `terraform plan` shows exactly what will be created, and the state file lets the team change or destroy the whole branch later. The two tools are often used together.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Ansible: agentless, SSH, push model, YAML playbooks, inventory of hosts, modules such as ios_command and ios_config.
Idempotence: rerunning the same playbook on a compliant device changes nothing.
Terraform: declarative, HCL, providers, state file, workflow init, plan, apply (and destroy).
Puppet and Chef: agent-based, pull model, mainly for servers.

course_blocks.text: 6.7 Recognize components of JSON-encoded data

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, RFC 8259) is a lightweight text format for structured data. It is easy for humans to read and for programs to parse, which is why it is the default format of REST APIs and controller responses. On the exam, you may be shown a JSON snippet and asked to identify its components, find a value, count elements or spot a syntax error.

items.definition: An unordered set of key/value pairs enclosed in curly braces `{ }`.
An ordered list of values enclosed in square brackets `[ ]`, separated by commas; the values can be of any type.
A key (always a string in double quotes), a colon, then a value: `"hostname": "R1"`.
Objects or arrays placed as values inside other objects or arrays, to represent hierarchy.

rows.label: Null
values: Means no value; lowercase, no quotes

items: Keys and string values use **double quotes** only; single quotes are invalid.
A **colon** separates each key from its value.
A **comma** separates pairs in an object and values in an array, but there is **no trailing comma** after the last one.
Every `{` needs a matching `}` and every `[` a matching `]`.
`true`, `false` and `null` are lowercase keywords; `"true"` in quotes is a string, not a boolean.
JSON has no comments, and whitespace between elements (spaces, line breaks, indentation) is ignored; inside a string, spaces are part of the value.

course_blocks.text: A valid JSON document describing a switch, with every data type:

An invalid version of a similar object. It contains four errors: the key `hostname` uses single quotes, `TRUE` is uppercase, a comma is missing after `"USERS"` (the pair before `"mtu"`), and there is a trailing comma after the last pair.

course_blocks.title: Reading nested data
course_blocks.body: Using the valid switch document above: (1) the top-level structure is an object with 7 keys. (2) `vlans` is an array of 3 objects; the name of the second VLAN is found at `vlans[1].name`, which is `"USERS"` (arrays are counted from 0 in most programming languages). (3) The trunk's allowed VLANs are at `uplink.allowedVlans`, an array of two numbers, 10 and 20. (4) `reachable` is the boolean `true`, while `location` is `null`, meaning no value was set. (5) `stackMembers` is a number, so it has no quotes, whereas `managementIp` is a string, even though it looks numeric.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Curly braces `{ }` mean an **object** (key/value pairs); square brackets `[ ]` mean an **array** (an ordered list). Do not confuse them. Watch the quotes: `"10"` is a string, `10` is a number; `"false"` is a string, `false` is a boolean. A trailing comma or a single quote makes the whole document invalid.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: JSON is built from objects `{ }` containing key/value pairs and arrays `[ ]` containing ordered values.
Six data types: string, number, boolean, null, object, array.
Keys are always double-quoted strings; true, false and null are lowercase and unquoted.
Commas separate elements, with no trailing comma; braces and brackets must balance.
Read nested data level by level, for example `uplink.allowedVlans` or `vlans[1].name`.

course_blocks.text: Preparing for CCNA v2.0 (expected from February 2027)

In May 2026 Cisco published the exam topics for **CCNA v2.0**, still under the code 200-301 and still a 120-minute exam. Third-party sources state that v2.0 replaces v1.1 on **3 February 2027**; this date does not appear in the topics document itself, so check Cisco's certification site for the version that applies on your exam date. Everything below comes from comparing the two official topic lists.

course_blocks.title: What stays the same
course_blocks.body: Most of the technical core carries over: subnetting, IPv6 addressing, VLANs and trunks, EtherChannel with LACP, Rapid PVST+, static routing, single-area OSPFv2, FHRP, NAT, ACLs, DHCP snooping, DAI, port security, IPsec VPN concepts, SNMP, syslog and Ansible. Parts 1 to 6 of this course remain your foundation; this part adds what is new.

course_blocks.text: New domain structure
v2.0 goes from six domains to five. The domains do not map one to one, so the table pairs each v2.0 domain with the v1.1 domains it mostly draws from.

rows.label: 1.0 Network Infrastructure and Connectivity
values: Diagnose and troubleshoot verbs for cabling, IPv4, IPv6 and clients; DHCPv4 server added; wireless adds interference and band selection. No longer listed: network components, topologies, TCP/UDP, switching concepts, VRFs, and IPv6 anycast and multicast address types

rows.label: 2.0 Switching and Network Access
values: Edge-port profiles (AP, phone, virtualized host, PoE), CDP/LLDP to validate documentation, troubleshooting with ping, traceroute, logs and packet capture; Rapid PVST+ moves from interpret to configure. No longer listed: wireless architectures and AP modes, WLAN physical connections, WLAN GUI, the device management access objective (Telnet, SSH, HTTP/HTTPS, console), and BPDU filter

rows.label: 3.0 IP Routing
values: OSPFv3 for IPv6 added (OSPF adjacencies now explicitly exclude authentication); routing table and forwarding decision merged into one interpret objective; FHRP narrowed to HSRP and VRRP status; static routing becomes troubleshoot

rows.label: 4.0 Network Services and Security
values: AAA client config, SFTP/SCP, DNS records, storm control and RA guard added; NAT becomes NAT/PAT on IOS XE. No longer listed: NTP, QoS, TFTP/FTP, the SSH remote access objective, WLAN WPA2 PSK in the GUI, and the descriptive security topics (threats, security program, password policy, AAA comparison)

rows.label: 5.0 AI, and Network Operations and Management
values: 6.0 Automation and Programmability (10%), plus SNMP and syslog from 4.0

Agentic AI, prompt design and management approaches added; Ansible becomes use, syslog becomes interpret. No longer listed: REST API, JSON, Terraform, SDN architecture, automation impact, and generative and predictive AI and ML as a stand-alone objective

course_blocks.title: Exam trap: verbs matter
course_blocks.body: v2.0 replaces many *describe* and *configure and verify* objectives with **troubleshoot**, **diagnose**, **interpret** and **validate**. Expect broken scenarios: a wrong mask, a missing route, a bad DNS record, an AI recommendation to evaluate. Cisco's v2.0 document also states that you may have to evaluate output and recommendations from agentic AI and digital network assistants.

items.definition: Know what it is, why it exists and its main characteristics. No configuration expected.
Read an output (routing table, FHRP status, syslog line) and draw the right conclusion.
Type working IOS commands from requirements, often in a lab.
Find the cause of a symptom from outputs, then pick or apply the fix.
Check that documentation or a design matches reality, for example with CDP or LLDP neighbors.
Pick the best option among several (a prompt, a tool) or run a tool such as Ansible to get a result.

course_blocks.text: OSPFv3 for IPv6 (v2.0 objective 3.3)

OSPFv3 is the version of OSPF that routes IPv6. The logic you know from OSPFv2 is unchanged: hellos, neighbor states up to FULL, DR/BDR on broadcast links, cost metric, areas and the SPF algorithm. What changes is **how it is enabled** (per interface, no `network` command), and the fact that neighbors talk using their **link-local addresses** (FE80::/10), with multicast **FF02::5** (all OSPF routers) and **FF02::6** (DR and BDR).

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# ipv6 router ospf 1
R1(config-rtr)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-rtr)# passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-rtr)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 1 area 0
R1(config-if)# exit
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:10::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 ospf 1 area 0

course_blocks.text: `ipv6 unicast-routing` is required for the router to forward IPv6 at all. The **router ID** is still a 32-bit value written like an IPv4 address. If the router has no IPv4 address on an up interface and you do not set `router-id`, the OSPFv3 process cannot pick one and does not start, so always configure it on IPv6-only routers. On recent IOS XE you may also see the newer syntax `router ospfv3 1` with `address-family ipv6 unicast`, and `ospfv3 1 ipv6 area 0` on the interface; the concepts are the same.

course_blocks.content:
R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor

            OSPFv3 Router with ID (1.1.1.1) (Process ID 1)

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Interface ID    Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/DR         00:00:34    3               GigabitEthernet0/0

R1# show ipv6 route ospf
O   2001:DB8:20::/64 [110/2]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/0

course_blocks.text: Read the neighbor table as in OSPFv2: neighbor RID, priority, state (FULL/DR means full adjacency with the DR) and dead timer. In the routing table, the code `O`, AD **110** and the next hop **FE80::2**: OSPFv3 routes point to the neighbor's link-local address, not its global address. Other useful commands: `show ipv6 ospf interface brief` and `show ipv6 protocols`.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: No adjacency in OSPFv3? Check the same things as in OSPFv2 (same area, same hello and dead timers, compatible network type, unique router IDs, interface not passive), plus the IPv6 specifics: `ipv6 unicast-routing` missing, or a router ID that could not be chosen. Mismatched global prefixes do not prevent the adjacency, because neighbors form over link-local addresses.

course_blocks.text: Troubleshooting with ping, traceroute, logs and packet capture (v2.0 objective 2.4)

A standard `ping` from a router uses the IP of the exit interface as source. An **extended ping** lets you choose the source, the count, the size and the DF bit. Sourcing from a LAN interface is the key trick: it proves that the far end also has a **return route** to that LAN, which a plain ping does not. Type `ping` alone for the interactive version, or give the options on one line.

course_blocks.content:
R1# ping 10.2.2.10 source GigabitEthernet0/1 repeat 20 size 1500 df-bit
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 20, 1500-byte ICMP Echos to 10.2.2.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
Packet sent with a source address of 10.1.1.1
Packet sent with the DF bit set
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (20/20), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/4 ms

R1# traceroute 10.2.2.10 source GigabitEthernet0/1 numeric
Type escape sequence to abort.
Tracing the route to 10.2.2.10
  1 192.168.12.2 1 msec 1 msec 1 msec
  2 192.168.23.3 2 msec 2 msec 2 msec
  3 10.2.2.10 3 msec *  2 msec

rows.label: . (ping)
values: Timeout: no reply within the timeout. Often a missing return route, an ACL or a host firewall.

rows.label: U (ping)
values: A router sent back an ICMP unreachable, for example no route or an ACL deny.

rows.label: M (ping)
values: Could not fragment: the packet with DF set is larger than a link MTU.

rows.label: * (traceroute)
values: No answer for that probe. The last hop that answers shows roughly where traffic stops.

course_blocks.text: `show logging` displays the logging configuration and the local buffer: look for interface flaps (`%LINK-3-UPDOWN`, `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN`), duplex mismatches (`%CDP-4-DUPLEX_MISMATCH`), err-disabled ports (`%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE`) or adjacency changes (`%OSPF-5-ADJCHG`). When logs and pings are not enough, a **packet capture** shows exactly what crosses an interface. IOS XE includes Embedded Packet Capture:

course_blocks.content:
R1# monitor capture CAP interface GigabitEthernet1 both
R1# monitor capture CAP match ipv4 host 10.1.1.10 any
R1# monitor capture CAP start
R1# monitor capture CAP stop
R1# show monitor capture CAP buffer brief
R1# monitor capture CAP export bootflash:cap1.pcap

course_blocks.text: Read a capture output by asking simple questions: does the request leave? Does a reply come back? Is the source address the one you expect (NAT)? Is there a TCP SYN with no SYN-ACK (service down or filtered), or a TCP RST (port closed)? The exported `.pcap` file opens in Wireshark.
Storm control and IPv6 RA guard (v2.0 objective 4.7)

**Storm control** protects a switch port against floods of broadcast, multicast or unknown unicast traffic, for example from a loop or a faulty NIC. You set a rising threshold (as a percentage of bandwidth, in bits per second or in packets per second) and optionally a falling threshold. Above the rising level, the switch drops that traffic type until it falls below the falling level. The `storm-control action` command adds a reaction: `shutdown` puts the port in err-disabled state, `trap` sends an SNMP trap.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
SW1(config-if)# storm-control broadcast level 20.00 10.00
SW1(config-if)# storm-control multicast level 30.00
SW1(config-if)# storm-control action trap

SW1# show storm-control GigabitEthernet1/0/10 broadcast
Interface  Filter State   Upper        Lower        Current
---------  -------------  -----------  -----------  ----------
Gi1/0/10   Forwarding       20.00%       10.00%        0.15%

course_blocks.text: **RA guard** protects IPv6 hosts against rogue **Router Advertisements**. Hosts use RAs to learn their default gateway and their SLAAC prefix, so a laptop sending fake RAs can become everyone's gateway (man in the middle) or break addressing. RA guard, applied on access ports facing hosts, drops RAs received there and only allows them from ports where real routers sit. It is the IPv6 counterpart of the idea behind DHCP snooping.

course_blocks.content:
SW1(config)# ipv6 nd raguard policy HOSTS
SW1(config-nd-raguard)# device-role host
SW1(config-nd-raguard)# exit
SW1(config)# interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/1 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy HOSTS

course_blocks.text: Secure file transfer with SFTP and SCP (v2.0 objective 4.2)

TFTP and FTP send files (and FTP credentials) in clear text. **SCP** and **SFTP** run over **SSH (TCP 22)**, so they encrypt both the login and the content. On IOS you use them to back up configurations and to copy software images. The router can act as a client (`copy scp:` or `copy sftp:` with a username in the URL), and as an SCP server so that an administrator can push a file to it from a workstation. The SCP server needs SSH working and AAA with exec authorization.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret Adm1n-Lab-Only
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default local
R1(config)# aaa authorization exec default local
R1(config)# ip scp server enable
R1(config)# end
R1# copy running-config scp://backup@10.0.0.50/configs/R1.cfg
R1# copy sftp://backup@10.0.0.50/images/c8000v-17.09.04a.SPA.bin bootflash:
R1# verify /md5 bootflash:c8000v-17.09.04a.SPA.bin

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: SCP and SFTP use **TCP 22** like SSH, not 20/21 (FTP) or UDP 69 (TFTP). If SSH is not working (no RSA keys, no domain name, wrong VTY transport), SCP and SFTP will not work either. After copying an image, check its hash with `verify` before changing the boot variable.

course_blocks.text: Diagnosing DNS records (v2.0 objective 4.4)

rows.label: A
values: Site reachable by IP but not by name, or name resolves to an old IP.

rows.label: AAAA
values: Dual-stack clients prefer IPv6: a wrong AAAA breaks or slows access while IPv4-only clients work.

rows.label: CNAME
values: Alias pointing to another name (www to a load balancer name).
Alias whose target no longer exists. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records on the same name.

rows.label: MX
values: Mail servers for a domain, with a preference (lowest value tried first). Points to a host name, not an IP.
Inbound mail lost or delivered to an old server; MX target with no A/AAAA record.

rows.label: NS
values: Authoritative name servers for a zone or delegated subdomain.
Whole zone or subdomain fails to resolve (lame delegation).

rows.label: PTR
values: Reverse lookup: IP to name, under in-addr.arpa or ip6.arpa.
Outgoing mail rejected as suspicious, logs show IPs instead of names, slow logins on services that do reverse lookups.

course_blocks.content:
C:\> nslookup -type=mx example.com
C:\> nslookup -type=aaaa www.example.com
$ dig www.example.com A +short
$ dig -x 203.0.113.25 +short

course_blocks.text: Method: first prove IP reachability (ping the IP), then query the record type the application actually uses, then compare with what it should be. Remember caching: after a fix, clients and resolvers keep the old answer until its **TTL** expires (`ipconfig /flushdns` on Windows clears the client cache). On IOS, `ip name-server` sets the resolver and `ip domain lookup` enables resolution; `no ip domain lookup` stops the router from trying to resolve mistyped commands.
Local users and AAA client for TACACS+ and RADIUS (v2.0 objective 4.1)

v1.1 asked you to compare AAA concepts; v2.0 asks you to **configure** a device as an AAA client so that administrators log in with central accounts. **TACACS+** (TCP 49) encrypts the whole payload and separates authentication, authorization and accounting, which suits device administration and per-command authorization. **RADIUS** (UDP 1812 authentication, 1813 accounting) encrypts only the password and is common for network access (802.1X, VPN), but also works for management logins. Always keep a local account as a fallback.

course_blocks.content:
R1(config)# username netadmin privilege 15 secret L0cal-Fallback-Only
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# tacacs server ISE-TAC
R1(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.10.10.5
R1(config-server-tacacs)# key Tac-Shared-Key
R1(config-server-tacacs)# exit
R1(config)# radius server ISE-RAD
R1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.10.10.6 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
R1(config-radius-server)# key Rad-Shared-Key
R1(config-radius-server)# exit
R1(config)# aaa authentication login VTY-LOGIN group tacacs+ local
R1(config)# aaa authorization exec VTY-LOGIN group tacacs+ local
R1(config)# aaa accounting exec default start-stop group tacacs+
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login authentication VTY-LOGIN
R1(config-line)# authorization exec VTY-LOGIN
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh

course_blocks.text: Here VTY logins try TACACS+ first and fall back to the local database. To use RADIUS instead, replace `group tacacs+` with `group radius`. Verify with `show aaa servers` (server state, requests, failures) and test a credential with `test aaa group tacacs+ netadmin <password> legacy`.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: The `local` fallback is used only when the server does **not answer** (unreachable, wrong key causing no valid reply). If the server answers and rejects the user, the login fails and the local database is not tried. Also, once `aaa new-model` is enabled, the `default` list applies to the console and VTY lines: create the local user first to avoid locking yourself out.

course_blocks.text: Agentic AI in network operations (v2.0 objective 5.1)

A chat assistant answers a question. An **AI agent** goes further: given a goal (“find why branch 12 is slow”), it plans steps, **calls tools** (run `show` commands through an API, query monitoring, read tickets), reasons on the results, and proposes or performs actions. In network operations, agents can triage alarms, correlate logs, draft a fix or a change request, and check the result afterwards.

course_blocks.code:
graph LR
  A[Goal from operator] --> B[Observe: telemetry, logs, show output]
  B --> C[Reason and plan]
  C --> D{Change needed?}
  D -- No --> E[Report findings]
  D -- Yes --> F[Human approval]
  F --> G[Act through tools or APIs]
  G --> B
course_blocks.caption: An agent loop with a human approval gate before any change.

course_blocks.title: Keep a human in the loop
course_blocks.body: Agents can be wrong with confidence. Good practice: read-only tools by default, **human approval** before any configuration change, least-privilege credentials for the agent, logging of every action, and a rollback plan. When the exam asks you to evaluate an AI recommendation, check it like a colleague's proposal: does the output really support it, and is the command correct and safe?

course_blocks.text: Prompt design for generative AI in operations (v2.0 objective 5.2)

items.definition: Decide what may be shared with which AI tool. Never paste passwords, keys, SNMP communities, full production configs, customer data or internal IP plans into a public tool; remove or mask them, or use an approved internal tool.
The role the model should take, for example a senior network engineer reviewing a change.
A precise task with context and constraints: platform, IOS version, what not to change.
How the answer must be shaped: a table, a numbered list, only IOS commands, JSON for a script.

course_blocks.title: A weak prompt and a better one
course_blocks.body: Weak: “Here is my router config with the enable secret and TACACS key, fix OSPF.” It leaks secrets, gives no symptom and no expected output. Better: “You are a senior Cisco network engineer. Two IOS XE routers do not form an OSPFv2 adjacency on Gi0/0. Below are the sanitized outputs of `show ip ospf interface Gi0/0` from both routers (passwords and keys removed). List the most likely causes in a numbered list, each with the line of output that supports it and the IOS command to fix it. Do not propose changes to other interfaces.”

course_blocks.text: Network management approaches (v2.0 objective 5.3)

rows.label: Device-based
values: Each device managed one by one through CLI, GUI or SNMP.
SSH to each switch to add a VLAN.

rows.label: Cloud-based
values: Devices register to a vendor cloud dashboard that pushes configuration and collects monitoring.

rows.label: Controller-based
values: An on-premises or hosted controller holds the intent and programs devices through southbound APIs.
Cisco Catalyst Center, a WLC for access points.

rows.label: Automation-based
values: Scripts or tools run the same tasks on many devices, repeatably.
An Ansible playbook that collects `show version` from 200 routers.

rows.label: Infrastructure as code
values: The desired state is described in versioned files (Git), reviewed, then applied automatically; the files are the source of truth.
VLAN and interface definitions in YAML, applied by a pipeline after a merge request.

course_blocks.text: What disappears or shrinks

The following points are drawn only from comparing the two official topic lists. A topic missing from the v2.0 list may still appear indirectly in a scenario, and basic knowledge (TCP versus UDP, what a router or a switch does) is assumed by many v2.0 objectives.

items: **Security Fundamentals** is no longer a stand-alone domain: its configuration topics (ACLs, Layer 2 security, VPN concepts, local users and AAA) move into 4.0 Network Services and Security. Threat vocabulary, security program elements, password policy and the AAA concept comparison are no longer listed.

**Automation**: REST API characteristics, JSON components, Terraform, the SDN architecture objectives (overlay, underlay, fabric, northbound and southbound APIs), automation impact and the generative and predictive AI and machine learning objective are no longer listed; AI now means agentic AI and prompt selection, and Ansible stays, now as *use* to execute commands.

**Fundamentals**: network components, topology architectures, TCP versus UDP, switching concepts and VRFs are no longer listed as objectives. For IPv6, v2.0 names only unicast and modified EUI-64, so anycast and multicast address types are no longer listed explicitly.

**Wireless**: Cisco wireless architectures, AP modes, WLC physical connections and the WLAN GUI objectives are gone; wireless remains through principles (band, channel, RF, security, interference), AP edge ports and client troubleshooting.

**Management access**: the v1.1 objective on device management access (Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS, console, TACACS+/RADIUS, cloud managed) is no longer listed as such; AAA becomes a configuration objective (4.1) and cloud management appears among management approaches (5.3).

**IP services**: NTP, QoS per-hop behavior, TFTP/FTP, the SSH remote access configuration objective and the generic DHCP/DNS role objective are no longer listed; DHCP becomes DHCPv4 troubleshooting (now including the server) and DNS becomes record diagnosis. SSH still underpins SCP/SFTP and AAA logins.
**STP**: BPDU filter is no longer in the list of protection features (root guard, loop guard and BPDU guard remain).

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: v2.0 topics were published in May 2026; third-party sources give 3 February 2027 as the switch date, so check Cisco's site.
Five domains: 25 / 25 / 20 / 20 / 10, with more troubleshooting verbs and AI output to evaluate.
OSPFv3: `ipv6 unicast-routing`, `ipv6 router ospf`, `ipv6 ospf 1 area 0` per interface, manual router ID on IPv6-only routers, link-local next hops.
New hands-on topics: extended ping and capture, storm control, RA guard, SCP/SFTP over TCP 22, DNS records, AAA client with local fallback.
AI topics: agents observe, reason and act through tools under human approval; prompts need classification, persona, instructions and output format.

course_blocks.text: Final review and exam day

This last part gathers the facts that are most often tested as exact values, then walks you through the final week, the day before, the exam itself and what happens afterwards. Use the tables as a self-test: cover the right-hand column and recite it.
Must-know values

items: **OSPF**: hello 10 s and dead 40 s on broadcast and point-to-point links (30/120 on NBMA). States: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full. DR/BDR: highest interface priority (default 1, 0 = never DR), then highest router ID, no preemption. Multicast 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers) and 224.0.0.6 (DR/BDR). Router ID order: manual `router-id`, highest loopback IPv4, highest active interface IPv4.

**STP / Rapid PVST+**: lowest bridge ID wins root (priority default 32768 plus VLAN ID, in steps of 4096). RSTP roles: root, designated, alternate, backup. RSTP states: discarding, learning, forwarding (legacy STP: blocking, listening, learning, forwarding, plus disabled). Short-method costs: 10 Mb/s = 100, 100 Mb/s = 19, 1 Gb/s = 4, 10 Gb/s = 2. Timers: hello 2 s, max age 20 s, forward delay 15 s.

**HSRP**: priority 100, preemption off by default, hello 3 s and hold 10 s, v1 multicast 224.0.0.2 and virtual MAC 0000.0C07.ACxx, v2 multicast 224.0.0.102 and MAC 0000.0C9F.Fxxx, UDP 1985. Roles: active and standby.

**VRRP**: priority 100, preemption on by default, advertisement every 1 s, multicast 224.0.0.18 (IP protocol 112), virtual MAC 0000.5E00.01xx. Roles: master and backup; the virtual IP can be a real interface IP (owner, priority 255).

**ACLs**: standard 1 to 99 and 1300 to 1999 (source only), extended 100 to 199 and 2000 to 2699. Place standard ACLs close to the destination, extended ACLs close to the source. Top-down first match, implicit `deny any` at the end, one ACL per interface, per direction, per protocol.
**Syslog**: 0 emergencies, 1 alerts, 2 critical, 3 errors, 4 warnings, 5 notifications, 6 informational, 7 debugging. Lower number = more severe; `logging trap 4` sends levels 0 to 4.

**SNMP**: v1 and v2c use clear-text community strings (v2c adds GetBulk and Inform); v3 adds users with noAuthNoPriv, authNoPriv or authPriv (authentication and encryption). Agent listens on UDP 161, traps and informs go to UDP 162.

**Wildcards and subnetting**: wildcard = 255.255.255.255 minus the mask (/26 gives 0.0.0.63). Block size = 256 minus the interesting octet of the mask. Usable hosts = 2^h minus 2. You should solve any subnet question in under a minute.

course_blocks.title: Exam trap
course_blocks.body: Classic swaps: HSRP preemption is **off** by default but VRRP preemption is **on**; OSPF DR election is **not** preemptive; a standard ACL goes **near the destination**; syslog level 7 is the **least** severe; SNMP traps go to **162**, not 161; TFTP is **UDP** 69.

course_blocks.text: The week before

items: Take two or three full timed mock exams and analyse every mistake; spend the remaining time on your two weakest domains with per-domain review.
Keep the daily subnetting drill and redo one mixed lab (VLANs, trunk, OSPF, NAT, ACL) from a blank configuration.
Reread every **Key points** summary and the tables above.
Check the logistics: exam confirmation, ID requirements, test center address or, for online delivery, the system test, webcam, quiet room and clear desk.

course_blocks.text: The day before

Do a light review only: the must-know tables and a few subnetting drills. Do not start a new topic or a full mock exam. Prepare your IDs, plan to arrive (or log in) early, and sleep. Fatigue costs more points than one extra hour of revision brings.
During the exam

items.title: Read the whole question
items.body: Read the full stem and every option before answering. Spot the constraint words: **NOT**, **EXCEPT**, *best*, *first*, *most likely*, and the number to pick (“Choose two”).

items.title: Eliminate, then decide
items.body: Remove the clearly wrong options first. Since going back is commonly reported as impossible, do not plan to flag a question and return: give your best answer now.

items.title: Watch the clock
items.body: About 1 minute per question, more for labs. Check your pace every 20 to 30 questions.

items.title: In a lab, read the whole task first
items.body: Note every requirement and every device involved before typing. Use `?` and `show` commands to discover interface names and the current state.

items.title: Configure, then verify
items.body: After each change, verify with the matching `show` command (`show ip interface brief`, `show vlan brief`, `show interfaces trunk`, `show ip route`, `show ip ospf neighbor`, `show access-lists`). If the task asks you to save, run `copy running-config startup-config`.

course_blocks.content:
R1# show running-config | section router ospf
R1# show ip interface brief
R1# copy running-config startup-config
Destination filename [startup-config]?
Building configuration...
[OK]

course_blocks.text: After the exam

You usually see a pass or fail result on screen at the end, and a **score report** follows in your Cisco certification account, with your performance per exam section. If you pass, your certification appears in the Cisco certification tracking system and is valid for three years. If you do not pass, use the section breakdown to target your weakest domains, then plan a retake. Cisco applies a waiting period between attempts and the rules can change, so **check Cisco's current retake policy** before booking.

course_blocks.title: Key points
items: Know the default values cold: AD, OSPF timers and election, STP costs and roles, HSRP/VRRP defaults, ACL ranges, syslog levels, SNMP versions, ports.
Final week: mock exams, mistake analysis, weak domains; the day before: light review and sleep.
Read every question fully, watch NOT/EXCEPT and the number of answers, and do not count on coming back.
Labs: read the whole task, configure, verify with `show`, save with `copy running-config startup-config` when asked.
After the exam, use the score report by section and check Cisco's current retake policy.

title: CompTIA A+
description: Certification vendor-neutral de référence pour débuter dans le support IT.
long_description: La CompTIA A+ valide l'ensemble des fondamentaux du support IT : matériel PC, systèmes d'exploitation (Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android), réseaux, cybersécurité de base, résolution d'incidents et procédures opérationnelles. C'est la seule certification vendor-neutral (non liée à un constructeur) universellement acceptée pour un premier poste dans le support.
importance: Souvent exigée pour un premier job helpdesk chez les grands comptes (Dell, HP, IBM, ainsi que dans la fonction publique US et de plus en plus en Europe). Elle rassure les recruteurs sur ta capacité à intervenir sur un parc hétérogène dès ton arrivée.
validity_note: CompTIA A+ = deux examens obligatoires (Core 1 : 220-1101, seuil 675/900 = 75 % · Core 2 : 220-1102, seuil 700/900 = 77,7 %). Chaque core dure 90 min pour 90 questions. Valeurs indiquées ici pour Core 2. Valide 3 ans, renouvelable via 20 CEUs (Continuing Education Units) ou une certif CompTIA supérieure. Grâce de 30 jours après expiration pour uploader tes CEUs.

title: AWS Cloud Practitioner
description: Fondamentaux AWS : services, tarification, sécurité et modèle cloud.
long_description: L'AWS Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02) est le point d'entrée officiel dans l'écosystème AWS. L'examen valide ta compréhension globale du cloud AWS : services principaux (EC2, S3, RDS, Lambda, VPC), modèles de tarification, modèle de responsabilité partagée, IAM, régions et zones de disponibilité, bonnes pratiques d'architecture Well-Architected. Elle ne demande pas de background technique lourd, mais une réelle compréhension du cloud.
importance: Certification à haute valeur commerciale : elle prouve que tu comprends AWS sans être forcément développeur. Fortement recommandée pour les chefs de projet, product managers, avant-vente et consultants qui interagissent avec des équipes cloud. C'est aussi le prérequis idéal avant Solutions Architect Associate.
validity_note: Valide 3 ans. L'examen officiel utilise un score scaled 700/1000 (≈ 70 %), affiché ici en équivalent brut sur 65 questions (dont 15 non notées côté AWS). Renouvellement en repassant l'examen, via une certif AWS Associate/Pro/Specialty, ou via AWS Cloud Quest (dispo dans les 6 mois avant expiration).

course_blocks.text: Introduction

Au 28 juillet 2026, l'examen en vigueur est **AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02)**. Cette version a commencé le 19 septembre 2023 et reste celle publiée dans le guide d'examen AWS courant. ([AWS Documentation][1])

L'examen vise une compréhension fondamentale et transversale du Cloud AWS, sans dépendre d'un rôle technique précis. Il comporte 65 questions à choix simple ou réponses multiples, dure 90 minutes, comprend 50 questions notées et 15 questions non notées, et utilise un score minimal de réussite de 700 sur 1 000. ([Amazon Web Services, Inc.][2]) ([AWS Documentation][1])

course_blocks.title: Niveau attendu
course_blocks.body: Le candidat doit savoir expliquer la valeur du Cloud AWS, la responsabilité partagée, les bonnes pratiques de sécurité, les principaux services, les coûts et les options de support. Le codage, l'implémentation détaillée, le dépannage approfondi et la conception d'architectures complexes sont hors périmètre du profil cible. ([AWS Documentation][1])

course_blocks.text: Domaine 1 : Concepts du cloud

items.definition: Capacité à expérimenter et à déployer rapidement sans attendre l'achat et l'installation d'une infrastructure physique. ([AWS Documentation][3])
Capacité à augmenter ou réduire automatiquement les ressources selon la demande. ([AWS Documentation][3])
Conception visant à maintenir le service malgré la panne d'un composant ou d'un emplacement. ([AWS Documentation][3])
Possibilité de déployer des charges de travail dans plusieurs zones géographiques à partir de l'infrastructure mondiale AWS. ([AWS Documentation][3])

rows.label: Évolutivité
values: Capacité d'une architecture à prendre en charge une croissance de charge en ajoutant ou en adaptant des ressources.

rows.label: Élasticité
values: Ajustement dynamique des ressources en fonction des variations réelles de la demande.

rows.label: Agilité
values: Rapidité d'expérimentation, de mise à disposition et d'évolution des solutions. ([AWS Documentation][3])

course_blocks.title: Application de billetterie
course_blocks.body: Une billetterie reçoit peu de trafic la plupart du temps, puis une forte demande lors de l'ouverture des ventes. Une architecture élastique augmente les ressources pendant le pic et les réduit ensuite, ce qui évite de payer en permanence pour la capacité maximale. ([AWS Documentation][3])

course_blocks.text: AWS Well-Architected Framework

items: Excellence opérationnelle : exploiter, observer et améliorer les systèmes et les processus.
Sécurité : protéger les informations, les systèmes et les actifs.
Fiabilité : assurer le fonctionnement prévu et la reprise après défaillance.
Efficacité des performances : utiliser efficacement les ressources selon les besoins.
Optimisation des coûts : obtenir la valeur attendue en évitant les dépenses inutiles.
Durabilité : réduire les ressources et les impacts environnementaux inutiles. ([AWS Documentation][3])

rows.label: Automatiser les changements et apprendre des incidents
Répartir une application entre plusieurs zones de disponibilité
Choisir un type d'instance adapté au profil de calcul
Supprimer les ressources inutilisées et ajuster leur taille
Appliquer le moindre privilège et chiffrer les données
Réduire le gaspillage de calcul et de stockage

course_blocks.text: Adoption et migration

AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (AWS CAF) aide les organisations à structurer leur transformation en reliant les objectifs métier, les personnes, la gouvernance, la plateforme, la sécurité et les opérations. Le blueprint met l'accent sur la réduction du risque métier, l'efficacité opérationnelle, la croissance et les résultats environnementaux, sociaux et de gouvernance. ([AWS Documentation][3])

rows.label: Répliquer progressivement une base de données
values: AWS Database Migration Service peut maintenir la source opérationnelle pendant une migration.

rows.label: Transférer un volume massif avec une connectivité limitée
values: AWS Snow Family permet un transfert physique de données.

rows.label: Recenser des serveurs et leurs dépendances
values: AWS Application Discovery Service collecte des informations de découverte.

rows.label: Centraliser le suivi d'un programme de migration
values: AWS Migration Hub fournit une vue de suivi. ([AWS Documentation][3]) ([AWS Documentation][4])

rows.label: Risque de surdimensionnement durable
values: Possibilité de redimensionner et d'arrêter les ressources inutiles. ([AWS Documentation][3])

course_blocks.text: Le **redimensionnement** consiste à choisir une capacité correspondant au besoin réel. L'automatisation réduit les tâches manuelles répétitives, et les économies d'échelle d'AWS contribuent à proposer une consommation à l'usage. Il faut aussi considérer les coûts souvent cachés du sur site : énergie, espace, refroidissement, maintenance, licences et personnel. ([AWS Documentation][3])

course_blocks.title: À retenir
items: Le cloud remplace une partie des coûts fixes par des coûts variables.
L'élasticité ajuste les ressources dans les deux sens.
AWS Well-Architected Framework comprend six piliers.
La migration doit être choisie selon les données, le délai, les dépendances et la connectivité.
Le redimensionnement et l'automatisation soutiennent l'efficacité économique. ([AWS Documentation][3])

course_blocks.text: Domaine 2 : Sécurité et conformité

AWS est responsable de la **sécurité du cloud**, notamment les centres de données, le matériel, le réseau physique et les couches d'infrastructure sous-jacentes. Le client est responsable de la **sécurité dans le cloud**, avec une portée qui varie selon le service choisi. ([AWS Documentation][5])

rows.label: Protection physique des centres de données
values: Gestion des identités et des autorisations

rows.label: Maintenance des couches gérées par le service
values: Respect des obligations qui concernent ses usages et ses données. ([AWS Documentation][5])

rows.label: Amazon EC2
values: Système d'exploitation invité, correctifs, applications, groupes de sécurité, identités et données.

rows.label: Amazon RDS
values: Configuration de la base, comptes, réseau, chiffrement, sauvegardes choisies et données, tandis qu'AWS gère davantage de couches d'infrastructure.

rows.label: AWS Lambda
values: Code, dépendances incluses, autorisations et données, tandis qu'AWS gère les serveurs et l'environnement d'exécution sous-jacent. ([AWS Documentation][5])

course_blocks.title: Service géré ne signifie pas sécurité automatique
course_blocks.body: Plus AWS gère de couches, moins le client administre d'infrastructure. Le client reste néanmoins responsable des données, des identités, des autorisations et de la configuration qu'il contrôle. ([AWS Documentation][5])

course_blocks.text: Gouvernance, conformité et journalisation

items.definition: Portail permettant d'accéder à des rapports de conformité AWS et à certains accords. ([AWS Documentation][5])
Service d'audit qui enregistre l'activité des API et les actions réalisées dans un compte. ([AWS Documentation][5])
Service qui enregistre l'état de configuration des ressources et permet d'évaluer leur conformité à des règles. ([AWS Documentation][5])
Service de surveillance pour les métriques, journaux, alarmes et événements opérationnels. ([AWS Documentation][5])
Service qui aide à collecter et organiser des preuves pour des audits. ([AWS Documentation][5])

course_blocks.text: Le chiffrement **au repos** protège les données stockées. Le chiffrement **en transit** protège les échanges sur le réseau, généralement avec TLS. AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) aide à créer et contrôler des clés de chiffrement, tandis qu'AWS CloudHSM fournit des modules matériels dédiés pour certains besoins de contrôle. ([AWS Documentation][5]) ([AWS Documentation][4])
Gestion des identités et des accès

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) contrôle l'authentification et l'autorisation dans un compte AWS. Les décisions d'accès reposent sur des identités, des politiques et des ressources. Le principe du moindre privilège consiste à accorder seulement les actions nécessaires sur les ressources nécessaires. ([AWS Documentation][5])

items.definition: Identité durable associée à une personne ou une application lorsque ce modèle est nécessaire. ([AWS Documentation][5])
Ensemble d'utilisateurs auquel des autorisations communes peuvent être attachées. ([AWS Documentation][5])

title: ITIL Foundation v5
description: Le référentiel mondial de la gestion des services IT.
long_description: ITIL est le framework le plus adopté au monde pour structurer la gestion des services IT. La certification Foundation valide ta compréhension du système de valeur ITIL, des sept principes directeurs, des quatre dimensions, du modèle d'amélioration continue et des principales pratiques (gestion des incidents, des problèmes, des changements, des demandes, des niveaux de service). C'est le socle indispensable avant de viser ITIL Practitioner, Managing Professional ou Strategic Leader.
importance: Prérequis explicite ou implicite dans la majorité des offres d'encadrement ITSM en France, en Belgique et au Canada. On la retrouve dans les fiches de poste 'Service Manager', 'Change Manager', 'Problem Manager', 'Chef de projet SI' ou 'Product Owner IT'. Elle apparaît comme un critère de sélection dans les grilles RH des grands comptes (banques, telco, secteur public).
validity_note: Depuis la modification de la politique de renouvellement PeopleCert, ITIL Foundation v5 est valide 3 ans à partir de la date de réussite. Pour la maintenir active, trois options avant expiration : accumuler des points CPD via PeopleCert Plus sur 3 ans, réussir une autre certification ITIL, ou repasser le même examen. Les badges officiels délivrés en 2026 portent d'ailleurs une date d'expiration en 2029, ce qui confirme la durée de 3 ans.

course_blocks.text: Introduction

Ce cours suit le syllabus **ITIL Foundation (Version 5)**, version 5.0 publiée en février 2026. Le blueprint officiel répartit l'examen en sept catégories: termes et définitions 30 %, quatre dimensions 10 %, cycle de vie 10 %, ITIL Value System 40 %, flux de valeur 5 %, ITIL et l'IA 2,5 %, ITIL et les autres référentiels 2,5 %.

La certification évalue surtout la mémorisation et la compréhension: 40 questions, 60 minutes, examen fermé, 26 bonnes réponses nécessaires, soit 65 %. Les questions peuvent être standard, négatives, à mot manquant ou basées sur une liste.

course_blocks.title: Version en vigueur
course_blocks.body: Le nom officiel public est **ITIL Foundation (Version 5)**. Le syllabus courant identifié est la version 5.0 de février 2026. Les pages officielles publiques consultées n'affichent pas de code d'examen autonome; elles identifient l'examen par ce nom. ITIL 4 reste disponible pendant la transition, mais ce cours n'utilise que le programme Version 5.

course_blocks.title: Piège d'examen
course_blocks.body: Les catégories **termes et définitions** et **ITIL Value System** représentent ensemble 70 % de l'examen. Un retour candidat Version 5 signale que les définitions exactes et les distinctions proches ont été la partie la plus exigeante, et que les examens blancs pouvaient sembler plus simples que l'épreuve réelle. ([Reddit][1])

course_blocks.title: Objectif du cours
items: Construire un vocabulaire précis avant d'aborder les modèles.
Relier produits, services, expérience, stratégie, flux de valeur et amélioration.
Préparer les niveaux de Bloom 1 et 2: rappeler et expliquer.

course_blocks.text: 1. Termes et définitions ITIL

Cette catégorie vaut **30 %** du blueprint. Elle couvre la gestion des produits et services numériques, l'expérience, la stratégie, la transformation, les offres de service, la co-création de valeur et les relations de service. ([Oxford College of Technology][2])

items.term: Gestion des produits et services numériques
items.definition: Ensemble coordonné d'activités permettant de diriger, contrôler, créer, exploiter et améliorer des produits et services reposant sur des technologies numériques.
Configuration de ressources d'une organisation conçue pour proposer de la valeur à un consommateur.
Moyen de permettre la co-création de valeur en facilitant les résultats recherchés par un consommateur, sans que celui-ci doive gérer seul certains coûts et risques.
Produit constitué de technologie numérique, ou fourni principalement grâce à elle.
Service dont la réalisation et la consommation dépendent principalement de technologies et d'informations numériques.
Élément matériel ou immatériel dont la propriété est transférée du fournisseur au consommateur.
Activité récurrente menée à tous les niveaux pour maintenir l'adéquation des produits, services et pratiques avec les besoins des parties prenantes.

items.term: Cycle de vie ITIL des produits et services
items.definition: Modèle de huit activités utilisées de manière non linéaire pour découvrir, concevoir, acquérir, construire, transitionner, exploiter, livrer et supporter des produits et services.
Fonctionnalité offerte pour répondre à un besoin: le produit ou service est adapté à l'objectif.
Assurance que le produit ou service répondra aux niveaux convenus: capacité, disponibilité, continuité et sécurité selon le contexte.
Perception et réaction d'une personne lorsqu'elle utilise un produit ou un service.
Capacité à créer de la valeur sans compromettre de manière injustifiée les ressources, les personnes et les possibilités futures.

rows.label: Question centrale
values: Qu'est-ce qui est conçu ou fourni ?

rows.label: Exemple
values: Mise à disposition sécurisée et supportée des accès.

rows.label: Question
values: La valeur peut-elle être maintenue de façon responsable ?

rows.label: Échec typique
values: Parcours frustrant malgré de bons indicateurs techniques.
Solution efficace aujourd'hui mais coûteuse ou nuisible à long terme.

course_blocks.title: Le mot « bien »
course_blocks.body: Dans le syllabus, `good` est un **nom**: un bien transféré au consommateur. Il ne signifie pas simplement « de bonne qualité ». Cette ambiguïté lexicale est typique des questions à mot manquant.

course_blocks.title: Cas pratique: portail de support
course_blocks.body: Un portail peut avoir une forte utilité parce qu'il permet de déclarer un incident, et une bonne garantie parce qu'il est disponible 24 h/24. Pourtant, sa valeur reste faible si le parcours est incompréhensible ou inaccessible. ITIL Version 5 oblige donc à considérer simultanément utilité, garantie, expérience et durabilité.

course_blocks.text: ITIL Version 5 bénéficie aux entreprises en donnant un langage commun, aux prestataires managés en clarifiant les relations et les résultats, aux éditeurs de produits numériques en reliant produit et service, et aux professionnels en fournissant un modèle commun de décision et d'amélioration. L'objectif officiel est précisément de rapprocher les communautés produit et service. ([itil.com][3])
1.2 Expérience, stratégie et transformation

items.definition: Ensemble des perceptions, émotions et réactions créées par les interactions avec une organisation, un produit ou un service.
Part de l'expérience produite par des interactions numériques.
Disposition d'une partie prenante à compter sur l'organisation, ses produits, ses services et ses comportements.
Expérience d'une personne lorsqu'elle utilise ou prévoit d'utiliser un produit ou service.
Expérience globale d'un client sur l'ensemble de sa relation avec une organisation.
Accord centré sur des résultats d'expérience mesurables, en complément ou au-delà de mesures purement techniques.
Approche qui fonde la conception sur les besoins, capacités, limites et contextes réels des personnes.
Approche choisie pour atteindre des objectifs dans un contexte donné.
Orientation qui guide les choix globaux de l'organisation.
Choix concernant l'usage du numérique pour soutenir ou transformer les objectifs de l'organisation.
Description concise du rôle et de l'intention générale de l'organisation.
Description de l'état futur souhaité.
Raison fondamentale pour laquelle l'organisation existe et crée de la valeur.
Capacité à donner une direction, influencer les comportements et permettre l'action collective.
Contexte marqué par la volatilité, l'incertitude, la complexité et l'ambiguïté.
Modification d'un état, d'un produit, d'un service, d'une pratique ou d'une manière de travailler.
Évolution importante et coordonnée qui modifie durablement la façon dont une organisation crée de la valeur.
Activités habituelles qui maintiennent les opérations courantes.
